heading: 10 Month Old Sleep Schedule: Two Naps, New Skills, and Night Waking
description: 10 month old sleep schedule: 12–16 hours a day (AASM), two naps, wake windows, an example day, and help with standing in the crib and separation anxiety.
body:
# 10 Month Old Sleep Schedule: Two Naps, New Skills, and Night Waking

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** September 3, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

A 10-month-old is a busy person. Crawling, cruising along the sofa, pulling up on anything with an edge: all of it is exciting, and all of it can spill over into sleep. Many babies this age have a dependable two-nap day, yet still wake at night, stand up in the crib and can't work out how to lie back down, or cry the moment a parent leaves the room. Here is what the sources say is normal, plus an example day and ways to handle the common snags.

## Short answer

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (endorsed by the AAP) recommends **12–16 hours of total sleep per 24 hours for babies 4–12 months**. KidsHealth describes babies of 8–12 months sleeping **9–12 hours at night** and usually taking **two naps**, each lasting anywhere from **30 minutes to 2 hours**. Most babies are past the third nap by now: Mayo Clinic puts its usual drop at about 9 months. Night waking can come back around this age. Two NHS services describe more frequent waking again at **8–9 months**, often linked with new motor skills and separation anxiety.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total sleep in 24 h | 12–16 hours (4–12 months) | AASM, endorsed by AAP; KidsHealth |
| Night sleep | A stretch of 9–12 hours (8–12 months) | KidsHealth |
| Naps | 2 a day, each 30 minutes to 2 hours | KidsHealth |
| Total day sleep | 2–4 hours (6–12 months) | Pregnancy, Birth and Baby |
| Awake time between sleeps | 2.5–4.5 hours (7–10 months); 3–6 hours (10–12 months) | Cleveland Clinic |
| When waking may return | Around 8–9 months | Newcastle Hospitals NHS; Derbyshire NHS |

## How much should a 10 month old sleep?

Sources broadly agree on the total but frame it differently:

- **AASM:** 12–16 hours in 24 hours, naps included.
- **KidsHealth:** 12–16 hours, including a 9–12 hour night stretch.
- **Pregnancy, Birth and Baby:** 11–16 hours in total for 6–12 months, with 10–14 hours at night.
- **Sleep Foundation:** by about 9 months, babies are generally sleeping 8–10 hours at night in addition to naps.

The previous version of this page gave a total of "13–15 hours". We could not match that figure to a primary source, so it has been removed.

**App examples (not clinical guidance):** Huckleberry suggests about 13.5 hours at 10 months, with 11–12 hours at night and 2–3 hours across two naps. Napper describes two naps of about 1–1.5 hours each.

## Example 2-nap day for a 10 month old

**Example only.** Your baby's best times depend on when they wake, how long the naps last, and how your family day runs.

| Time | What happens | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 7:00 a.m. | Wake up, milk, breakfast soon after | Bright light and a cheerful start |
| 10:00–11:15 a.m. | Morning nap | About 3 hours after waking |
| 11:15 a.m. | Lunch, milk, play | |
| 2:45–4:00 p.m. | Afternoon nap | About 3.5 hours after nap 1 |
| 4:00 p.m. | Snack, outside time | Practice standing and sitting down again |
| 5:45 p.m. | Dinner | |
| 6:45 p.m. | Bath, pajamas, milk, two books | Keep the steps the same |
| 7:30 p.m. | Asleep in the crib | About 3.5 hours after nap 2 |

This day gives about 2.5 hours of naps. The awake periods of 3–3.5 hours sit inside Cleveland Clinic's ranges for this age.

## How many naps at 10 months?

Two naps is the norm. Mayo Clinic suggests a morning and an early-afternoon nap for babies from 4 months to a year, says the third nap is usually dropped by about 9 months, and notes that some babies give up the morning nap at 10–12 months. Boys Town National Research Hospital places the move from two naps to one later, at **15–18 months**. Sources disagree, so if your 10-month-old resists the morning nap for a few days, it may be a short phase rather than a real transition.

Signs that one long midday nap might be worth a trial:

- The morning nap gets later and later, pushing the afternoon one toward evening.
- Your baby plays happily through the second nap opportunity on most days for two weeks or more.
- Bedtime becomes a long battle even though the day looks well spaced.

Before switching, try moving the first nap a bit later instead. For the full picture, see our [baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age).

## 10 month old wake windows

Ten months is where two clinical bands meet. Cleveland Clinic lists **2.5–4.5 hours** for 7–10 months and **3–6 hours** for 10–12 months; Sleep Foundation's matching bands are **1.5–6 hours** and **3–7.5 hours**. The two app examples are much narrower: Huckleberry gives **3–3.75 hours** at 10 months and Napper about **3–4 hours**.

For a two-nap day, that usually means something like 3 hours before the morning nap, a little longer before the afternoon one, and the longest stretch before bed *(practical suggestion)*. If the morning nap starts getting refused, a slightly longer first window is often worth trying before you think about one nap. None of these numbers come from the AAP or AASM, so treat them as a starting point. The [wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age) page shows the full chart.

## Standing in the crib at night

Tresillian notes that when babies start moving around more or standing up in the cot, sleep can be disturbed and they may wake more. Many babies this age can pull up but not yet get down again.

What can help:

1. **Practice during the day.** Show your baby how to bend their knees and sit down from standing, using a low table or the crib rail.
2. **At night, guide rather than entertain.** Tresillian suggests using a calm tone with simple words like "time to lie down" and then showing or guiding them down.
3. **Keep the response short and the same each time.** Lay them down, say the same phrase, and leave.
4. **Check the crib.** KidsHealth advises removing hazards your baby could reach from a seated or standing position, such as mobiles, wall hangings, curtains, and blind cords.

## Separation anxiety and bedtime

KidsHealth explains that separation anxiety usually appears between 8 months and 1 year, as babies understand that a parent who leaves still exists somewhere else. A baby who slept well may begin calling out or crying in the night and calm down as soon as a parent appears.

Approaches KidsHealth suggests:

- **A short, warm exit ritual.** Say goodbye in a pleasant, loving, and firm way, and keep it brief.
- **A quiet night response.** Reassure your baby softly that you are there, give a soothing pat, then leave quickly. Long cuddles, feeds, or chatting may encourage more waking.
- **Avoid big changes if you can.** KidsHealth suggests not starting childcare with an unfamiliar person during this window, where possible.

## Night waking at 10 months

Newcastle Hospitals NHS says it is normal for some babies to start waking more often again at around 8–9 months, and Derbyshire NHS describes the same pattern. Sleep Foundation's wake-windows page notes that sleep disturbances may be more common around 9 months.

Before deciding what to change, rule out the basics: illness, teething discomfort, hunger, a room that is too warm or cold, or a nap that ended too close to bedtime. If the waking persists and your baby is otherwise well, a consistent settling plan usually helps. Our [sleep training methods guide](/sleep-training-methods-explained) compares the main options.

## What can make it worse

- **A morning nap dropped too early,** leading to an overtired afternoon and a hard bedtime.
- **An afternoon nap that ends late,** leaving too little awake time before bed.
- **Changing responses each night,** which makes it harder for your baby to know what to expect.
- **A long, playful night visit** after every cry.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Contact your pediatrician if your baby snores loudly, pauses in breathing, or breathes with effort during sleep; seems unwell or has a fever; is eating much less; or if night waking is leaving you exhausted and unable to cope.

## Frequently asked questions

**How many naps does a 10 month old need?**  
Usually two, each between 30 minutes and 2 hours (KidsHealth).

**What is a good bedtime for a 10 month old?**  
There is no single correct time. Choose one that leaves about as much awake time after the last nap as your baby manages earlier in the day.

**Why is my 10 month old suddenly waking at night?**  
Common reasons include new skills such as standing, separation anxiety, illness, and schedule changes. NHS services describe more waking at 8–9 months as normal for some babies.

**My 10 month old stands up in the crib and cries. What should I do?**  
Practice sitting down during the day, then at night calmly lay them down with the same short phrase (Tresillian).

**Is my 10 month old ready for one nap?**  
Most babies are not. Mayo Clinic says the morning nap is often dropped at 10–12 months, while Boys Town gives 15–18 months.

## Two naps, tracked over time (Yorix)

**Yorix** records naps and night wakings and suggests the next nap window from your baby's recent days. That can help you see whether a skipped morning nap is a one-off or a pattern. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [Baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age)
- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)
- [Sleep training methods explained](/sleep-training-methods-explained)
- [The Ferber method](/ferber-method-baby-sleep)
- [Sleep regression ages](/sleep-regression)
- [9 month old sleep schedule](/9-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [11 month old sleep schedule](/11-month-old-sleep-schedule)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026. App pages are used only as labeled examples.

2. Nemours KidsHealth. "Baby Sleep: 8- to 12-Month-Olds." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleep812m.html>.
3. Nemours KidsHealth. "Separation Anxiety." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sep-anxiety.html>.
4. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby (Australian Government). "Baby sleep patterns by age." Last reviewed May 2025. <https://www.pregnancybirthbaby.org.au/babies/sleep-and-settling/sleep-patterns-for-babies>.
5. Sleep Foundation. "The Ferber Method for Sleep Training." Updated 15 July 2025. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/ferber-method>.
6. Sleep Foundation. "Newborn Wake Windows: What's Normal by Age." Updated 13 October 2026. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/newborn-wake-windows>.

title: 3 Month Old Sleep Schedule: Naps & Night Stretches | Yorix
heading: 3 Month Old Sleep Schedule: Naps, Night Stretches, and an Example Day
description: A 3 month old sleep schedule: how much sleep at 12 weeks (14–17 hours per NSF), how many naps, longer night stretches, night feeds, and an example day.
body:
# 3 Month Old Sleep Schedule: Naps, Night Stretches, and an Example Day

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** September 3, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Around 12 weeks, many parents notice the first glimmers of order: a longer stretch after the late-evening feed, a baby who stays bright and chatty a little longer in the morning, naps that start to land at roughly similar times. It is a halfway stage. Your 3-month-old is no longer a newborn in sleep terms, but not yet ready for the more clock-based days that tend to come later.

## Short answer

A **3 month old sleep schedule** is still flexible. The National Sleep Foundation's expert panel recommends **14–17 hours of sleep per 24 hours for babies 0–3 months**; the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's recommendations only begin at 4 months. KidsHealth says many babies this age take **2–3 daytime naps** followed by a longer night stretch, and that "sleeping through the night" at this stage means about **5 or 6 hours**. Formal sleep training is generally considered too early: Sleep Foundation places readiness at 4–6 months.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total sleep, 0–3 months | 14–17 hours per 24 hours | National Sleep Foundation (Hirshkowitz et al., 2015); KidsHealth |
| Naps | 2–3 for many babies at 1–3 months | KidsHealth |
| "Sleeping through" at this age | A stretch of about 5–6 hours | KidsHealth |
| Longest night stretch by about 3 months | Around 5 hours for some babies | Newcastle Hospitals NHS; Derbyshire NHS |
| Awake time between sleeps | 1–2 hours (1–3 months) or 1.25–2.5 hours (3–4 months) | Cleveland Clinic |

## What changes in sleep around 3 months

Several developments come together at about this age:

- **The body clock is switching on.** Sleep Foundation explains that from about 8 to 9 weeks, melatonin and cortisol begin following a daily rhythm. The Sydney Children's Hospitals Network says many babies around 3 months start staying awake longer in the day and sleeping longer at night.
- **Night stretches lengthen for some.** Newcastle Hospitals NHS says some babies skip a night feed by 3 months and sleep around 5 hours at a time. Tresillian describes night sleep at 3 months lengthening to up to 5–6 hours, often twice a night, with one to three brief rousings inside those stretches.
- **But not for everyone.** KidsHealth stresses that the range of "normal" at 1–3 months is still very wide. Plenty of healthy 12-week-olds still wake every few hours.

## How much should a 3 month old sleep?

Because the AASM does not set a figure for babies under 4 months, the most commonly used number comes from the National Sleep Foundation: **14 to 17 hours** for newborns up to 3 months. KidsHealth and Sleep Foundation both quote this range. Other services describe wider spreads. Tresillian says most babies of 3–6 months sleep about 14 or 15 hours, while Pregnancy, Birth and Baby lists 11–19 hours for birth to 3 months.

The panel behind the NSF figures added a caveat worth knowing: durations outside the range can still be appropriate for some individuals, but being far outside it is rare. In practical terms, a content, feeding, growing baby who sleeps 13 hours is not a cause for alarm. A baby who seems unusually hard to wake or is sleeping far more than before is worth a call.

**App examples (not clinical guidance):** Huckleberry suggests about 15 hours with 4–5 naps at 3 months; Napper describes 14–17 hours with 3–4 naps. Both sit near the NSF range but suggest more naps than KidsHealth.

## A 3 month old schedule: example day

This is **an example only**. At this age, follow your baby's cues first and the clock second. The times assume a 7:00 a.m. start.

| Time | Activity | What to watch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 7:00 a.m. | Wake, feed, curtains open | Morning light helps the developing body clock |
| 8:15–9:30 a.m. | Nap | Yawns, glazed look, turning away |
| 9:30 a.m. | Feed, then floor time and tummy time | Short bursts are enough |
| 11:00 a.m.–12:30 p.m. | Nap | A walk in the pram can count |
| 12:30 p.m. | Feed, cuddles, play | |
| 2:00–3:15 p.m. | Nap | |
| 3:15 p.m. | Feed | |
| 4:45–5:20 p.m. | Short late-afternoon nap | Helps the baby reach bedtime calmly |
| 6:30 p.m. | Bath or wash, feed, song | Keep the same order every evening |
| About 7:30 p.m. | Down for the night | Expect one or more night feeds |
| Late evening or night | Feed(s), kept dim and brief | |

Add it up and you get roughly 4 hours 25 minutes of daytime sleep, with night sleep broken by feeds. Some 3-month-olds take more, shorter naps; some take three longer ones. Both patterns are fine.

## Naps at 3 months

Naps are often still irregular in length. One nap might last 35 minutes and the next almost 2 hours. Rather than chasing a fixed number, look at the whole day: is your baby getting enough sleep across 24 hours to be mostly content when awake?

Helpful habits at this stage:

- Offer a nap when you see early tiredness signs, before crying starts.
- Use a short, repeatable wind-down: dim the room, change the diaper, a song, into the sleep sack.
- Let some naps happen on the go. Newcastle Hospitals NHS suggests daytime sleep in a pram or a lighter room can help babies learn that long, dark, quiet sleep is for night.

For a wider view of how nap counts fall across the first two years, see our [baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age).

## 3 month old wake windows

Around 12 weeks a baby can usually manage a little more time awake than in the newborn weeks, but not much. What the charts say:

| Who says it | Age it covers | Time awake between sleeps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cleveland Clinic | 1–3 months, then 3–4 months | 1–2 hours, then 1.25–2.5 hours |
| Sleep Foundation | 1–4 months | 1–3 hours |
| Huckleberry (app example) | 3 months | 60–120 minutes |
| Napper (app example) | 3 months | 1–2 hours |

A sensible place to begin is about **75 to 90 minutes**, feeds included, and to go shorter after a poor nap *(practical suggestion)*. Huckleberry's list of sleepy cues at this age includes going quiet and still, staring into space, and resting the head against you. Wake windows are not an official AAP or AASM measure, so use them only as a rough guide; our [wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age) chart shows how they change month to month.

## Night feeds at 3 months

Night feeds are still normal for most 3-month-olds, especially breastfed babies. HealthyChildren.org (AAP) notes that most formula-fed babies no longer need a middle-of-the-night feed somewhere **between 2 and 4 months**, or once they weigh more than about 12 pounds, though this varies a lot between babies. Breastfed babies often keep at least one night feed for longer; there is no single cut-off that suits every baby.

A few ways to keep night feeds sleepy:

- Low light only, no screens.
- Change the diaper only if it is dirty or very wet.
- Put your baby back down soon after the feed, rather than waiting for deep sleep in arms.

## Is there a 3 month sleep regression?

Many parents notice changes between 3 and 4 months. Sleep Foundation describes newborn sleep as falling into one- to three-hour segments and says this begins to change by around 3 to 4 months, as sleep starts to mature. Some babies wake more or nap more briefly during that shift. If your 3-month-old's sleep has suddenly worsened, our [4 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/4-months) guide explains the process. Rule out illness, hunger, and discomfort first.

## Day-night contrast and the bedtime routine

KidsHealth suggests starting a bedtime routine now if you haven't already, using familiar, relaxing steps in the same order. It doesn't have to be long. Many families use something like a bath or wash, a feed, a short song, and into bed.

During the day, the NHS suggests opening the curtains, playing, and not worrying much about everyday noise while your baby naps. Derbyshire NHS adds that getting up at about the same time each morning helps line up your body clock and your baby's. At night, keep everything quiet, dim, and dull.

## Why sleep training is usually too early at 3 months

Sleep Foundation says babies generally aren't ready for sleep training until **4 to 6 months**, because the rhythms that support longer independent sleep are still developing. HealthyChildren.org adds that regular sleep cycles don't really appear until about 4 months.

What you *can* practice now is gentle: putting your baby down drowsy but not fully asleep some of the time, and giving them a moment to settle before you step in. If you are curious about later options, our [sleep training methods guide](/sleep-training-methods-explained) compares them.

## Safe sleep at 3 months

Rolling often starts around now. KidsHealth says swaddling is fine until babies begin to roll, which typically happens at about 3 to 4 months, and that the first attempts to roll over are the signal to stop. HealthyChildren.org (AAP) warns against weighted swaddles, sleepers, and blankets at any age.

The rest of the AAP basics still apply: back to sleep every time, a firm, flat crib or bassinet with only a fitted sheet, and room-sharing without bed-sharing.

## What can make a 3-month-old's sleep harder

- **Keeping your baby awake in the day "so they sleep at night."** KidsHealth notes that overtired infants often have more trouble sleeping at night.
- **Long daytime naps in a pitch-dark room**, which can blur day and night for some babies (Newcastle Hospitals NHS).
- **Lively night feeds:** lights, chatting, and play.
- **Comparing with other babies.** Ranges at this age are genuinely wide.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Call your pediatrician if your baby is feeding poorly or having fewer wet diapers, seems much sleepier or harder to wake than usual, has a fever, breathes with effort or makes unusual noises during sleep, or if you are simply concerned. A fever in a baby under 12 weeks old warrants a prompt call (HealthyChildren.org symptom checker).

## Frequently asked questions

**How much should a 3 month old sleep?**  
The National Sleep Foundation recommends 14–17 hours per 24 hours for babies up to 3 months.

**How many naps does a 3 month old take?**  
KidsHealth says many take 2–3 naps; app guidance suggests 4–5 shorter naps for some babies. Nap length decides how many your baby needs.

**Should my 3 month old sleep through the night?**  
Not necessarily. At this age, "through the night" usually means a 5–6 hour stretch (KidsHealth), and many babies still wake for feeds.

**Can I sleep train a 3 month old?**  
Sleep Foundation places readiness at 4–6 months. For now, focus on a calm routine and drowsy-but-awake practice.

**When should I stop swaddling my 3 month old?**  
Once your baby starts trying to roll over (KidsHealth).

## See the rhythm as it forms (Yorix)

**Yorix** keeps a single log of naps, feeds, and night wakings, then highlights the rhythm that is starting to show, such as when the longest night stretch tends to begin. It suggests the next sleep window as your baby's days settle. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

- [4 month old sleep schedule](/4-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)
- [Baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age)

body:
# 4 Month Old Sleep Schedule: Naps, Bedtime, and How Much Sleep Is Enough

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** September 3, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Four months is often the first age at which a day starts to look like a plan: a morning nap, a midday nap, something in the afternoon, and a bedtime you can roughly predict. This guide gives you two example days (one with three naps, one with four), the daily sleep totals that experts recommend, and what to do when the plan falls apart by 10 a.m.

## Short answer

A **4 month old sleep schedule** usually has **3 or 4 naps**, a bedtime in the early evening, and one or more night feeds. On **how much a 4 month old should sleep**, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) recommends **12–16 hours in 24 hours, including naps**, for babies aged 4 to 12 months, and says the AAP endorses this. KidsHealth puts typical daytime sleep at this stage at **about 3–4 hours**. Short naps of 30–45 minutes are common and not a sign that something is wrong.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | Typical range | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total sleep per 24 hours | 12–16 hours, naps included | AASM (endorsed by the AAP); KidsHealth; Derbyshire NHS |
| Daytime sleep | About 3–4 hours | KidsHealth (4–7 months) |
| Number of naps | At least 2 (KidsHealth); 2–3 for 3–6 months (Pregnancy, Birth and Baby) | KidsHealth; Pregnancy, Birth and Baby |
| Wake windows | 1.25–2.5 hours (3–4 months) / 1–3 hours (1–4 months) | Cleveland Clinic / Sleep Foundation |
| Typical nap length | Often 30–40 minutes at 4–5 months; up to 2 hours | Tresillian; Pregnancy, Birth and Baby |

## How much should a 4 month old sleep?

The AASM range is **12 to 16 hours per 24 hours**, counting naps and night sleep together. Derbyshire Community Health Services (NHS) uses the same range from around 4 months. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby, Australia's government parenting service, gives a slightly narrower **12 to 15 hours** for 3–6 months, and Tresillian says most babies of this age sleep about 14 or 15 hours.

A range this wide exists because babies genuinely differ. Derbyshire's advice is a good test: if your baby is growing and is alert and happy when awake, they are very likely getting enough sleep.

Baby apps publish their own targets, and they don't agree with each other. As **examples only**: Huckleberry suggests aiming for about 14.5 hours with 3–4 naps, while Napper describes 12–15 hours with 2–3 naps. Both sit inside the AASM range, which is the number to go by.

## Example 4 month old schedules (3-nap and 4-nap days)

These are **examples, not prescriptions**. Shift every time to match when your baby actually woke up.

**Example A: a 4-nap day** (often fits babies whose naps are short)

| Time | What's happening | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 6:30 a.m. | Wake up, feed | Open curtains; daylight helps the body clock |
| 7:50–8:35 a.m. | Nap 1 (45 min) | First window here is about 1 h 20 min |
| 8:35–10:15 a.m. | Feed, floor play, tummy time | |
| 10:15–11:00 a.m. | Nap 2 (45 min) | |
| 11:00 a.m.–12:45 p.m. | Feed, outing | |
| 12:45–2:00 p.m. | Nap 3 (1 h 15 min) | |
| 2:00–4:00 p.m. | Feed, play | |
| 4:00–4:30 p.m. | Nap 4 (30 min catnap) | If your baby dozes off in a stroller or carrier, move them onto their back on a firm sleep surface as soon as possible (HealthyChildren.org / AAP) |
| 4:30–6:15 p.m. | Feed, quiet play | |
| 6:15 p.m. | Bath or wash, feed, song | Same steps each evening |
| About 6:45 p.m. | Asleep for the night | One or more night feeds still expected |

Rough total: about 3 hours 15 minutes of naps, plus close to 12 hours in the crib overnight. Take off the time spent awake for feeds and you land somewhere around 14 hours, inside the 12–16 hour range.

**Example B: a 3-nap day** (often fits babies who take one or two longer naps)

| Time | What's happening | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 7:00 a.m. | Wake up, feed | |
| 8:45–10:15 a.m. | Nap 1 (1 h 30 min) | Longer morning nap |
| 10:15 a.m.–12:30 p.m. | Feeds and play | |
| 12:30–2:00 p.m. | Nap 2 (1 h 30 min) | |
| 2:00–4:15 p.m. | Feed, walk | |
| 4:15–4:50 p.m. | Nap 3 (35 min) | Keep this one short so bedtime isn't pushed late |
| 4:50–7:00 p.m. | Feed, wind-down | |
| About 7:15 p.m. | Asleep for the night | |

Rough total: about 3 hours 35 minutes of naps, plus about 11 hours of actual sleep overnight once feeds are taken out.

### 3 naps or 4: how to choose

Look at nap *length*, not the calendar. If most naps end at 30–45 minutes, your baby builds up sleepiness again sooner and usually needs a fourth nap to reach bedtime without a meltdown. If one or two naps reliably run over an hour, three naps tend to fit. Many babies switch back and forth for a few weeks, and a mix of 3-nap and 4-nap days in the same week is normal.

## 4 month old wake windows

How long can a 4 month old stay awake? Cleveland Clinic gives **1.25–2.5 hours** for 3–4 months, and Sleep Foundation gives **1–3 hours** for 1–4 months. Start at the shorter end, especially for the first window of the day and after a short nap. Watch for yawning, eye rubbing, staring off, or fussing, and begin your wind-down then.

The apps disagree on which window is longest. Huckleberry describes morning windows as usually the shortest, while Napper says the first window is often the longest. That disagreement is a good reminder to follow your baby rather than a rule. Our [wake windows by age chart](/wake-windows-by-age) compares the sources in one table.

**Wake windows for a 4 month old, side by side:**

| Source | Wake window at about 4 months |
| --- | --- |
| Cleveland Clinic (3–4 months) | 1.25–2.5 hours |
| Sleep Foundation (1–4 months) | 1–3 hours |
| Napper, 4-month page (app example) | About 1.5–2.5 hours |
| Napper, wake-window chart (app example) | 75–120 minutes |

On a four-nap day the windows sit near the short end; once your baby moves toward three naps they stretch toward 2 hours or a little more *(practical suggestion)*. If a 4 month old wake window of 2 hours ends in tears every time, shorten it by 15 minutes and watch for a week.

## Short naps at 4 months: why they happen

Tresillian, an Australian early-parenting service, explains that at 4–5 months a baby's sleep cycle lasts around **30–50 minutes**, and that it's very common to wake after **30–40 minutes**. In other words, a single cycle and then awake is developmentally ordinary.

What can help a nap last longer:

- Offer the nap before your baby is overtired.
- Keep the wind-down short and identical: same room, same song, same sleeping bag.
- If your baby stirs at the half-hour mark, pause briefly before going in. Mayo Clinic suggests that from about 4 months, you can check on a baby who cries after being put down, offer soothing words, and give them a little time to settle.
- Accept that some naps will stay short. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby notes naps at 3–6 months last *up to* 2 hours, so anything shorter is still within the normal spread.

## Bedtime for a 4 month old

No official body sets a bedtime for this age. In practice, bedtime follows the day: the time of the last nap, plus a wake window, plus a short routine. After a day of short naps, moving bedtime earlier is usually easier than stretching a tired baby to the "normal" time. As an **app example**, Huckleberry describes 6:00–8:00 p.m. as a common range.

KidsHealth encourages a soothing, repeatable routine at this age and putting your baby down drowsy but still awake, so they practice the last step of falling asleep in their own bed. HealthyChildren.org (AAP) makes the same point.

## Night feeds and night waking at 4 months

Many 4-month-olds still feed once or more overnight, and that is expected. Newcastle Hospitals NHS notes that some babies sleep around 5 hours at a stretch by 3 months, but many begin waking more again at 4–5 months. Derbyshire NHS adds that babies do not routinely sleep through the night until around age 1, and that by 5 months some may sleep up to 8 hours.

If wakings suddenly multiply, our page on the [4 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/4-months) explains what changes in sleep around this age. Before you blame a regression, rule out hunger, illness, and discomfort.

## Swaddling, pacifiers, and rolling

- **Swaddling:** stop as soon as your baby shows signs of trying to roll (HealthyChildren.org / AAP). KidsHealth notes rolling typically starts around 3–4 months, so this is often the age to move to a wearable sleep sack.
- **Pacifier:** KidsHealth says it is fine to offer one at sleep time without forcing it, and you don't need to put it back in if it falls out once your baby is asleep.
- **Rolling over in sleep:** keep placing your baby on their back. If they can roll both ways on their own, HealthyChildren.org says you don't need to keep turning them back, as long as the crib is clear.

## What can make a 4 month schedule harder

- **Copying clock times from someone else's baby.** The examples above are anchored to a wake-up time, so if yours woke at 7:40, everything shifts.
- **A late, long last nap** that leaves no sleep pressure for bedtime.
- **Changing several things at once:** new room, new routine, and dropping a nap in the same week.
- **Bright, busy evenings.** Keep the last hour calm and dim.
- **Unsafe sleep fixes:** inclined sleepers, extra blankets, pillows, or weighted products. HealthyChildren.org says a surface that inclines more than 10 degrees is not safe for infant sleep.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Call if your baby is feeding less, has fewer wet diapers, has a fever, breathes noisily or with effort during sleep, is hard to wake, or if you are simply worried. It's also worth asking before you start any formal sleep training. Our [sleep training methods guide](/sleep-training-methods-explained) explains the options.

## Frequently asked questions

**How much should a 4 month old sleep?**  
12–16 hours in 24 hours, naps included (AASM, endorsed by the AAP).

**How many naps does a 4 month old take?**  
Usually 3 or 4. KidsHealth says at least two at this stage; Pregnancy, Birth and Baby gives 2–3 for 3–6 months. Short naps often mean an extra nap is needed.

**What is a good bedtime for a 4 month old?**  
Whatever time follows the last nap plus a wake window, often early evening. Move it earlier after a day of short naps.

**Is it normal for my 4 month old to nap only 30–45 minutes?**  
Yes. Tresillian notes waking after 30–40 minutes is very common at 4–5 months.

**Should a 4 month old still eat at night?**  
Often yes. Many babies wake for feeds well beyond 4 months, and NHS services say sleeping through the night routinely comes closer to age 1.

**When should I stop swaddling?**  
When your baby starts trying to roll (HealthyChildren.org / AAP).

## Plan the day around your real baby (Yorix)

**Yorix** turns the naps and feeds you log into a day plan that adjusts after every short nap, with a predicted next sleep window and bedtime. The in-app AI coach can explain why today's plan moved. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

body:
# 5 Month Old Sleep Schedule: Moving to 3 Naps and Steadier Nights

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** September 3, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Five months is often the age when a day finally starts to look like a plan. Many babies can now stay happily awake for a couple of hours, and a fourth catnap begins to feel unnecessary. At the same time, plenty of 5-month-olds still wake at night, take 30-minute naps, or roll onto their tummy and protest about it. This guide covers what is typical, how a 3-nap day can look, and what tends to help.

## Short answer

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (endorsed by the AAP) recommends **12–16 hours of sleep per 24 hours, naps included, for babies 4–12 months old**. KidsHealth says babies of 4–7 months usually take **at least two naps** and about **3–4 hours of daytime sleep** in total. Many 5-month-olds are on **three naps**, with a short late-afternoon nap still common. Night waking is normal for many babies: two NHS services report that around **4–5 months** waking often comes back after an earlier calmer phase.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total sleep in 24 h | 12–16 hours (4–12 months) | AASM, endorsed by AAP |
| Daytime sleep | About 3–4 hours, at least 2 naps (4–7 months) | KidsHealth |
| Usual nap count | 2–3 naps, each up to about 2 hours (3–6 months) | Pregnancy, Birth and Baby |
| Awake time between sleeps | 2–4 hours (5–7 months) | Cleveland Clinic |
| Sleep cycle length | About 30–50 minutes at 4–5 months | Tresillian |
| Longest night stretch | Up to about 8 hours by 5 months for some | Derbyshire NHS; Newcastle Hospitals NHS |

## How much sleep does a 5 month old need?

The AASM range of 12 to 16 hours is wide on purpose. Some babies thrive near the bottom of it, others near the top. Tresillian puts the typical figure for 3–6 months at about 14–15 hours.

Night length varies a lot at this age:

- Newcastle Hospitals NHS says that by 5 months about half of babies settle for an 8-hour stretch on some nights.
- Derbyshire NHS describes night stretches of up to 8 hours by about 5 months, with a full night of sleep more typical closer to the first birthday.
- Pregnancy, Birth and Baby gives up to 6–8 hours for the longest stretch at 3–6 months.

**App examples (not clinical guidance):** Huckleberry aims for about 14.5 hours, with 11–12 hours at night and 3–4 naps. Napper describes 12–15 hours, with about 10–11 hours at night and 2–3 naps.

## Example 3-nap day for a 5 month old

**Example only.** Shift the times to match your baby's wake-up time, and treat the nap lengths as rough guides.

| Time | What happens | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 6:45 a.m. | Wake for the day, milk feed | Open the curtains straight away |
| 8:45–10:00 a.m. | Nap 1 | Often the most reliable nap of the day |
| 10:00 a.m. | Milk feed, play on the floor | Practice rolling both ways |
| 12:15–1:45 p.m. | Nap 2 | The longest nap for many babies |
| 1:45 p.m. | Milk feed, outing | Daylight and fresh air |
| 4:00–4:40 p.m. | Nap 3 (short) | Keep it brief to protect bedtime |
| 6:15 p.m. | Bath, pajamas, milk feed, book | Same order every night |
| 7:00 p.m. | Asleep in the crib | |
| Overnight | 0–2 feeds, depending on your baby | Dim lights, no play |

This example adds up to about 3 hours 25 minutes of daytime sleep, inside the KidsHealth 3–4 hour range. Mayo Clinic notes that a third nap is typically dropped by about 9 months, so there is usually no rush to cut it now.

## From 4 naps to 3: signs and timing

You will probably not need to "decide" this. Your baby's day tends to make it obvious.

| Sign | What it may mean |
| --- | --- |
| The last nap of the day is fought or skipped | The day may have room for only three naps now |
| Bedtime keeps drifting later | Too much daytime sleep for the current night |
| Your baby is calm after 2+ hours awake | Longer awake periods are coming in |
| The first two naps lengthen | The rest of the day is shifting |

Huckleberry (app example) links the switch to babies managing about 2–3 hours of awake time. Cleveland Clinic's wake window range for 5–7 months is 2–4 hours. Our [wake windows guide](/wake-windows-by-age) shows the full chart.

## Is 3 to 2 naps too early at 5 months?

For most babies, yes. Mayo Clinic suggests two naps (for example, around 9 a.m. and 1 p.m.) from 4 months to a year, and puts the loss of the third nap at about 9 months. App guidance from Huckleberry suggests the 3-to-2 transition by about 8 months. If a 5-month-old seems to "refuse" the third nap, look first at whether the nap is simply scheduled too close to the second one or too close to bedtime.

Signs that two naps are not enough yet include crankiness by late afternoon, a meltdown at bedtime, or more night waking.

## 5 month old wake windows

Five months straddles two chart bands, which explains why advice online ranges so widely:

- **Cleveland Clinic:** 1.25–2.5 hours up to 4 months, then 2–4 hours from 5 to 7 months.
- **Sleep Foundation:** 1.5–4.5 hours for 5–7 months.
- **Huckleberry (app example):** babies awake about 1.5–2.5 hours tend to need 4 naps; once the fourth nap goes, most need 2–3 hours.
- **Napper (app example):** about 2–3 hours, often longest first thing in the morning.

In practice, a 5-month-old on four naps is usually near 1.5–2 hours, and one on three naps nearer 2–2.5 hours *(our reading of the ranges above)*. No medical body sets wake windows, so let your baby's cues have the final say. See the [wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age) chart for the months before and after.

## Why naps are often 30–40 minutes

Tresillian says sleep cycles at 4–5 months last around 30–50 minutes, and waking after 30–40 minutes is very common. A short nap is not a sign that something is wrong. It may help to:

- Wait a few minutes before going in after a short nap, in case your baby resettles.
- Keep the room similar for every nap: same sleep sack, same space, similar light.
- Look at the full day. If your baby is mostly content and night sleep is fine, short naps may simply suit them right now.

## Night waking at 5 months

Both Newcastle Hospitals NHS and Derbyshire NHS describe night waking often returning at **4–5 months**, after many babies had a calmer spell. HealthyChildren.org says that babies who are held or rocked all the way to sleep may struggle to get back to sleep when they wake at night.

Practical steps:

- **Pause before you respond.** KidsHealth suggests waiting a few minutes before going in, because some babies settle on their own.
- **Put your baby down drowsy but awake** at least for bedtime (KidsHealth, HealthyChildren.org).
- **Keep night feeds calm and quiet.** Whether your baby still needs a night feed depends on many factors; ask your pediatrician if you are unsure.
- **Use comfort that you can keep doing.** Mayo Clinic suggests that from about 4 months, short check-ins with soothing words can help.

## Is there a 5 month sleep regression?

There is no separate clinical "5-month regression." What parents call by that name is usually the same sleep shift that begins around 3 to 4 months (Sleep Foundation) together with a busier body and brain. If sleep worsened suddenly and your baby is also unwell, feeding less, or in pain, talk with your pediatrician. Otherwise, our [4 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/4-months) guide explains what is going on.

## Rolling, solids, and other 5-month changes

- **Rolling.** HealthyChildren.org (AAP) says to keep placing your baby on their back, but once they roll both ways on their own, you do not need to turn them back over. Keep the crib bare. Swaddling should already have stopped once your baby showed signs of rolling (KidsHealth).
- **Solids.** The AAP recommends breast milk only for about the first 6 months. HealthyChildren.org lists readiness signs such as good head control, sitting supported, and interest in food. Cleveland Clinic warns against adding cereal to a bottle. There is no fetched evidence that starting solids early improves sleep, so we don't recommend it for that purpose.
- **Crying peak passing.** Tresillian notes that normal crying peaks earlier in infancy and decreases naturally from about 5 months.

## What can make it worse

- An overtired baby at bedtime because the last nap was dropped too early.
- A third nap that runs late and pushes bedtime back.
- New props at every wake-up (rocking, then feeding, then a car ride), so your baby never gets a chance to learn one way to settle.
- A bedroom that changes from night to night.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Contact your pediatrician if your baby snores loudly or pauses in breathing during sleep, is feeding much less, has fewer wet diapers, has a fever or seems unwell, or if sleep problems leave you struggling to cope. Your own wellbeing matters too.

## Frequently asked questions

**How many naps should a 5 month old take?**  
Most take 2–3 naps (Pregnancy, Birth and Baby; KidsHealth says at least two). Many have three at this age.

**How long should a 5 month old be awake between naps?**  
Cleveland Clinic suggests 2–4 hours for 5–7 months. Most 5-month-olds are near the shorter end.

**What time should bedtime be for a 5 month old?**  
There is no fixed rule. Pick a bedtime that leaves a reasonable awake period after the last nap and fits your family. Many families choose an early evening time.

**Is it normal for a 5 month old to wake up at night?**  
Yes. NHS services report that night waking often returns at 4–5 months.

**Should I drop to two naps at 5 months?**  
Usually not. The third nap typically goes at about 9 months (Mayo Clinic).

## Plan the 3-nap day (Yorix)

**Yorix** logs naps, night wakings, and feeds, then suggests the next nap window based on your baby's recent days. That can make the move from four naps to three easier to see. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

description: Baby feeding schedule by age: how often and how much breast milk or formula from newborn to 12 months, when to start solids, hunger cues, and red flags.
body:
# Baby Feeding Schedule by Age: How Often and How Much, Birth to 12 Months

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** September 3, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Feeding is the part of baby care that most often brings parents to a search bar: is my baby eating enough, too often, too much? The honest answer from pediatric sources is that babies vary, and that following your baby's hunger and fullness signals matters more than any chart. Still, typical ranges help you know what to expect. Here they are, by age, with the sources for every number.

## Short answer

Most healthy, full-term babies are **fed on demand** rather than by the clock. HealthyChildren.org (AAP) says breastfed newborns usually nurse **about every 2 hours, 10–12 times in 24 hours**, while formula-fed newborns eat **every 2–3 hours, at least 8 times a day**, taking about **1–2 ounces** per feed after the first days. By the end of the first month, many formula-fed babies take **3–4 ounces every 3–4 hours**. The AAP recommends **breast milk only for about the first 6 months**, then adding solid foods while continuing breast milk or formula. Your pediatrician's growth checks are the real measure of whether feeding is going well.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | Answer | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Breastfeeds per day, newborn | About 10–12 (roughly every 2 hours) | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |
| Formula feeds per day, newborn | At least 8 (every 2–3 hours) | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |
| Formula per feed, end of month 1 | 3–4 oz (90–120 ml), every 3–4 hours | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |
| Formula per day, maximum | About 32 oz (960 ml) | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |
| Wet diapers after day 4–5 | At least 5–6 a day | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |
| Start of solid foods | About 6 months | AAP; Cleveland Clinic |

## Baby feeding chart by age

These are typical ranges, not targets. Every baby's needs are different.

| Age | Breastfed | Formula-fed | Solid foods |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First days | Colostrum, about a teaspoon per feed; may want to feed about every hour at first (NHS) | About ½ oz per feed in the first day or two (HealthyChildren.org) | None |
| Weeks 1–4 | About every 2 hours, 10–12 feeds a day (HealthyChildren.org); 8–12 feeds (Cleveland Clinic) | Every 2–3 hours, at least 8 feeds, about 1–2 oz each (HealthyChildren.org); 6–10 feeds (Cleveland Clinic) | None |
| End of month 1 | Feeds slowly space out | 3–4 oz about every 3–4 hours (HealthyChildren.org) | None |
| 1–6 months | On demand; total daily intake stays similar from 4 weeks to 6 months (Cleveland Clinic) | 3–4 oz per feed, about 24–30 oz a day (Cleveland Clinic); no more than about 32 oz a day (HealthyChildren.org) | None. Exclusive breast milk for about 6 months (AAP) |
| About 6 months | Continue | 6–8 oz at each of 4–5 feeds (HealthyChildren.org); Cleveland Clinic lists 3–4 oz per feed, totals vary | Start solids when ready |
| 6–8 months | Continue | Continue | 2–3 meals a day (Cleveland Clinic) |
| 9–12 months | Continue | Continue | 3–4 meals plus 1–2 snacks a day (Cleveland Clinic) |

**Note on differences:** HealthyChildren.org and Cleveland Clinic give different per-feed amounts at about 6 months. Both say babies regulate their own intake. Ask your pediatrician what fits your baby's growth.

HealthyChildren.org also offers a rough guide for formula of about **2½ ounces per pound of body weight per day**, within the 32-ounce upper limit.

## Newborn feeding: the first weeks

- **Feed early and often.** The NHS explains that frequent breastfeeding in the first days stimulates milk supply, and feeds become fewer but longer once mature milk comes in.
- **Don't let a newborn go too long.** HealthyChildren.org advises waking a formula-fed newborn who sleeps longer than 4–5 hours in the first weeks and starts missing feeds. KidsHealth says newborns should be woken to feed every 3–4 hours until they are gaining weight well.
- **Watch the diapers.** HealthyChildren.org says 2–3 wet diapers a day in the first few days, then **at least 5–6 a day** after day 4–5, suggests your baby is getting enough.

For how feeding and sleep fit together in these weeks, see our [newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule).

## Breastfed vs formula-fed: why schedules differ

Breast milk digests quickly, so breastfed babies usually feed more often, in smaller amounts. HealthyChildren.org notes that formula-fed babies often settle into a more regular pattern, such as every 3–4 hours. Neither pattern is better; they are just different.

For bottle feeding, HealthyChildren.org suggests:

- **Start on demand** and let a routine emerge from your baby's own timetable.
- **Let your baby decide when they're done.** If they get fidgety or distracted, they're probably full. If they finish the bottle and keep smacking their lips, they may want a little more.
- **Talk to your pediatrician** if your baby consistently seems to want much more or much less than the usual range.

## Hunger and fullness cues

| Early hunger cues | Fullness cues |
| --- | --- |
| Licking lips, sticking tongue out | Slowing down or stopping sucking |
| Rooting (turning toward the breast) | Getting fidgety or easily distracted |
| Hands to mouth repeatedly | Relaxed hands and body |
| Opening mouth, fussing | Turning away from the breast or bottle |

Source: HealthyChildren.org (hunger cues; bottle fullness signs). HealthyChildren.org stresses that **crying is a late hunger sign**, and that babies also suck for comfort, so not every cry or suck means hunger. It also notes that some babies keep sucking even when full, so pausing during a feed can help them notice.

## Night feeds and feeding schedules

Night feeds are normal in the early months. HealthyChildren.org says that between **2 and 4 months**, or when they weigh more than about 12 pounds, most formula-fed babies no longer need a middle-of-the-night feed, although this varies widely. Breastfed babies often feed at night for longer.

If you want to know how feeds interact with naps and bedtime, our age guides cover this, starting with the [4 month old sleep schedule](/4-month-old-sleep-schedule). Night feeds and settling are also covered in our guide to [baby night wakings](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents).

## Example feeding days

**Examples only.** Your baby may feed more or less often. Follow their cues and your pediatrician's advice.

**Example: formula-fed 3-month-old (about 4 oz per feed, within the 24–30 oz Cleveland Clinic range)**

| Time | Feed |
| --- | --- |
| 6:30 a.m. | Bottle |
| 9:45 a.m. | Bottle |
| 1:00 p.m. | Bottle |
| 4:15 p.m. | Bottle |
| 7:15 p.m. | Bottle before bed |
| About 11:00 p.m. | Bottle |
| About 3:00 a.m. | Bottle, if your baby wakes hungry |

That makes 7 feeds of about 4 oz, or roughly 28 oz in 24 hours.

**Example: 8-month-old on breast milk or formula plus solids (2–3 meals a day)**

| Time | Feed |
| --- | --- |
| On waking | Breast or bottle |
| Mid-morning | Breakfast (solids) |
| Late morning | Breast or bottle |
| Early afternoon | Lunch (solids) |
| Late afternoon | Breast or bottle |
| Early evening | Dinner (solids) |
| Before bed | Breast or bottle |

## Starting solid foods

The AAP recommends breast milk alone for about the first 6 months, then continuing breastfeeding alongside foods for as long as you and your child wish, for 2 years or beyond. Cleveland Clinic also places the start at around 6 months.

**Signs of readiness** (HealthyChildren.org; Cleveland Clinic):

- Good head control and able to sit in a high chair or feeding seat.
- Watching you eat, reaching for food, opening their mouth for a spoon.
- Moving food from a spoon to the back of the mouth rather than pushing it out.

**Key points:**

- **Don't add cereal to a bottle.** Cleveland Clinic advises spoon-feeding instead.
- **Common allergens early.** HealthyChildren.org says there is no evidence that waiting to introduce foods like eggs, dairy, soy, peanut products, or fish beyond 4–6 months prevents allergy. Cleveland Clinic suggests introducing them at about six months.
- **No juice before 12 months** (HealthyChildren.org).
- **Water:** healthy babies don't need extra water before solids. Once solids start, a little water from a cup is fine, up to about 1 cup (8 oz) a day (HealthyChildren.org).

## What can make feeding harder

- **Watching the clock instead of your baby,** especially in the newborn weeks.
- **Pushing a baby to finish every bottle,** which can override their fullness signals.
- **Feeding to sleep every time,** if you later want your baby to settle without a feed. This is a sleep habit, not a feeding problem.
- **Starting solids before your baby is ready.**

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Contact your pediatrician promptly if your baby (HealthyChildren.org symptom checker):

- isn't feeding well, can't finish feeds, or has to be woken for every feed (HealthyChildren.org calls feeding "the one reliable measure" of a newborn's wellbeing);
- has fewer wet diapers than the ranges above;
- is sleeping much more than normal or is hard to wake;
- vomits green (bile-colored) fluid;
- has a fever, especially if under 12 weeks old;
- isn't gaining weight, or you are worried about how much they eat.

Breastfeeding problems such as pain or poor latch are common and fixable. Ask your midwife, health visitor, or a lactation consultant for help.

## Frequently asked questions

**How often should a newborn eat?**  
Breastfed newborns usually feed about every 2 hours (10–12 times a day). Formula-fed newborns feed every 2–3 hours, at least 8 times a day (HealthyChildren.org).

**How much formula should a 2 month old drink?**  
Many babies take 3–4 oz per feed from the end of the first month, about every 3–4 hours (HealthyChildren.org). Your baby may take more or less.

**When can I stop night feeds?**  
HealthyChildren.org says most formula-fed babies no longer need a middle-of-the-night feed between 2 and 4 months, but this varies. Check with your pediatrician.

**When should my baby start solids?**  
At about 6 months, when they show signs of readiness (AAP; Cleveland Clinic).

**Is it OK to feed on demand instead of a schedule?**  
Yes. For most healthy, full-term babies, HealthyChildren.org recommends following your baby's hunger cues.

## Feeds and sleep in one place (Yorix)

**Yorix** logs breast and bottle feeds alongside naps and night wakings, so you can see how feeding times line up with sleep and share a clear record at checkups. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule)
- [Surviving night wakings](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents)
- [3 month old sleep schedule](/3-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [4 month old sleep schedule](/4-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [5 month old sleep schedule](/5-month-old-sleep-schedule)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. HealthyChildren.org / AAP. "How Often and How Much Should Your Baby Eat?" Last updated 2 April 2024. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/feeding-nutrition/Pages/How-Often-and-How-Much-Should-Your-Baby-Eat.aspx>.
2. HealthyChildren.org / AAP. "Amount and Schedule of Baby Formula Feedings." Last updated 16 May 2022. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/formula-feeding/Pages/Amount-and-Schedule-of-Formula-Feedings.aspx>.
3. HealthyChildren.org / AAP. "Starting Solid Foods." Last updated 23 June 2026. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/feeding-nutrition/Pages/Starting-Solid-Foods.aspx>.
4. Cleveland Clinic. "Feeding Your Baby in the First Year." <https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/9693-feeding-your-baby-the-first-year>.
5. NHS. "Breastfeeding: the first few days." <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/breastfeeding-and-bottle-feeding/breastfeeding/the-first-few-days/>.
6. Nemours KidsHealth. "Sleep and Your Newborn." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleepnewborn.html>.
7. HealthyChildren.org symptom checker. "Newborn Illness – How to Recognize." <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/tips-tools/symptom-checker/Pages/symptomviewer.aspx?symptom=Newborn+Illness+-+How+to+Recognize>.

description: How many naps a baby needs by age, how long naps last, and when babies drop from 3 to 2 and from 2 to 1 nap, with example nap days and source-backed ranges.
body:
# Baby Nap Schedule by Age: Nap Chart and Nap Transitions

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** September 3, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Naps shrink in number long before they shrink in importance. A newborn may sleep six or more times between dawn and dusk; a toddler usually settles on one long afternoon nap. This guide covers **how many naps your baby needs at each age**, how long those naps tend to last, and the two transitions that cause the most confusion: **3 naps to 2** and **2 naps to 1**.

Looking for how long your baby should stay awake between naps? That's a separate question, covered in our [wake windows by age chart](/wake-windows-by-age).

## Short answer

Nap count drops in steps across the first two years. Sleep Foundation says newborns may take **six or more naps** a day. KidsHealth describes **2–3 daytime naps** for most babies from around 4 months, and **two naps** as typical at 8–12 months. Most toddlers move to **one nap by about 18 months** (KidsHealth); Boys Town National Research Hospital puts the usual 2-to-1 switch at **15–18 months**. Very few children stop napping before age 2.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Newborn naps per day | 6 or more | Sleep Foundation |
| Naps from about 4 months | 2–3 (some babies still take a late-afternoon catnap) | KidsHealth; Mayo Clinic |
| Dropping the third nap | Around 9 months | Mayo Clinic |
| Two naps to one | Usually 15–18 months; most by 18 months | Boys Town; KidsHealth |
| Stopping naps altogether | Under 2.5% before age 2; 94% by age 5 | Staton et al., 2020 meta-analysis |

## Baby nap chart: how many naps by age

| Age | Naps per day | Typical daytime sleep | Notes | Sources |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0–3 months | Many: 6 or more is common in the newborn weeks; 2–3 longer naps for many by 1–3 months | Varies widely; newborns sleep on and off around the clock | Naps follow feeds, not the clock | Sleep Foundation; KidsHealth (1–3 months) |
| 3–6 months | 2–3, sometimes a 4th short one | About 3–4 hours (4–7 months) | Each nap up to about 2 hours; 30–40 minute naps are common at 4–5 months | Pregnancy, Birth and Baby; KidsHealth; Tresillian |
| 6–12 months | 2, with a 3rd late-afternoon nap for some until around 9 months | 2–4 hours | Naps of 30 minutes to 2 hours both occur | Pregnancy, Birth and Baby; KidsHealth (8–12 months); Mayo Clinic |
| 12–18 months | 2 moving to 1 | Varies during the switch | Mixed one-nap and two-nap days are common | Boys Town; KidsHealth |
| 18 months–3 years | 1 | 1–2 hours | Usually after lunch | Pregnancy, Birth and Baby (after 12 months); Mayo Clinic |
| 3–5 years | 1 or none | Shrinking | Mayo Clinic: by age 5 most children have stopped napping | Mayo Clinic; Staton et al. |

*Note on app charts:* baby-sleep apps publish their own nap charts. For example, Huckleberry lists 4–5 naps at 3 months and 3–4 naps at 4–5 months, which is more than the 2–3 that KidsHealth and Pregnancy, Birth and Baby describe. Both pictures can be true for different babies; the clinical sources are the ones we use for the chart.

For a typical day at one specific age, see the month guides: [1](/1-month-old-sleep-schedule), [2](/2-month-old-sleep-schedule), [3](/3-month-old-sleep-schedule), [4](/4-month-old-sleep-schedule), [5](/5-month-old-sleep-schedule), [6](/6-month-old-sleep-schedule), [7](/7-month-old-sleep-schedule), [8](/8-month-old-sleep-schedule), [9](/9-month-old-sleep-schedule), [10](/10-month-old-sleep-schedule), [11](/11-month-old-sleep-schedule), [12](/12-month-old-sleep-schedule), and [15 months](/15-month-old-sleep-schedule).

## How long should baby naps be?

There is no single "right" nap length, and the sources describe a broad spread:

- **3–6 months:** Pregnancy, Birth and Baby says each nap lasts up to about 2 hours. Tresillian notes that at 4–5 months a sleep cycle is around 30–50 minutes, so waking after 30–40 minutes is very common.
- **8–12 months:** KidsHealth says some babies nap for 30 minutes while others nap for up to 2 hours.
- **Toddlers:** Pregnancy, Birth and Baby describes one nap of 1 to 2 hours after 12 months, and Mayo Clinic says most children still sleep 1–2 hours in the afternoon until about age 3.

Mayo Clinic suggests letting babies from 4 months to 1 year nap as long as they want, *unless* they then have trouble falling asleep at night. Late-day naps are usually the ones to trim.

## The 3 to 2 nap transition

**When:** Mayo Clinic suggests cutting out a late-afternoon third nap at about **9 months**, which helps bring bedtime earlier. As an app example, Huckleberry describes most babies finishing the 3-to-2 switch by 8 months.

**Signs your baby may be ready** (practical signs; no clinical body publishes a checklist):

- The third nap is refused or takes ages to start on most days.
- When it does happen, the third nap pushes bedtime uncomfortably late.
- Your baby copes well with the longer gap before bed on days the nap is skipped.

**How to make the switch:**

1. Let the first two naps run a little longer if your baby will take it.
2. On days without a third nap, bring bedtime earlier, even by 30–60 minutes, so the afternoon isn't too long.
3. Expect a messy week or two, with some three-nap days mixed in. That's part of the process.

Our [7 month old sleep schedule](/7-month-old-sleep-schedule) shows a three-nap and a two-nap day side by side.

## The 2 to 1 nap transition

**When:** Boys Town National Research Hospital describes **15–18 months** as the most common window, and KidsHealth says most toddlers are down to one nap by 18 months. Mayo Clinic gives an earlier picture, noting that babies 10–12 months old often drop the morning nap. Sources clearly differ here, so think of roughly 12–18 months as the range, with mid-toddlerhood being typical.

**What the switch usually looks like:** Boys Town describes gradually keeping a toddler awake longer in the morning, so that two naps (for example around 9:30 and 2:30) turn into a single midday nap closer to noon, often with lunch moving earlier. Toddlers who weren't quite ready may need an earlier bedtime or a slightly later morning wake-up for a while.

**Daycare tip:** Boys Town also points out that daycare nap times may not match your child's readiness exactly. Ask how the room handles toddlers who are mid-transition.

The [15 month old sleep schedule](/15-month-old-sleep-schedule) walks through the switch to one nap step by step.

## Example nap days by stage (examples only)

These show the *shape* of a day. Adjust every time to your child's wake-up time and cues.

**Around 6 months: three naps**

| Time | Sleep |
| --- | --- |
| 6:45 a.m. | Wake for the day |
| 9:00–10:15 a.m. | Nap 1 |
| 12:30–1:45 p.m. | Nap 2 |
| 4:15–4:45 p.m. | Short nap 3 |
| About 7:15 p.m. | Bedtime |

**Around 10 months: two naps**

| Time | Sleep |
| --- | --- |
| 6:30 a.m. | Wake |
| 9:15–10:30 a.m. | Morning nap |
| 2:00–3:15 p.m. | Afternoon nap |
| About 7:00 p.m. | Bedtime |

Mayo Clinic offers 9 a.m. and 1 p.m. as one starting point for babies aged 4 months to 1 year; the example above is a later variation.

**Around 18 months: one nap**

| Time | Sleep |
| --- | --- |
| 7:00 a.m. | Wake |
| About 12:30–2:15 p.m. | Midday nap |
| About 7:30 p.m. | Bedtime |

## Short naps and nap strikes: what to try

- **Under 6 months, short is common.** A 30–40 minute nap may simply be one sleep cycle (Tresillian). Offering an extra nap later in the day often works better than trying to stretch every nap.
- **Start the nap drowsy but awake.** KidsHealth recommends putting infants down sleepy but not yet asleep, so they learn to fall asleep on their own.
- **Keep a short, steady nap routine.** KidsHealth suggests soft music, dim lights, and a quiet story. Mayo Clinic says naps at about the same time each day tend to work best.
- **Light or dark room?** Advice varies. Mayo Clinic says a dark, quiet room can help babies sleep. Newcastle Hospitals NHS suggests avoiding long daytime naps in dark rooms, so babies learn that dark, quiet rooms are for night. A reasonable middle path is a dim (not blacked-out) room for naps, with the darkest setting saved for night.
- **A sudden nap strike** around a transition age often signals the next step, but check for illness, teething discomfort, or hunger first.

## What can make naps harder

- **Dropping a nap too early** because of one bad week. Short-lived refusals are common.
- **A very late final nap** that leaves your baby wide awake at bedtime.
- **Inconsistent places** for every nap, every day. Some flexibility is fine, but a predictable main nap spot helps.
- **Unsafe nap spots.** Naps count too: back to sleep, on a firm, flat surface with nothing loose in the crib. HealthyChildren.org (AAP) advises moving a baby who falls asleep in a car seat, swing, or carrier to a safe flat surface as soon as possible.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Bring it up if your baby is regularly very sleepy during the day despite good night sleep, snores or struggles to breathe when asleep, is suddenly much sleepier or harder to wake than usual, or isn't feeding or growing well. KidsHealth also suggests looking at bedtime and the nap schedule if a child seems tired, rubs their eyes, or acts out during the day.

## Frequently asked questions

**How many naps does a baby need?**  
It depends on age: many in the newborn weeks, usually 2–3 from about 4 months, 2 in the second half of the first year, and 1 for most toddlers by 18 months (Sleep Foundation; KidsHealth).

**When do babies go from 3 naps to 2?**  
Mayo Clinic suggests dropping the late-afternoon third nap at about 9 months.

**When do babies go from 2 naps to 1?**  
Most commonly at 15–18 months (Boys Town), with most toddlers on one nap by 18 months (KidsHealth).

**How long should a baby nap?**  
Anywhere from about 30 minutes to 2 hours is described as normal for infants. Toddlers typically take one nap of 1–2 hours.

**When do toddlers stop napping?**  
Fewer than 2.5% stop before age 2, and 94% have stopped by age 5, according to a 2020 meta-analysis.

**Should naps be at the same time every day?**  
Mayo Clinic says babies get the most out of naps taken at about the same time and length each day, though real days will vary.

## See the nap pattern, not just today (Yorix)

**Yorix** shows how your baby's naps change week to week, including nap count, total day sleep, and how the last nap affects bedtime. That makes it easier to spot when a nap transition is starting rather than guessing from one bad day. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)
- Month-by-month schedules: [newborn](/newborn-sleep-schedule) · [1 month](/1-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [2 months](/2-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [3 months](/3-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [4 months](/4-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [5 months](/5-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [6 months](/6-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [7 months](/7-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [8 months](/8-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [9 months](/9-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [10 months](/10-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [11 months](/11-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [12 months](/12-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [15 months](/15-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Sleep regressions by age](/sleep-regression)
- [Contact naps](/contact-naps)
- [Short naps](/short-naps)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026. App pages are used only as labeled examples.

1. Sleep Foundation. "Newborn Wake Windows: What's Normal by Age." Updated 13 October 2026. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/newborn-wake-windows>. Newborns may take six or more naps a day.
2. Nemours KidsHealth. "Naps." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/naps.html>. 2–3 naps from about 4 months; most toddlers down to one nap by 18 months; nap routine.
3. Nemours KidsHealth. "Infant Sleep: 1- to 3-Month-Olds." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleep13m.html>.
4. Nemours KidsHealth. "Baby Sleep: 4- to 7-Month-Olds." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleep47m.html>.
5. Nemours KidsHealth. "Baby Sleep: 8- to 12-Month-Olds." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleep812m.html>.
6. Mayo Clinic Staff. "Baby naps: Daytime sleep tips." 7 May 2025. <https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/infant-and-toddler-health/in-depth/baby-naps/art-20047421>.
