heading: The Ferber Method: Check-In Chart, Step-by-Step Plan, and When to Stop
description: The Ferber method step by step: the 7-night check-in interval chart, what to do on night wakings, the age to start, when to stop, and what research shows.
body:
# The Ferber Method: Check-In Chart, Step-by-Step Plan, and When to Stop

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** September 3, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

The Ferber method is one specific, structured way to sleep train. This page goes deep on that single method: the interval chart, exactly what a check-in looks like, how to handle 2 a.m. wakings, and the signs that it is not working. If you are still choosing between approaches, start with our [overview of sleep training methods](/sleep-training-methods-explained).

## Short answer

The **Ferber method** (also called graduated extinction, "Ferberizing," progressive waiting, or the interval method) means putting your baby down awake after a bedtime routine, leaving the room, and returning for **brief check-ins at gradually longer intervals**. Sleep Foundation describes check-ins of **under one to two minutes**, with no picking up or feeding, and says the method usually works **within a few nights to a week**. It suggests that **around 6 months** is a sensible starting age for many babies. If there is no improvement after **seven days**, Sleep Foundation (summarizing Dr. Ferber) advises stopping to rethink.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | Answer | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Usual starting age | Around 6 months, when many babies can self-soothe | Sleep Foundation |
| Length of a check-in | Under 1–2 minutes | Sleep Foundation |
| First wait, night 1 | 3 minutes | Sleep Foundation; Cleveland Clinic |
| Longest wait in the chart | 30 minutes (night 7) | Sleep Foundation |
| Typical time to work | A few nights to a week | Sleep Foundation |
| Stop and reassess if | No improvement after 7 days | Sleep Foundation |

## Who created it and what "graduated extinction" means

Pediatrician Richard Ferber popularized the method in a 1985 book, with a revised edition in 2006 (Sleep Foundation). Cleveland Clinic calls it the best-known form of graduated extinction. The aim is to help a baby stop associating falling asleep with a parent's presence.

It sits between two extremes. Full extinction ("cry it out") involves no check-ins at all. Gentler options keep a parent in the room. Ferber keeps a fixed structure but builds in regular reassurance visits.

## The Ferber check-in chart

These are the intervals published by Sleep Foundation, in minutes of waiting before each check-in.

| Night | First wait | Second wait | Third and later waits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 3 | 5 | 10 |
| 2 | 5 | 10 | 12 |
| 3 | 10 | 12 | 15 |
| 4 | 12 | 15 | 17 |
| 5 | 15 | 17 | 20 |
| 6 | 17 | 20 | 25 |
| 7 | 20 | 25 | 30 |

Two notes from the sources:

- **The numbers are flexible.** Both Sleep Foundation and Cleveland Clinic say Dr. Ferber accepted that families may adapt the times. Cleveland Clinic quotes a pediatrician whose families sometimes use 10, then 20, then 30 minutes.
- **The direction matters more than the exact minutes.** Waits should get longer within a night and from one night to the next.

## How to do the Ferber method: step by step

1. **Pick a start date with no big disruptions.** Avoid illness, travel, or a houseguest week.
2. **Agree on the plan with every adult who will do bedtime.** Write the chart down and keep a timer handy.
3. **Do a calm, predictable bedtime routine.** For example: bath, pajamas, milk, a book, a song.
4. **Put your baby in the crib awake.** Sleep Foundation stresses not letting them fall asleep in your arms or while feeding, since the goal is to fall asleep independently.
5. **Say goodnight and leave**, even if your baby starts to cry.
6. **Wait for the first interval** on the chart.
7. **Check in briefly.** Keep the lights off and your voice soft. You can pat or shush, but don't pick your baby up or feed them (Sleep Foundation; Cleveland Clinic).
8. **Leave again while they are still awake** and wait for the next, longer interval.
9. **Repeat until your baby falls asleep.** The next night, move one row down the chart.

## What to do when your baby wakes in the night

Sleep Foundation says that if your child falls asleep and then wakes later, you can **restart the intervals** for that night. Before starting the method, decide with your pediatrician whether your baby still needs a night feed. If they do, keep that feed and use the check-in pattern for other wakings.

Many parents choose a simple rule, for example: "a feed only if it has been at least X hours since the last one, otherwise check-ins." Agree on the number in advance so you are not deciding at 3 a.m.

## Right age for Ferber

- **Sleep Foundation:** around 6 months, because many babies can self-soothe and resettle by then.
- **Sleep Foundation's sleep training guide:** most babies are not ready before 4–6 months.
- **App example:** Huckleberry notes that Dr. Ferber's own lower limit is about 3–4 months, but suggests waiting until at least 6 months for this kind of method.

**Avoid it in the newborn months.** Mayo Clinic advises not leaving babies to cry alone in the first month. Ferber can also be adapted for older children, for example by making reassurance depend on staying in bed (Sleep Foundation). If you're weighing Ferber against leaving your baby without check-ins, see [the cry it out method](/cry-it-out-method).

## When the Ferber method is not a good fit

Sleep Foundation says behavioral methods like Ferber are not enough on their own for children with:

- heavy snoring, which may be a sign of a breathing disorder;
- neurodevelopmental conditions such as Down syndrome or autism spectrum disorder;
- sleep problems linked with medical, mental health, or unstable home circumstances.

Talk to your pediatrician first if any of these apply, or if your baby is unwell, has reflux symptoms, or has feeding or weight concerns.

## When to stop or pause

- **No improvement after 7 days:** stop and reassess (Sleep Foundation).
- **Illness, teething pain, or vomiting during crying:** pause and comfort your baby. Restart once they are well.
- **It feels unbearable for your family:** another method may fit better. Sleep Foundation lists the chair method, pick-up/put-down, no-cry approaches, full extinction, and scheduled awakenings as alternatives.

Expect a possible bump: Sleep Foundation describes "post-extinction bursts," where crying returns for a short time after it seemed to be over. It says these are normal and that consistency helps them pass.

## Does Ferber work, and is it harmful?

| Study | What was tested | Main finding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mindell et al., 2006 (AASM review, 52 studies) | Behavioral treatments for bedtime problems and night wakings | 94% of studies reported the treatments were effective; over 80% of children improved, with gains lasting 3–6 months; graduated extinction was among the supported methods |
| Gradisar et al., 2016 (randomized trial, 43 infants aged 6–16 months) | Graduated extinction vs bedtime fading vs sleep education | Both methods improved sleep compared with control, with no adverse stress responses and no effect on attachment or child emotions and behavior 12 months later |
| Price et al., 2012 (5-year follow-up, 225 families) | Behavioral sleep techniques used at 8–10 months | No evidence of differences in child mental health, stress, parent–child relationship, or maternal wellbeing at age 6 |

These studies support the method's safety for healthy, typically developing babies. They don't prove it is the best choice for every family.

## What can make it harder

- **Starting during a nap transition, illness, or travel.**
- **Going in "just this once" outside the plan.** Sleep Foundation warns that a single lapse may reinforce the need for a parent's presence.
- **Long, stimulating check-ins** with lights on, picking up, or feeding.
- **A late, overtired bedtime** or an afternoon nap that ended too close to bed.

## Frequently asked questions

**How long does the Ferber method take?**  
Sleep Foundation says it usually works within a few nights to a week.

**What age can you start the Ferber method?**  
Sleep Foundation suggests around 6 months. Don't use it for newborns.

**Can I pick up my baby during a check-in?**  
The standard method says no. Keep check-ins short, quiet, and hands-on only for a pat or a touch.

**What if my baby cries for longer than the chart allows?**  
Keep doing check-ins at the current interval for that night. If there is no improvement after a week, stop and reassess.

**Does the Ferber method work for naps?**  
The sources we checked describe it for bedtime and night wakings. Many families start with nights and leave naps more flexible.

**Is the Ferber method the same as cry it out?**  
No. Cry it out has no check-ins; Ferber adds timed reassurance visits (Cleveland Clinic).

## Track your Ferber week (Yorix)

**Yorix** can log bedtime, how long it took your baby to fall asleep, and each night waking, so you can see whether the week is moving in the right direction. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [Sleep training methods explained](/sleep-training-methods-explained)
- [10 month old sleep schedule](/10-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Surviving night wakings](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents)
- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)
- [Cry it out method](/cry-it-out-method)
- [When to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026. App pages are used only as labeled examples.

1. Sleep Foundation. "The Ferber Method for Sleep Training." Updated 15 July 2025. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/ferber-method>.
2. Cleveland Clinic. "What Is the Ferber Method of Sleep Training Your Baby?" 27 January 2025. <https://health.clevelandclinic.org/ferber-method>.
3. Sleep Foundation. "Sleep Training: What It Is, When to Start, and How to Do It." Updated 21 July 2025. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/sleep-training>.
4. Mayo Clinic Staff. "Baby naps: Daytime sleep tips." 7 May 2025. <https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/infant-and-toddler-health/in-depth/baby-naps/art-20047421>.
5. Mindell JA, et al. "Behavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children." *Sleep*, 2006. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17068979/> (abstract via Europe PMC).
6. Gradisar M, et al. "Behavioral Interventions for Infant Sleep Problems: A Randomized Controlled Trial." *Pediatrics*, 2016. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27221288/> (abstract via Europe PMC).
7. Price AM, et al. "Five-year follow-up of harms and benefits of behavioral infant sleep intervention: randomized trial." *Pediatrics*, 2012. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22966034/> (abstract via Europe PMC).
8. App example: Huckleberry. "Ferber Method for sleep training - What age to start?" Updated 15 October 2026. <https://huckleberrycare.com/blog/ferber-method-for-sleep-training-what-age-to-start>.

title: Newborn Sleep Schedule: What's Normal Week by Week | Yorix
heading: Newborn Sleep Schedule: What's Normal, Week by Week
description: Is there a newborn sleep schedule? What's normal in the first weeks, how many hours newborns sleep, feeding at night, day-night cues, and red flags to know.
body:
# Newborn Sleep Schedule: What's Normal, Week by Week

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** September 3, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

If you searched for a **newborn sleep schedule** at 3 a.m., here is the honest headline: in the first weeks there isn't one, and that is how it is supposed to be. What you *can* have is a loose rhythm (feed, a short awake time, sleep, repeat) and a sense of what's normal so you know when not to worry and when to call.

## Short answer

Newborns sleep in short pieces around the clock because hunger, not daylight, runs their day. Total daily sleep varies hugely: Sleep Foundation and Pregnancy, Birth and Baby give **11–19 hours**, while NHS pages describe anything from about 8 to 18 hours as normal. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine's sleep-duration recommendations start at 4 months, so there is no official target for newborns. Sleep Foundation says sleep may start to become more predictable around 2 months, and a clock-based routine usually comes later.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total sleep per day | 11–19 hours; NHS: about 8 up to 18 hours | Sleep Foundation; Pregnancy, Birth and Baby; NHS |
| Longest stretch | Often 1–2 hours at a time; rarely more than 3 hours | HealthyChildren.org (AAP); Newcastle Hospitals NHS |
| Feeds | Breastfed: often every 2 hours, 10–12 times a day; formula: every 2–3 hours, at least 8 a day | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |
| Awake time between sleeps | About 30 minutes to 1.5 hours | Sleep Foundation; Cleveland Clinic |
| Wet diapers after day 4–5 | At least 5–6 a day | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |

## Why newborns can't follow a sleep schedule yet

Three things make a fixed timetable impossible in the early weeks:

- **No body clock yet.** Newcastle Hospitals NHS explains that babies are born without a body clock and can't tell night from day; it develops over time. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby says a newborn's sleep responds to hunger and fullness rather than light and dark.
- **Tiny stomachs.** HealthyChildren.org (AAP) compares a newborn's stomach to the size of an egg, which is why small, frequent feeds are the norm.
- **Short sleep cycles.** A newborn's sleep cycle is about **45 to 60 minutes**, according to Pregnancy, Birth and Baby, so waking often is built in.

That's why parenting services advise following your baby's cues for now rather than the clock.

## How much do newborns sleep? Why every source gives a different number

| Source | Newborn total sleep per 24 hours |
| --- | --- |
| Sleep Foundation (newborn schedule page) | 11–19 hours |
| Pregnancy, Birth and Baby (birth to 3 months) | 11–19 hours |
| KidsHealth (citing the National Sleep Foundation) | 14–17 hours; some newborns up to 18–19 |
| HealthyChildren.org (AAP) | About 16–17 hours, often only 1–2 hours at a time |
| Mayo Clinic (first month) | About 16 hours |
| Derbyshire NHS | Commonly 16–18 hours until around 4 months |
| NHS Best Start in Life | Around 8 hours for some newborns, up to around 18 for others; both normal |
| Newcastle Hospitals NHS | 8 to 20 hours in the first few months |

The spread is not a mistake. Some figures are averages, some are "recommended" ranges, and some are the extremes seen in healthy babies. The practical message is the same everywhere: a wide range is normal, and **how your baby feeds, grows, and behaves when awake tells you more than the total**.

## Newborn sleep week by week (what to expect)

Every baby moves at their own pace. Use these stages as rough landmarks, not deadlines.

**Weeks 1–2: feeding drives everything.** Expect frequent waking. The Sydney Children's Hospitals Network says a baby in the first weeks may wake as often as every 40 minutes and need a feed every 2 to 3 hours overnight. KidsHealth advises waking a newborn who sleeps for long stretches every 3–4 hours to feed until they show good weight gain, which usually happens within the first couple of weeks. Follow your own pediatrician's advice on this.

**Weeks 3–6: a little more awake.** Short alert periods appear, often after feeds. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby says the circadian rhythm starts to develop at around **4 to 6 weeks**, so your baby begins to respond more to light and dark. Day-night confusion (long daytime sleeps, wakeful nights) is common now.

**Weeks 6–9: patterns start to show.** Sleep Foundation explains that at about **8 to 9 weeks**, the release of melatonin and cortisol starts following a daily rhythm. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby notes that some babies begin sleeping for longer periods at around 8 weeks.

**Weeks 9–12: longer night stretches for some.** Newcastle Hospitals NHS says that by 3 months some babies skip a night feed and sleep around 5 hours at a time. The Sydney Children's Hospitals Network says many babies around 3 months stay awake longer in the day and sleep longer at night. Others take longer, and that is normal too.

## A flexible newborn day (example only)

Instead of clock times, think in loops. One loop is roughly: **feed → short awake time → sleep**. A newborn might repeat it 8–12 times in 24 hours.

| Part of the loop | What it might look like | Tip |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Feed | Breast or bottle when you see early hunger cues | HealthyChildren.org: crying is a late hunger sign |
| Awake | A diaper change, a cuddle, a few minutes of face time or tummy time | Often just 30–60 minutes, feed included |
| Wind down | Dim the room, hold close, swaddle if your baby isn't trying to roll | Keep it short; newborns tire fast |
| Sleep | On the back, in a bassinet or crib | Anywhere from a short catnap to a few hours |

*Example of a single morning (illustration only):* 7:10 feed, 7:40 diaper and a chat, 8:00 asleep in the bassinet, 9:40 awake and hungry, and the loop starts again. Tomorrow will look different, and that's fine.

## Helping your newborn tell day from night

You can't speed up the body clock, but you can give it clear signals. NHS advice:

- **Daytime:** open curtains, play and talk, and don't worry about everyday household noise while your baby naps.
- **Night-time:** keep lights low, talk little, change diapers only when needed, and put your baby down as soon as they've been fed and changed.

KidsHealth adds that it can take a few weeks for a baby's brain to learn the difference, and that there are no tricks to hurry it.

Newcastle Hospitals NHS suggests that daylight and outdoor time in the day help, and that starting the day at a similar time each morning can support the body clock over a couple of weeks.

## What's normal in newborn sleep (and looks scary but usually isn't)

- **Noisy, twitchy sleep.** Babies spend more of their sleep in active (REM-like) sleep. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby says they may breathe shallowly, twitch, flutter their eyes, and make noises.
- **Falling asleep at the breast or bottle.** NHS calls this common in the early weeks; you can keep feeding until your baby is done.
- **Only sleeping when held.** Tresillian describes this as normal behavior in the early weeks. You can hold your baby while you are awake and alert, then move them to their own flat, clear sleep space.
- **Waking every 1–3 hours.** Pregnancy, Birth and Baby says a baby this age may wake after one or two sleep cycles, so every 1 to 3 hours.

## Safe sleep in the newborn weeks

The AAP's guidance, explained on HealthyChildren.org:

- **Back to sleep** for every nap and night.
- **A firm, flat surface** with only a fitted sheet. No pillows, bumpers, quilts, or soft toys.
- **Room-share without bed-sharing**, ideally for at least the first 6 months. HealthyChildren.org says this can lower SIDS risk by as much as 50%. NHS also advises keeping your baby in your room for at least the first 6 months, day and night.
- **Not too warm:** dress your baby in about one layer more than you'd wear.
- **Swaddling** is optional; stop once your baby tries to roll, and never use weighted swaddles or blankets.
- **Pacifiers:** HealthyChildren.org suggests waiting until breastfeeding is established, around 3 to 4 weeks, before offering one.

If your baby falls asleep in a car seat, swing, or carrier, move them to a flat sleep surface as soon as you can.

## Red flags: when sleepiness is not normal

Newborns are sleepy, but there's a difference between sleepy and hard to rouse. HealthyChildren.org (AAP) advises seeking medical help right away if a newborn seems increasingly sleepy, unresponsive, or hard to wake.

**Call emergency services (911 in the US)** if your baby can't be woken, is very weak or floppy, grunts or moans with each breath, or has bluish or gray lips, tongue, or face (HealthyChildren.org symptom checker).

**Call your doctor now** if your newborn has to be woken for every feed or can't finish feeds, is sleeping much more than usual, has a fever while under 12 weeks old (don't give fever medicine before being seen), or looks or acts abnormal in any way (HealthyChildren.org symptom checker). Fewer wet diapers than expected (fewer than 5–6 a day after the first 4–5 days, per HealthyChildren.org) is another reason to call.

## Looking after yourself in the newborn weeks

NHS advice for parents is practical: sleep when your baby sleeps, share night duties with a partner if you can, and accept help from friends or family. If you are formula feeding, a partner can take some feeds; if you are breastfeeding, they can take over early-morning changes. Newcastle Hospitals NHS suggests going to bed early to make the most of your baby's longest stretch at the start of the night. If you feel unable to cope, speak to your doctor, midwife, or health visitor.

## Frequently asked questions

**Can I put my newborn on a sleep schedule?**  
Not in the first weeks. Sleep Foundation says newborns don't follow a predictable schedule for roughly the first two months. A loose feed–awake–sleep loop works better.

**How many hours should a newborn sleep?**  
There's no official target. Published figures range from about 11 to 19 hours, and NHS pages call totals from around 8 to 18 hours normal.

**Should I wake my newborn to feed?**  
In the early weeks, often yes. KidsHealth suggests feeding every 3–4 hours until good weight gain is established. Ask your pediatrician what applies to your baby.

**Why does my newborn sleep all day and stay awake at night?**  
Their body clock isn't working yet. Bright, normal days and quiet, dim nights help it develop over the first weeks.

**When will my baby sleep longer at night?**  
Some babies manage around 5-hour stretches by about 3 months (Newcastle Hospitals NHS). Many take longer.

**My newborn only sleeps on me. Is that normal?**  
Very common in the early weeks (Tresillian). Hold your baby while you are awake, and move them to their own safe sleep space before you sleep.

## Keep track without keeping it in your head (Yorix)

**Yorix** keeps feeds, diapers, and sleep in one timeline both parents can see, so nobody has to remember which side was last or when the last wet diaper happened. As patterns appear in the weeks ahead, it suggests the next sleep window. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [1 month old sleep schedule](/1-month-old-sleep-schedule) (a closer look at weeks 4–7)
- [2 month old sleep schedule](/2-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)
- [Baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age)
- [3 month old sleep schedule](/3-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Baby feeding schedule](/baby-feeding-schedule)
- [Sleep regressions by age](/sleep-regression)
- [Dream feed](/dream-feed)
- [Newborn grunting in sleep](/newborn-grunting-in-sleep)

body:
# Sleep Training Methods Explained: A Side-by-Side Comparison

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** September 3, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

"Sleep training" covers a family of approaches, not one technique. They differ in how much crying is involved, how close the parent stays, and how quickly families tend to see change. This guide lays them out together, so you can choose the one that fits your baby's temperament and your own limits.

## Short answer

Sleep training means helping a baby learn to fall asleep and resettle without being fed, rocked, or held all the way to sleep. Sleep Foundation says most babies are **not ready before 4–6 months**, and many families start around 6 months. In a review of 52 studies for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, behavioral approaches were reported effective in **94% of studies**, with over 80% of children improving. Follow-up trials found **no evidence of harm** to emotions, behavior, stress, or attachment. No single method is "best": the right one is the approach you can carry out consistently.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | Answer | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Earliest readiness | Usually 4–6 months | Sleep Foundation |
| A common start time | Around 6 months; some wait until 9 months | Sleep Foundation |
| Studies reporting benefit | 94% of 52 studies | Mindell et al., 2006 (AASM) |
| Children who improved | Over 80%, maintained for 3–6 months | Mindell et al., 2006 |
| Long-term follow-up | No differences in harms or benefits at age 6 | Price et al., 2012 |

## Is your baby ready?

Sleep Foundation suggests looking for these signs:

- Your baby is **at least 4–6 months old** (before this, the circadian rhythm that supports longer sleep is still forming).
- Your baby **sometimes falls asleep on their own** at bedtime, even if they still wake later.
- Your pediatrician has no concerns about **growth, feeding, or health**.

Sleep Foundation notes that some families wait until **9 months**, when most babies no longer need to feed at night. Ask your pediatrician whether your baby still needs a night feed before you begin, and build any feeds into the plan. For age-by-age readiness and self-soothing, see our full guide on [when to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training).

## Sleep training methods at a glance

| Method | Also called | Parent's role | Crying | How fast | Research support |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Extinction | Cry it out (CIO), full extinction | Leaves after bedtime and doesn't return until morning (except for safety or illness) | Most, for a short time | Often fastest | Strong support (AASM review) |
| Graduated extinction | Ferber method, interval method, progressive waiting | Brief check-ins at lengthening intervals | Moderate | A few nights to a week | Supported (AASM review; 2016 and 2012 trials) |
| Check and console | Variation of Ferber | Checks in before crying builds, then stretches the gaps to about 15 minutes | Less | Up to a week | Variant of graduated extinction |
| Chair method / fading | Camping out | Sits by the crib, moves a little farther away each night | Some, with the parent in sight | Slower | Limited direct trials |
| Pick up / put down | — | Picks up to calm, puts down drowsy, repeats | Less | Slow, demanding for parents | Limited direct trials |
| Bedtime fading | — | Temporarily moves bedtime later, then 15 minutes earlier every few days | Minimal if done correctly | Gradual | Supported (AASM review; 2016 trial) |
| No-cry / gentle | Gentle sleep training | Consistent routine, quick responses, slow changes to sleep associations | Least | Slowest | Limited direct trials |

Sources: Sleep Foundation (sleep training and Ferber guides), Cleveland Clinic, KidsHealth New Zealand (bedtime fading), Mindell et al. 2006, Gradisar et al. 2016, Price et al. 2012. "Limited direct trials" means we found no trial of that method in the sources we checked, not that it fails to work.

## Each method in more detail

### Extinction (cry it out)

After a calm bedtime routine and a goodnight cuddle, the parent leaves and doesn't go back for crying. Sleep Foundation says supporters find it works quickly, while many parents find it very hard to listen to. In the AASM review, unmodified extinction had strong evidence behind it. Always go in if your baby may be sick, hurt, or unsafe. Our [cry it out guide](/cry-it-out-method) covers the age limits, newborns, the stress-hormone and attachment studies, and the "fuss it out" variation.

### Graduated extinction (Ferber)

This is the most familiar middle path. You leave the room and return for very short, calm check-ins, waiting a little longer each time and a little longer each night. Sleep Foundation recommends check-ins of under one to two minutes, without picking up or feeding. The full 7-night interval chart, plus what to do with night wakings, is in our dedicated [Ferber method guide](/ferber-method-baby-sleep).

### Check and console

A softer version of Ferber. In Sleep Foundation's description, the parent leaves and comes back after a minute or two to offer a few loving words or a light pat, before crying escalates. The gaps then grow to around 15 minutes. It can take up to a week and demands more of parents. Some babies get more upset with each visit, and if that happens, Sleep Foundation suggests another method may suit better.

### Chair method (fading, camping out)

The parent stays in the room, first standing or sitting beside the crib, then moving a little farther away each night until they are outside the door. Sleep Foundation notes that crying is still common, that some parents find it harder because they can see their baby, and that it usually takes longer than CIO or Ferber.

### Pick up / put down

Place your baby down drowsy but awake. If they cry, pick them up to calm them, then lay them down again before they fall asleep, and repeat as needed. Sleep Foundation says it suits babies of about 4–8 months best and requires a lot of patience.

### Bedtime fading

This method works on timing rather than on crying. KidsHealth New Zealand describes starting with a temporary bedtime close to when your child usually falls asleep, then, once they fall asleep quickly, moving bedtime 15 minutes earlier every few days. In the 2016 randomized trial by Gradisar and colleagues, bedtime fading improved sleep compared with a control group, as did graduated extinction.

### No-cry or gentle methods

These lean heavily on a consistent routine and on slowly changing how your baby falls asleep, such as feeding or rocking a little less each night. Sleep Foundation says they are less stressful but take longer, and that parents may lose more sleep along the way.

## What the research says about safety

Concerns about crying and attachment are common and reasonable. The studies we checked found:

- **AASM task force review (2006):** across 52 studies, behavioral treatments produced reliable, lasting improvements in bedtime problems and night waking.
- **Randomized trial (2016):** in 43 babies aged 6–16 months, neither graduated extinction nor bedtime fading caused adverse stress responses, and there were no effects on attachment, emotions, or behavior a year later.
- **Five-year follow-up (2012):** in 225 families, children whose parents learned sleep techniques at 8–10 months were no different at age 6 from other children on mental health, stress, closeness to parents, or maternal depression.

These findings apply to healthy, typically developing babies. Sleep Foundation adds that behavioral methods alone are not enough for children with breathing problems such as heavy snoring, or for some neurodevelopmental conditions.

## How to choose a method

| If this sounds like you | Consider |
| --- | --- |
| You want the quickest change and can tolerate crying | Extinction or Ferber |
| You need to see your baby is OK during crying | Ferber or check and console |
| You want to stay in the room | Chair method |
| Your baby fights bedtime but sleeps fine once asleep | Bedtime fading |
| You'd rather go slowly with as little crying as possible | Pick up / put down or a no-cry approach |

## Before you start: a short checklist

1. **Health first.** No illness, ear pain, or feeding concerns. Check with your pediatrician if unsure.
2. **A predictable routine.** Sleep Foundation calls the bedtime routine a key part of every method.
3. **A sensible schedule.** An overtired baby will find any method harder. Our [wake windows guide](/wake-windows-by-age) can help.
4. **Everyone agrees.** All caregivers use the same responses.
5. **The right week.** Avoid travel, a new childcare setting, or a nap transition.
6. **Safe sleep basics.** Back to sleep, a bare crib, and room-sharing without bed-sharing (HealthyChildren.org / AAP).

## What can make sleep training harder

- **Inconsistency,** such as rocking to sleep on some nights and not others.
- **Starting too young,** before about 4–6 months.
- **Switching methods every few nights** before any one has had a fair trial.
- **Ignoring signs of illness or pain** during crying.

Sleep Foundation also reminds parents that rough nights happen, especially with travel, illness, or teething, and that keeping a sleep diary can help you stay on track.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Talk to your pediatrician before starting if your baby was premature, has a medical condition, snores loudly, or has feeding or weight concerns. Also check in if a method isn't helping after a fair trial, or if you are feeling low, hopeless, or unable to cope.

## Frequently asked questions

**What age can you start sleep training?**  
Sleep Foundation says most babies aren't ready before 4–6 months.

**Which sleep training method is best?**  
None is best for everyone. Extinction and graduated extinction have the strongest research base; gentler methods take longer but involve less crying.

**Does sleep training harm attachment?**  
Studies we checked found no harm to attachment, stress, emotions, or behavior, including at a five-year follow-up.

**How long does sleep training take?**  
It depends on the method. Ferber often works within a week (Sleep Foundation); chair, pick up/put down, and no-cry methods usually take longer.

**Do you have to sleep train?**  
No. Sleep Foundation notes that some babies learn to sleep through without formal training.

**Can I sleep train for naps too?**  
Many families start with bedtime and nights first, then apply the same responses to naps once nights improve.

## See whether it's working (Yorix)

**Yorix** logs bedtimes, how long settling takes, and night wakings, so you can compare week one with week two instead of relying on memory. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [The Ferber method: chart and steps](/ferber-method-baby-sleep)
- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)
- [5 month old sleep schedule](/5-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [10 month old sleep schedule](/10-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Surviving night wakings](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents)
- [Cry it out method: age and research](/cry-it-out-method)
- [When to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

2. Sleep Foundation. "The Ferber Method for Sleep Training." Updated 15 July 2025. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/ferber-method>.
3. Cleveland Clinic. "What Is the Ferber Method of Sleep Training Your Baby?" 27 January 2025. <https://health.clevelandclinic.org/ferber-method>.
4. KidsHealth New Zealand. "Bedtime Fading For Managing Sleep Problems." <https://www.kidshealth.org.nz/bedtime-fading-for-managing-sleep-problems>.
5. Mindell JA, et al. "Behavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children." *Sleep*, 2006. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17068979/> (abstract via Europe PMC).
6. Gradisar M, et al. "Behavioral Interventions for Infant Sleep Problems: A Randomized Controlled Trial." *Pediatrics*, 2016. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27221288/> (abstract via Europe PMC).
7. Price AM, et al. "Five-year follow-up of harms and benefits of behavioral infant sleep intervention: randomized trial." *Pediatrics*, 2012. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22966034/> (abstract via Europe PMC).
8. HealthyChildren.org / AAP. "How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby Safe: AAP Policy Explained." Last updated 11 September 2026. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/A-Parents-Guide-to-Safe-Sleep.aspx>.

description: Why babies wake at night, what's normal by age, hunger vs comfort, safe sleep when you're exhausted, sharing the night shift, and when parents need help.
body:
# Baby Waking at Night: How to Get Through It (and Look After Yourself)

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** September 3, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

At 3 a.m., advice about "drowsy but awake" can feel like it was written for someone else. This guide is for the parent who is up again: what is normal at each age, how to tell hunger from a need for comfort, how to stay safe when you are exhausted, and how to protect your own sleep and mental health. It combines our earlier pages on night wakings and on parent stress.

## Short answer

Night waking is normal for babies. HealthyChildren.org (AAP) says newborns may wake **as often as every one or two hours**, and two NHS services describe most babies **not settling all night, every night, until about their first birthday**. In a Lullaby Trust survey quoted by the NHS, **59% of parents of babies under 12 months** said their baby slept less than 4 hours at a time. What helps most is a quick, calm, dim response; a sleep space that stays safe even when you are half asleep; shared night duties; and getting help early if you feel low or unable to cope.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How often newborns wake | As often as every 1–2 hours | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |
| Babies sleeping under 4 hours at a time | 59% of parents of babies under 12 months reported this | Lullaby Trust survey, via NHS |
| When waking often comes back | Around 4–5 months and again 8–9 months | Newcastle Hospitals NHS; Derbyshire NHS |
| Settled all night, every night | Usually not before about 1 year | Newcastle Hospitals NHS; Derbyshire NHS |
| Baby blues | Usually pass within 2 weeks of birth | NHS |

## What's normal: night waking by age

| Age | What many babies do at night | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0–3 months | Wake every 1–3 hours, mainly to feed | Pregnancy, Birth and Baby; HealthyChildren.org |
| Around 3 months | Some manage a stretch of about 5 hours | Newcastle Hospitals NHS; Derbyshire NHS |
| 3–6 months | Some sleep 5–8 hours or longer, but not all | NHS |
| 4–5 months | Waking often increases again | Newcastle Hospitals NHS; Derbyshire NHS |
| By 6 months | Most sleep 9 hours or more at night, with brief awakenings | KidsHealth |
| 8–9 months | More waking again for some babies | Newcastle Hospitals NHS; Derbyshire NHS |
| About 12 months | Many are settled most nights, though plenty still wake | Newcastle Hospitals NHS |

If your baby wakes more than this table suggests, it doesn't automatically mean something is wrong. Ranges are wide. It is worth checking the daytime schedule, though: our [wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age) chart can help.

## Hunger or comfort?

HealthyChildren.org says babies suck for comfort as well as hunger, and that it can be hard at first to tell the difference. Sometimes a baby just needs a cuddle or a diaper change.

| More likely hunger | More likely comfort or something else |
| --- | --- |
| Rooting, lip-licking, hands to mouth, opening mouth (HealthyChildren.org) | Settles quickly with a pat, a voice, or being held |
| A long gap since the last feed | Woke soon after a full feed |
| Feeds actively and then relaxes | Sucks briefly, then dozes |
| Newborn weeks, or a growth spurt | Older baby with the same waking time every night |

HealthyChildren.org also says crying is a **late** hunger sign. In the early months, feeding on demand is recommended for most healthy, full-term babies. Whether an older baby still needs a night feed is a question for your pediatrician, as it depends on growth and feeding.

## Getting through a night waking

### Respond early and keep it boring

Newcastle Hospitals NHS suggests going to your baby as soon as you can so they don't become very upset, because a distressed baby takes longer to settle. Keep lights low and the room quiet. HealthyChildren.org adds that night feeds should not be playtime.

### Try a calm sequence of soothing

HealthyChildren.org suggests building up slowly when your baby cries: look at them first, then use your voice softly, and only then move on to a pacifier, a light touch, or picking them up, pausing between steps.

### Put your baby back down before they're deeply asleep

HealthyChildren.org says babies who are held or rocked all the way to sleep may struggle to get back to sleep when they wake. Laying them down a little awake gives them practice.

### Decide on the plan before night falls

Agree in daylight what you will do at each waking: who goes, whether to feed, how long to try settling. Fewer decisions at 3 a.m. means less stress.

## Safe sleep when you're exhausted

Tired parents are more likely to fall asleep holding their baby. HealthyChildren.org warns that sleeping with a baby on a bed, sofa, or armchair raises the risk of sudden unexpected infant death, and recommends:

- **Avoid feeding on a couch or armchair.**
- **Clear the area of pillows and bedding** if you think you might doze off.
- **Use tools to stay awake:** a snack and water, a podcast, an alarm every few minutes, or another adult nearby while you feed.
- **If you do fall asleep while feeding,** move your baby onto their back in their own crib or bassinet as soon as you wake.
- **Keep the crib bare and place your baby on their back** for every sleep.

## Protecting your own sleep

The NHS and HealthyChildren.org offer practical ideas:

- **Rest when your baby sleeps**, even if the chores wait. Set an alarm if you worry about oversleeping (NHS).
- **Go to bed soon after the last evening feed** (HealthyChildren.org).
- **Split the night.** If you formula feed, a partner can share feeds. If you breastfeed, they can take nappy changes and early mornings, and once feeding is established, sometimes give expressed milk (NHS).
- **Ask friends or relatives** to watch the baby while you nap, or to stay for a few days if you are on your own (NHS).
- **Get outside daily.** The NHS notes that regular exercise, even a short walk with the pram, can help you feel less tired.

## Parent stress and mental health

Feeling exhausted and overwhelmed is common. HealthyChildren.org says caring for a new baby is one of the hardest things you'll do. But exhaustion can also hide something that needs treatment.

The NHS lists symptoms of postnatal depression including:

- finding it hard to enjoy anything;
- feeling hopeless, guilty, or unable to cope;
- constant worry or anxiety;
- **trouble sleeping even when you have the chance to rest**;
- difficulty bonding with your baby;
- thoughts of harming yourself or your baby.

The "baby blues" usually pass within two weeks of birth. If low mood lasts longer, gets worse, or you're struggling, the NHS says to speak to your GP, midwife, or health visitor, even if you have only some of the signs. Symptoms can start up to a year after birth, and partners can be affected too. Treatment helps.

### Where to get help

- **United States:** National Maternal Mental Health Hotline, **1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262)**: call or text, free, confidential, 24/7 (HRSA). It is not a crisis line. **In a crisis, call or text 988; in an emergency, call 911.**
- **United Kingdom:** your GP, midwife, or health visitor; Samaritans on **116 123** (NHS). In England, you can refer yourself to NHS talking therapies.
- **Anywhere:** if you feel you might harm yourself or your baby, put your baby somewhere safe, such as their crib, and call emergency services.

## What can make night wakings worse

- **A day with too little sleep.** KidsHealth notes that overtired babies often sleep worse at night.
- **A late last nap** that leaves your baby not tired enough at bedtime.
- **Bright lights, screens, and play** during night feeds.
- **A different response every night,** so your baby can't predict what happens.
- **Illness, teething, or a growth spurt.** These usually pass. See a doctor if your baby seems unwell.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Call your pediatrician if your baby has a fever (urgently if under 12 weeks), seems unusually sleepy or hard to wake, is feeding poorly or having fewer wet diapers, breathes with effort or pauses in breathing, snores loudly, or cries inconsolably in a way that is new. Mention night waking at checkups too, especially if it is wearing you down.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is it normal for my baby to wake every 2 hours?**  
In the newborn months, yes: HealthyChildren.org says newborns may wake every 1–2 hours. In older babies, check daytime sleep and settling habits, and ask your pediatrician if you are worried.

**When do babies stop waking at night?**  
Many babies still wake in their first year. Two NHS services say most are about 1 year old before they settle all night, every night.

**How do I know if my baby is hungry at night or wants comfort?**  
Look for early hunger cues such as rooting and hands to mouth, and consider the time since the last feed. Babies also suck for comfort (HealthyChildren.org).

**How can I cope with sleep deprivation as a new parent?**  
Rest when your baby sleeps, share the night with a partner or helper, go to bed early, and ask for help (NHS; HealthyChildren.org).

**When is tiredness a sign of postnatal depression?**  
If you can't sleep even when your baby sleeps, or you feel hopeless or unable to cope, speak to a doctor (NHS).

## Nights, made a little more predictable (Yorix)

**Yorix** records every night waking and feed, so you can spot patterns (for example, wakings that cluster after a late nap) and share the log with a partner who takes the next shift. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)
- [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule)
- [Sleep training methods explained](/sleep-training-methods-explained)
- [Baby feeding schedule by age](/baby-feeding-schedule)
- [White noise for baby sleep](/white-noise-for-baby-sleep)
- [Baby waking every hour](/baby-waking-every-hour)
- [Split nights](/split-nights)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. HealthyChildren.org / AAP. "Safe Sleep Tips for Sleep-Deprived New Parents." Last updated 13 September 2026. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/Safe-Sleep-Tips-for-Sleep-Deprived-Parents.aspx>.
2. HealthyChildren.org / AAP. "How Often and How Much Should Your Baby Eat?" Last updated 2 April 2024. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/feeding-nutrition/Pages/How-Often-and-How-Much-Should-Your-Baby-Eat.aspx>.
3. HealthyChildren.org / AAP. "Getting Your Baby to Sleep." Last updated 4 June 2024. <https://www.healthychildren.org/english/ages-stages/baby/sleep/pages/getting-your-baby-to-sleep.aspx>.
4. HealthyChildren.org symptom checker. "Newborn Illness – How to Recognize." <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/tips-tools/symptom-checker/Pages/symptomviewer.aspx?symptom=Newborn+Illness+-+How+to+Recognize>.
5. NHS Best Start in Life. "Your baby's sleep patterns" (Lullaby Trust survey). <https://www.nhs.uk/best-start-in-life/baby/baby-basics/newborn-and-baby-sleeping-advice-for-parents/your-babys-sleep-patterns/>.
6. NHS. "Helping your baby to sleep." <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/caring-for-a-newborn/helping-your-baby-to-sleep/>.
7. NHS. "Sleep and tiredness after having a baby." <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/support-and-services/sleep-and-tiredness-after-having-a-baby/>.
8. NHS. "Postnatal depression: overview." <https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/conditions/post-natal-depression/overview/>.
9. Newcastle Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust. "Sleep (infants 0–12 months)." <https://www.newcastle-hospitals.nhs.uk/services/great-north-childrens-hospital/childrens-sleep-service/sleep-infants-0-12-months/>.
10. Derbyshire Community Health Services NHS. "How much will my baby sleep in their first year?" <https://derbyshirefamilyhealthservice.nhs.uk/our-services/0-5-years/your-babys-first-year/sleep>.
11. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby (Australian Government). "Baby sleep patterns by age." Last reviewed May 2025. <https://www.pregnancybirthbaby.org.au/babies/sleep-and-settling/sleep-patterns-for-babies>.
12. Nemours KidsHealth. "Baby Sleep: 4- to 7-Month-Olds." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleep47m.html>.
13. Nemours KidsHealth. "Sleep and Your Newborn." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleepnewborn.html>.
14. HRSA Maternal and Child Health Bureau. "National Maternal Mental Health Hotline: FAQ." Last reviewed November 2023. <https://mchb.hrsa.gov/national-maternal-mental-health-hotline/faq>.

body:
# Wake Windows by Age: A Chart From Newborn to 12 Months

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** September 3, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

A **wake window** is simply the stretch of time your baby spends awake between one sleep and the next. Parents look up **wake windows by age** because timing a nap a little too early or too late can turn an easy settle into a long one. Below you will find the published ranges side by side, why they disagree, and a simple way to work out your own baby's number.

## Short answer

Wake windows grow from well under two hours in the first weeks to several hours by the end of the first year. Sleep Foundation gives **0.5 to 1.5 hours for 0–1 month** and **1 to 3 hours for 1–4 months**; Cleveland Clinic gives **0.5 to 1 hour from birth to 1 month** and **3 to 6 hours at 10–12 months**. These are rough guides from clinicians and health writers, not an official standard: we found no wake-window table from the AAP or the AASM. Your baby's tired cues should win whenever the clock and the baby disagree.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Newborn wake windows (0–1 month) | 0.5–1.5 hours / 0.5–1 hour | Sleep Foundation / Cleveland Clinic |
| Around 3–4 months | 1–3 hours (1–4 months) / 1.25–2.5 hours (3–4 months) | Sleep Foundation / Cleveland Clinic |
| 10–12 months | 3–7.5 hours / 3–6 hours | Sleep Foundation / Cleveland Clinic |
| Total sleep, 4–12 months | 12–16 hours per 24 hours, naps included | AASM (endorsed by the AAP) |

## Wake windows by age: the chart

Two medically reviewed or clinician-quoted sources publish a full table. They overlap, but not perfectly, so we show both rather than inventing a single "right" number.

| Baby's age | Sleep Foundation | Cleveland Clinic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0–1 month | 0.5–1.5 hours | 0.5–1 hour |
| 1–3 months | 1–3 hours (listed as 1–4 months) | 1–2 hours |
| 3–4 months | 1–3 hours (listed as 1–4 months) | 1.25–2.5 hours |
| 5–7 months | 1.5–4.5 hours | 2–4 hours |
| 7–10 months | 1.5–6 hours | 2.5–4.5 hours |
| 10–12 months | 3–7.5 hours | 3–6 hours |

**How to read this chart.** The upper ends are very wide on purpose. A 9-month-old who is happy after five hours awake is inside Sleep Foundation's range; another who melts down at three hours is still normal. Start near the lower end for your baby's age and move up only if your baby keeps resisting sleep.

**Want one age in detail?** Each of our month guides has its own wake-window section with an example day: [1 month (incl. 4 weeks)](/1-month-old-sleep-schedule), [2 months](/2-month-old-sleep-schedule), [3 months](/3-month-old-sleep-schedule), [4 months](/4-month-old-sleep-schedule), [5 months](/5-month-old-sleep-schedule), [6 months](/6-month-old-sleep-schedule), [7 months](/7-month-old-sleep-schedule), [8 months](/8-month-old-sleep-schedule), [9 months](/9-month-old-sleep-schedule), [10 months](/10-month-old-sleep-schedule), [11 months](/11-month-old-sleep-schedule), [12 months](/12-month-old-sleep-schedule), and [15 months](/15-month-old-sleep-schedule).

## Why wake-window numbers differ between sources

You will see different figures on almost every site, and that is not because one of them is wrong. A few reasons:

- **No formal guideline exists.** The AASM recommends total daily sleep (12–16 hours for 4–12 months), not how long a baby should stay awake between sleeps. Wake-window charts come from clinical experience and are summaries, not research cut-offs.
- **Age bands are drawn differently.** Sleep Foundation groups 1 to 4 months together; Cleveland Clinic splits that into two bands.
- **Days are uneven.** Sleep Foundation notes that a baby's wake windows can change from one day to the next, and Cleveland Clinic says they can even vary from one nap to the next.

Baby-app makers publish their own charts too. These are useful as examples of how others apply the idea, but they are not clinical sources (see the next table).

## Wake windows at 3, 4, 5, and 6 months

This is the age when most parents start thinking in wake windows, and when the published numbers diverge the most. The first two columns are clinical sources; the last two are **app examples only**, included so you can see the spread.

| Age | Cleveland Clinic | Sleep Foundation | Huckleberry (app example) | Napper (app example) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3 months | 1–2 h (1–3 mo) or 1.25–2.5 h (3–4 mo) | 1–3 h | 1–2 h | 75–120 min |
| 4 months | 1.25–2.5 h | 1–3 h | 1.5–2.5 h | 75–120 min |
| 5 months | 2–4 h | 1.5–4.5 h | 1.5–2.5 h | 2–3 h |
| 6 months | 2–4 h | 1.5–4.5 h | 2–3 h | 2–3 h |

What this tells you in practice: at 3–4 months, roughly one to two and a half hours is where all four overlap. By 6 months, two to three hours is the shared middle. If your baby sits outside that middle but is feeding well, growing, and mostly content, there is no reason to force the number.

## Newborn wake windows (0–3 months)

In the first weeks, a baby may manage only a feed, a diaper change, and a cuddle before needing sleep again. Sleep Foundation describes newborn windows of as little as 30–45 minutes and as much as 90 minutes. Mayo Clinic puts it a little differently: in the first month, a newborn awake for one to two hours most often needs to sleep again.

Two things are different at this age:

1. **Don't try to stretch them.** Sleep Foundation says there is no need to extend a newborn's wake windows to get longer sleep, because most infants lengthen them on their own. KidsHealth adds that keeping a baby up during the day in the hope of better nights tends to backfire, since overtired infants often sleep worse.
2. **Feeding sets the rhythm.** Hunger drives newborn sleep far more than the clock. If you want the broader picture of the first weeks, read our [newborn sleep schedule guide](/newborn-sleep-schedule).

## Does feeding count as awake time?

Yes, in most definitions. Sleep Foundation defines a wake window as starting when your baby wakes and ending the next time they fall asleep, so a feed in between is part of the window. If your baby dozes off at the breast or bottle, that drowsy stretch is where the window ends.

## Tired cues: when the window is closing

Numbers get you into the right neighborhood; cues tell you the exact moment. Sleep Foundation lists crying, yawning, eye rubbing, blinking more often, and staring off to the side. Cleveland Clinic says activity levels usually drop as a baby gets sleepy. Tresillian, an Australian parenting service, adds grimacing, frowning, clenched fists, jerky movements, and sudden overactivity.

Over a few days you will usually notice your baby's own signal. Cleveland Clinic gives this example: if a 4-month-old reliably shows sleepy signs about two hours into a window, lay them down a few minutes before that point.

## A simple wake window calculator you can do on paper

There is no formula that predicts every nap, but this method turns the chart into a starting point for *your* baby:

1. **Write down when your baby woke up.** Count from the moment they woke, not from when you got them out of the crib.
2. **Pick the lower end of the range for their age** from the chart above, for example about 1.25 hours at 4 months using Cleveland Clinic's band.
3. **Start a wind-down about 10 minutes before that time**, so your baby is in a calm, dim space as the window closes.
4. **Adjust after a short nap.** If the last nap was much shorter than usual, aim for the earlier side of the next window.
5. **Note what actually happened for three or four days**: when cues appeared, how long settling took, and how long the nap lasted. Patterns show up quickly.

*Worked example (illustration only):* a 4-month-old wakes at 6:45 a.m. Starting from 1.25 hours, the first nap target is about 8:00 a.m., with the wind-down starting around 7:50. If the baby shows sleepy cues at 7:40, follow the baby, not the math.

## What can make wake windows go wrong

- **Treating the top of the range as a goal.** Upper limits are where *some* babies cope, not where every baby should be.
- **Ignoring the previous nap.** A 25-minute nap rebuilds less rest than a long one, so the next window usually needs to be shorter.
- **Over-stimulation at the end of the window.** Bright screens, visitors, or rough play just before sleep make settling harder.
- **Unsafe shortcuts.** Letting a baby finish a nap in a swing, bouncer, or car seat is a common way to "fix" a mistimed window. HealthyChildren.org (AAP) advises moving a baby who falls asleep in a sitting device to a firm, flat surface as soon as you can.

## When wake windows stop mattering

Sleep Foundation notes that many parents stop counting wake windows once their child is down to one or two naps, and that most children nap two times a day or fewer between 12 and 18 months. At that point, a steady nap time and bedtime usually matter more. See [baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age) for how naps drop over time.

Sleep regressions can also throw the numbers off for a while. During one, Sleep Foundation says windows may suddenly get shorter or longer.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Sleep Foundation suggests checking in if your baby regularly sleeps a lot more or less than the recommended total for their age, or if you notice snoring or thrashing during sleep. Call sooner if your baby is unusually hard to wake, is feeding poorly, has fewer wet diapers, or simply seems unwell.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is a wake window?**  
The time your baby stays awake between two sleeps, from waking up until falling asleep again.

**How long should wake windows be at 4 months?**  
Cleveland Clinic gives 1.25–2.5 hours for 3–4 months; Sleep Foundation gives 1–3 hours for 1–4 months. More detail is in our [4 month old sleep schedule](/4-month-old-sleep-schedule).

**What are normal newborn wake windows?**  
Roughly 30 minutes to 1.5 hours in the first month, according to Sleep Foundation and Cleveland Clinic.

**My baby gets tired before the window ends. Should I keep them up?**  
No. Sleep Foundation's advice is to look at the baby's cues; the chart is only a starting point.

**Are wake windows backed by research?**  
Only loosely. Official recommendations cover total sleep per day, not awake time between naps, so wake-window charts are experience-based guides.

**Is there a wake window calculator?**  
The paper method above works for most families. Apps such as Yorix can do the counting from your logged sleep.

## Let Yorix do the counting (Yorix)

**Yorix** starts a wake-window timer when you log the end of a nap and suggests the next sleep window based on your baby's age and the day you have actually logged. You can ask the in-app AI coach why a window changed. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [Baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age)
- Month-by-month schedules: [newborn](/newborn-sleep-schedule) · [1 month](/1-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [2 months](/2-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [3 months](/3-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [4 months](/4-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [5 months](/5-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [6 months](/6-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [7 months](/7-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [8 months](/8-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [9 months](/9-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [10 months](/10-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [11 months](/11-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [12 months](/12-month-old-sleep-schedule) · [15 months](/15-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Sleep regression ages](/sleep-regression)
- [Dream feed](/dream-feed)
- [Short naps](/short-naps)
- [False starts](/false-starts)

3. American Academy of Sleep Medicine. "Recharge with sleep: Pediatric sleep recommendations promoting optimal health." <https://aasm.org/recharge-with-sleep-pediatric-sleep-recommendations-promoting-optimal-health/>. 12–16 hours per 24 hours for 4–12 months; endorsed by the AAP.

title: Baby White Noise: Safe Volume, Placement & Weaning | Yorix
heading: Baby White Noise: Does It Help, and How to Use a Sound Machine Safely
description: Does white noise help babies sleep? What the studies show, why sound machines can get too loud, AAP placement and volume advice, and how to wean off it.
body:
# Baby White Noise: Does It Help, and How to Use a Sound Machine Safely

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** September 3, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

A steady hum from a fan, a shushing app, or a dedicated sound machine is one of the most common tools in a baby's room. It can mask a barking dog or a sibling's footsteps, and for some babies it becomes a familiar part of falling asleep. The catch is volume: sound machines can be loud enough to be a hearing concern if they are used carelessly. Here is what the evidence actually shows, and how to use one sensibly.

## Short answer

White noise may help some babies fall asleep. In a small 1990 trial, **80% of newborns fell asleep within 5 minutes** with white noise, compared with 25% without it. Volume is the main safety issue. A 2014 study in *Pediatrics* found that **all 14 infant sleep machines tested, at maximum volume, exceeded 50 dBA at 30 cm**, the noise limit recommended for hospital nurseries, and three exceeded 85 dBA. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises that if you use a sleep machine, you **place it as far from your baby as possible, keep the volume as low as possible, and limit how long it runs**.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the evidence says | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Does it help newborns settle? | 16 of 20 (80%) asleep within 5 minutes vs 5 of 20 (25%) | Spencer et al., 1990 |
| Can machines be too loud? | All 14 machines exceeded 50 dBA at 30 cm at maximum volume | Hugh et al., 2014 |
| Loudest machines | 3 of 14 exceeded 85 dBA | Hugh et al., 2014 |
| Distances tested | 30, 100, and 200 cm from the machine | Hugh et al., 2014 |
| AAP guidance | As far away as possible, as low as possible, limited duration | AAP; HealthyChildren.org |

## Does white noise help babies sleep?

The most quoted trial is small and old. Spencer and colleagues studied 40 newborns aged 2–7 days in a randomized trial. With white noise, 16 of 20 fell asleep within five minutes; without it, only 5 of 20 did. The authors concluded white noise "may help" parents settle unsettled babies.

What this means in practice:

- **It can help with settling,** especially in a noisy home.
- **It isn't proven to make babies sleep longer overall,** and the trial didn't test months of nightly use.
- **The AAP mentions possible benefits** of sleep machines alongside the hearing concern, which is why its advice is about safer use rather than avoidance.

## Is white noise safe for babies?

The concern is not the sound itself but **how loud and how close** it is, and for **how long**.

In the 2014 *Pediatrics* study, researchers played 14 infant sleep machines at full volume and measured them at three distances, adjusted for a 6-month-old's ear canal. At 30 cm (about a foot), every machine was louder than 50 dBA, the noise limit recommended for babies in hospital nurseries. Three exceeded 85 dBA, a level that, over more than 8 hours, would exceed adult workplace limits for accumulated noise exposure. The authors warned that these machines can produce sound levels that may damage infant hearing.

HealthyChildren.org (AAP) puts it simply: some machines can produce hazardous noise levels, so if you use one, keep it as far from your baby's head as possible and use it for a short time only. The AAP's environmental health guidance repeats the same three rules: far away, low volume, limited duration. The AAP's 2023 technical report on noise adds that infants cannot remove themselves from loud situations and depend on adults to do it for them.

## How loud should white noise be?

The sources we checked give a clear principle (as quiet as works), but the AAP pages we opened do not give a single decibel figure for home use. Here is how to read the numbers you will see online:

| Figure you may see | Where it comes from | How to use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 50 dBA | The hospital nursery noise limit used as the benchmark in the 2014 *Pediatrics* study | A sensible upper reference point; quieter is better |
| 85 dBA | Adult occupational limit for long exposure, cited in the same study | Far too loud for a baby's room |
| "No louder than 50 dB and 7 feet (200 cm) away" | Widely quoted on parenting sites, including Huckleberry, which attributes it to the AAP | **Not verified:** we could not find these exact numbers in the AAP pages and abstracts we opened |

**A practical check (our suggestion, not an official rule):** stand where your baby's head will be. If you need to raise your voice to talk over the machine, it is too loud. A free sound-meter app can give a rough reading, though phone measurements are not precise.

## Where to put a sound machine

- **Across the room, not in or on the crib.** Distance lowers the volume that reaches your baby's ears (the 2014 study measured the effect at 30, 100, and 200 cm).
- **Cords out of reach.** KidsHealth warns that cords within reach of a crib, from a sitting or standing position, are a hazard.
- **Nothing added to the sleep space.** The AAP's safe sleep advice is a bare crib with only a fitted sheet. Plush toys with built-in sound don't belong in it.
- **Pointed away from the crib,** if the device has a speaker direction.

## How long should it run?

The AAP advises limiting the duration. Options families use:

- Running it only while your baby falls asleep, using a timer.
- Lowering it once your baby is in deep sleep.
- Keeping all-night use for genuinely noisy situations, such as traffic or a shared room, at the lowest volume that works.

## Types of noise: white, pink, brown, or nature sounds

You will see "pink noise" and "brown noise" marketed for babies. These are names for sounds with more energy at lower pitches, which many people find softer to listen to. In the sources we checked, we found **no study comparing noise colors for infant sleep**, so we can't recommend one over another. Whichever you pick, the same rules apply: steady sound, low volume, and distance. Avoid tracks that loop with sudden changes, music with lyrics, or a sound that suddenly cuts out.

## When to stop using white noise

There is no medical age at which white noise must stop. Families usually phase it out when:

- the home is quieter, or the baby no longer seems to rely on it to settle;
- the baby moves to a new room or bed;
- travel makes carrying a machine inconvenient.

To wean gently, lower the volume a little every few nights, or use it for falling asleep only and let a timer switch it off. These are practical suggestions, not clinical guidance.

## What can make it worse

- **Maximum volume, close to the crib.**
- **Using it to drown out a baby who seems unwell.** White noise should never replace checking on your baby.
- **Relying on it for every sleep, everywhere,** so your baby struggles without it.
- **A device inside the sleep space** or cords within reach.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask your pediatrician if your baby doesn't startle at loud sounds, doesn't turn toward voices as they get older, or if you have concerns about hearing. Also talk to them if your baby only sleeps with very loud noise, or if sleep problems persist despite good habits.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is it safe to use white noise all night?**  
The AAP advises limiting duration. If you need it all night, keep it as far away and as quiet as possible.

**How far should a white noise machine be from a baby?**  
The AAP says as far away as possible. The often-quoted "7 feet" figure is attributed to the AAP online, but we could not verify it in AAP documents.

**What decibel is safe for babies?**  
The 2014 study used 50 dBA (the hospital nursery limit) as its benchmark. Aim for well below what you would need to talk over.

**Can babies become dependent on white noise?**  
Some may get used to it as a sleep cue. Gradually lowering the volume can help if you want to stop.

**Is pink noise better than white noise for babies?**  
We found no infant study comparing them.

## A calmer sleep space, logged (Yorix)

**Yorix** lets you note when white noise was used and compare how quickly your baby fell asleep and how long they stayed asleep, so you can tell whether it's actually helping. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)
- [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule)
- [Surviving night wakings](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents)
- [Sleep training methods explained](/sleep-training-methods-explained)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026. App pages are used only as labeled examples.

1. Spencer JA, et al. "White noise and sleep induction." *Archives of Disease in Childhood*, 1990. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2405784/> (abstract via Europe PMC).
2. Hugh SC, et al. "Infant sleep machines and hazardous sound pressure levels." *Pediatrics*, 2014. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24590753/> (abstract via Europe PMC).
3. American Academy of Pediatrics. "Noise" (environmental health). Last updated 11 January 2024. <https://www.aap.org/en/patient-care/environmental-health/promoting-healthy-environments-for-children/noise/>.
4. HealthyChildren.org / AAP. "How Noise Affects Your Child's Health." Last updated 20 October 2023. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/all-around/Pages/how-noise-affects-your-child.aspx>.
5. Balk SJ, et al. "Preventing Excessive Noise Exposure in Infants, Children, and Adolescents." *Pediatrics*, 2023 (AAP technical report). <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37864408/> (abstract via Europe PMC).
6. Nemours KidsHealth. "Baby Sleep: 8- to 12-Month-Olds" (crib hazards). <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleep812m.html>.
7. HealthyChildren.org / AAP. "How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby Safe: AAP Policy Explained." Last updated 11 September 2026. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/A-Parents-Guide-to-Safe-Sleep.aspx>.
8. App example: Huckleberry. "Can white noise help babies sleep?" Updated 3 September 2026. <https://huckleberrycare.com/blog/white-noise-for-babies-sleep>.
