description: 1 month old sleep schedule for weeks 4–7: how much sleep is normal, 4 week old wake windows, an example day built around feeds, and a first bedtime routine.
body:
# 1 Month Old Sleep Schedule: Weeks 4 to 7, Wake Windows, and a First Routine

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

By about four weeks, the blur of the first days has usually eased a little. Feeding is more practiced, you've seen a few longer sleeps, and you may be wondering whether it's time for a "schedule." This page covers that narrow stretch from roughly **4 to 7 weeks**: what a realistic day looks like, how long a 4-week-old can stay awake, and how to start a first, simple bedtime routine. For the bigger picture of the first weeks (why newborns can't follow a clock, safe sleep, and red flags), see our [newborn sleep schedule guide](/newborn-sleep-schedule).

## Short answer

At 1 month there is **no fixed schedule** to aim for. Sleep Foundation says newborns don't follow a predictable day-night pattern for roughly the first two months. What you can expect: **about 14–17 hours of sleep in 24 hours** (National Sleep Foundation panel; KidsHealth) in pieces that follow feeds, with **wake windows of about 30–90 minutes**. Breastfed babies feed about every 2–3 hours and bottle-fed babies about every 3–4 hours (KidsHealth). The body clock begins to develop around **4–6 weeks** (Pregnancy, Birth and Baby), so this is a good time to start a short, repeatable bedtime routine. Expect it to work as a cue, not a switch.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total sleep, 0–3 months | 14–17 hours per 24 hours | National Sleep Foundation (Hirshkowitz et al., 2015); KidsHealth |
| Sleep in the first month | About 16 hours a day | Mayo Clinic |
| Wake windows around 4 weeks | 0.5–1.5 h (0–1 month), then 1–3 h (1–4 months) / 0.5–1 h, then 1–2 h (1–3 months) | Sleep Foundation / Cleveland Clinic |
| Feeds | About every 2–3 hours (breastfed) or 3–4 hours (bottle-fed) | KidsHealth |
| Body clock starts developing | Around 4–6 weeks | Pregnancy, Birth and Baby |
| Sleep cycle length | About 45–60 minutes | Pregnancy, Birth and Baby |

## How much does a 1 month old sleep?

Mayo Clinic says babies sleep about 16 hours a day in the first month. The National Sleep Foundation panel recommends 14–17 hours for 0–3 months. The AASM has no figure under 4 months, and Cleveland Clinic explains why: research hasn't tied a specific amount of sleep to health benefits at this age, so "normal" is very wide.

**App example (not clinical guidance):** Huckleberry suggests aiming for about 15.5 hours at 1 month.

Sleep usually comes in pieces. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby says babies under 3 months may wake after one or two sleep cycles, so every 1 to 3 hours. Cleveland Clinic describes sleeps of about 30 minutes to 3 hours in the first two months.

## 4 week old wake window (and weeks 5–7)

Four weeks sits right on the line between two age bands in most charts, which is why numbers you find online jump around:

| Source | Up to 1 month | From 1 month |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sleep Foundation | 0.5–1.5 hours | 1–3 hours (1–4 months) |
| Cleveland Clinic | 0.5–1 hour | 1–2 hours (1–3 months) |
| Napper (app example) | 35–60 minutes (0–4 weeks) | 60–90 minutes (4–12 weeks) |
| Huckleberry (app example) | 30–90 minutes at 1 month | — |

**In practice:** most 4–7 week olds manage somewhere around **45 to 75 minutes**, feed included, which is where all four sources overlap *(our reading of the table, not an official figure)*. Mayo Clinic puts it simply: after a newborn has been awake for 1 to 2 hours, they most often need to sleep again. Sleep Foundation adds that there's no need to stretch a newborn's wake windows to get longer sleeps, because most babies lengthen them on their own.

Watch the baby more than the clock. Sleep Foundation lists yawning, eye rubbing, blinking more often, staring off to the side, and crying as signs of tiredness. It suggests laying your baby down a few minutes before they get too tired or upset.

## Example day for a 1 month old (example only)

At this age a "schedule" is really a repeating loop of **feed, a short awake time, then sleep**. This is **an example only**. Your baby's loops will be longer or shorter, and no two days will match.

| Time | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| 7:00 a.m. | Feed; open the curtains |
| 7:50 a.m. | Asleep (about 50 minutes awake) |
| 9:30 a.m. | Feed, diaper, a few minutes of tummy time |
| 10:30 a.m. | Asleep |
| 12:15 p.m. | Feed, cuddle, short walk outside |
| 1:10 p.m. | Asleep (maybe in the stroller) |
| 3:00 p.m. | Feed and play |
| 3:50 p.m. | Asleep |
| 5:30 p.m. | Feed |
| 6:30–8:00 p.m. | Short naps and feeds as your baby needs them |
| About 9:00–10:30 p.m. | Bedtime routine and a feed before the longest stretch |
| Night | Feeds roughly every 2–4 hours, kept dark and quiet |

**Why such a late bedtime?** Huckleberry (app example) notes that at 1 month the longest stretch often doesn't start until about 10 p.m. or later, and that bedtime usually moves earlier over the next couple of months.

## Feeding sets the pace

- **How often:** KidsHealth says breastfed babies feed about every 2–3 hours and bottle-fed babies about every 3–4 hours.
- **Long sleepers:** KidsHealth advises waking a baby every 3–4 hours to feed until they show good weight gain, which usually happens in the first couple of weeks. After that, HealthyChildren.org says healthy, growing babies usually don't need to be woken to feed. Check with your pediatrician if growth, feeding, or diapers aren't on track.

**App example:** Huckleberry describes an "eat, play, sleep" pattern for the early months and cautions that it may need adjusting by 3–5 months, as wake windows grow.

## A first bedtime routine for a 1 month old

You don't need a long ritual. The goal is a short, repeatable set of signals. The NHS lists ideas such as a bath, night clothes and a fresh diaper, dim lights, a lullaby, and a goodnight cuddle. Sleep Foundation describes cuddling, rocking, walking, and feeding as part of a relaxing newborn routine. A simple version:

1. Dim the lights about 15 minutes before the last evening feed.
2. Change the diaper and put on a clean sleepsuit or sleep sack.
3. Feed in a quiet, low-lit room.
4. Sing the same short song.
5. Lay your baby on their back in the bassinet.

KidsHealth says it may take a few weeks for a baby's brain to learn the difference between night and day, and there are no tricks to speed this up. Do the routine anyway: you're building the cue for later.

**Help the body clock along.** The NHS suggests opening curtains, playing, and not worrying about everyday noise during daytime naps. At night, keep lights low, talk little, and change diapers only when needed.

## Holding, crying, and "bad habits"

At 1 month, comforting is not spoiling. The CDC says you can't spoil a baby by holding or responding to them, and Mayo Clinic advises not letting babies cry alone in the first month. Cleveland Clinic says babies younger than 3 months can't yet regulate their emotions and rely on you to soothe them back to sleep. HealthyChildren.org suggests helping your baby fall asleep with soothing sensations like rocking or sucking. Our [contact naps guide](/contact-naps) covers safe ways to handle a baby who only sleeps on you.

The CDC also notes that infant crying is often worse in the first few months and gets better. If you feel overwhelmed, put your baby down somewhere safe and step away for a few minutes.

## Sleep safety reminders

Every sleep, day or night: on the back, on a firm, flat surface with only a fitted sheet, in your room but not in your bed (KidsHealth; HealthyChildren.org). If your baby falls asleep in a car seat, swing, or on a feeding pillow, move them to their sleep space. KidsHealth warns against weighted blankets, sleepers, or swaddles. If you use a pacifier while breastfeeding, the Sydney Children's Hospitals Network suggests waiting until about 4–6 weeks.

## What can make it harder

- **Keeping your baby awake** in the day to "save" sleep for night. KidsHealth says overtired infants sleep worse.
- **Bright, lively night feeds.** Cleveland Clinic suggests avoiding talking or playing during night feeds.
- **Comparing with a friend's baby.** The range of normal is wide.
- **Skipping sleep yourself.** Share night duties if you can (NHS).

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Call your doctor right away for a fever in a baby under 12 weeks, a baby who is unusually hard to wake or too sleepy to feed, fewer wet diapers than usual, breathing that looks like hard work, or if you are worried (HealthyChildren.org symptom checker). Also speak up if you are feeling low or anxious.

## Frequently asked questions

**Can I put my 1 month old on a sleep schedule?**  
Not a clock-based one. Sleep Foundation says newborns don't follow a predictable pattern for about the first two months. A feed-play-sleep loop and an evening routine are enough.

**How long should a 4 week old be awake?**  
Roughly 30–90 minutes, often about 45–75 minutes including the feed (Sleep Foundation; Cleveland Clinic; app charts).

**How much should a 1 month old sleep?**  
About 14–17 hours in 24 hours (National Sleep Foundation panel); Mayo Clinic says about 16 hours in the first month.

**When should a 1 month old go to bed?**  
Often late, around 9–10:30 p.m., at the start of the longest stretch. Bedtime tends to move earlier over the next months.

**Should I start a bedtime routine at 1 month?**  
Yes, if you'd like. Keep it short and calm; it becomes more useful as the body clock develops.

## Count the minutes for you (Yorix)

**Yorix** times each wake window from the moment you log the end of a sleep and shows when the next sleep is likely. Feeds and diapers sit in the same log, which is handy at 3 a.m. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

# 11 Month Old Sleep and Feeding Schedule: Two Naps, Three Meals

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

At 11 months, the day often looks almost like a toddler's: three meals, a couple of snacks, milk feeds, two naps, and a bedtime that's fairly predictable. Parents searching at this age usually want two things at once: a **sleep schedule** and a **feeding schedule** that fit together. This page covers both, plus what to do when your baby starts refusing one of the naps a few weeks before the first birthday.

## Short answer

Sleep needs haven't changed since six months: **12 to 16 hours a day**, most of it (9 to 12 hours) at night, plus **two naps** for most babies (KidsHealth). Clinical wake-window charts for the last quarter of the first year are wide, **3 to 6 hours** at Cleveland Clinic and up to **7.5 hours** at Sleep Foundation; the apps aim for about **3 to 4**. For food, HealthyChildren.org (AAP) says babies of 8–12 months need about **750–900 calories a day**, with roughly **400–500 of them (about 24 ounces) still from breast milk or formula**, spread over three meals and snacks. No cow's milk as a drink and no juice before 12 months.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Item | 11-month figure | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sleep across the day and night | 12 to 16 h | KidsHealth; AASM |
| Night portion | 9 to 12 h | KidsHealth |
| Naps | Two, as a rule | KidsHealth; Mayo Clinic |
| Awake between sleeps | 3 to 6 h (Cleveland Clinic), 3 to 7.5 h (Sleep Foundation) | Cleveland Clinic; Sleep Foundation |
| Calories | 750–900 a day, about 400–500 from breast milk or formula (about 24 oz) | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |
| Water | 4–8 oz a day from about 6 months | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |
| Juice and cow's milk | Not before 12 months | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |

## How much sleep at 11 months?

KidsHealth gives 12–16 hours for 8–12 months, with a night stretch of 9–12 hours and naps from about 30 minutes to 2 hours. Newcastle Hospitals NHS says that by the age of 1 most of a baby's sleep happens at night, and that many babies keep waking at night through the first year.

**App examples (not clinical guidance):** Huckleberry puts the 11-month total near 13.5 hours. Napper keeps its 12–15 hour range and describes two daytime sleeps.

## 11 month old nap schedule

Most 11-month-olds still need **two naps**. Here the sources pull in different directions. Mayo Clinic writes that the morning nap often disappears between 10 and 12 months. KidsHealth and Boys Town Pediatrics both place the move to a single nap later, closer to a year and a half. That spread is why a few skipped morning naps shouldn't automatically mean "one nap now."

**If your baby starts refusing a nap:**

- Huckleberry (app example) says nap resistance at 11 months is often a sign the baby needs *longer wake windows*, not fewer naps, and suggests trying 3.5–3.75 hour windows.
- Try that for a week before changing to one nap *(practical suggestion)*.
- If you do move to one nap, Mayo Clinic suggests moving the afternoon nap and bedtime about half an hour earlier.

When the switch does come, the [15 month old sleep schedule](/15-month-old-sleep-schedule) walks through it step by step.

## 11 month wake windows

- Cleveland Clinic, 10 to 12 months: 3 to 6 hours.
- Sleep Foundation, same band: 3 to 7.5 hours.
- Huckleberry, 11 months (app example): 3 to 3.75 hours.
- Napper, 11 months (app example): 3 to 4 hours, sometimes a little more before bed.

These are guides, not rules. The clinical charts are wide on purpose, and wake windows have no official AAP or AASM standard.

## Feeding schedule for an 11 month old

HealthyChildren.org (AAP) publishes a sample menu for 8- to 12-month-olds. Laid out as a day, it looks like this. Amounts are the AAP's; the clock times are **our example only**.

| Time (example) | Meal | What the AAP sample menu suggests |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 7:00 a.m. | Breakfast | 2–4 oz cereal or 1 mashed or scrambled egg; 2–4 oz fruit; breast milk or 4–6 oz formula |
| 9:00 a.m. | Snack | Breast milk or 4–6 oz formula; 2–4 oz diced cheese or cooked vegetables |
| 11:30 a.m. | Lunch | 2–4 oz yogurt, cottage cheese, beans, or meat; 2–4 oz yellow or orange vegetables; breast milk or 4–6 oz formula |
| 3:30 p.m. | Snack | 1 whole-grain cracker or teething biscuit; 2–4 oz yogurt or soft fruit; 2–4 oz water |
| 5:30 p.m. | Dinner | 2–4 oz poultry, meat, or tofu; 2–4 oz green vegetables; 2–4 oz pasta or potato; 2–4 oz fruit; breast milk or 4–6 oz formula |
| Before bed | Milk | Breast milk or 6–8 oz formula, or water, then water or toothbrushing |

**Drinks.** HealthyChildren.org suggests 4–8 oz of water a day from about 6 months, no cow's milk as a drink before 12 months, and no juice before 12 months. Offer drinks in a cup; the AAP suggests finishing the move from bottles to cups between 12 and 18 months.

**Sleep-friendly feeding tips:**

- Keep the last milk feed **before** the bath or book, not as the last step of falling asleep. Nationwide Children's advises keeping bedtime feeds out of the bedtime routine after 6 months.
- Brush after that final milk. In the AAP's Brush, Book, Bed wording, nothing should touch the teeth after the toothbrush.
- **Never put your baby to bed with a bottle** (HealthyChildren.org).

## Sample 11 month old day: sleep and food together (example only)

**Example only.** Shift the whole day to match your baby.

| Time | Sleep | Food |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 6:45 a.m. | Wake | Milk |
| 7:15 a.m. | | Breakfast |
| 9:45–11:00 a.m. | Morning nap | |
| 11:15 a.m. | | Lunch |
| 1:00 p.m. | | Snack and milk |
| 2:30–3:45 p.m. | Afternoon nap | |
| 3:50 p.m. | | Fruit or yogurt snack with water in a cup |
| 5:20 p.m. | | Family dinner |
| 6:40 p.m. | Bedtime routine | Last milk before the bath, then teeth |
| 7:15 p.m. | Asleep | |

**App examples:** Huckleberry's sample has a 6:30 a.m. start, naps beginning at 9:30 and 2:15, and lights out at 7:15. Napper's starts at 7:00, naps at 10:30 and 3:00 for an hour each, and bedtime from 7:30.

## Bedtime and night at 11 months

- **Routine.** KidsHealth suggests a warm bath followed by stories or singing. The AAP's Brush, Book, Bed adds brushing and a book at a regular bedtime.
- **Drowsy but awake.** KidsHealth describes putting your baby down awake and, if they cry, waiting a few minutes before brief soothing.
- **Separation.** KidsHealth says separation anxiety often develops between 8 months and 1 year, so a short, confident goodnight helps.
- **Standing up.** If your baby pulls up in the crib and can't get down, see our [10 month old sleep schedule](/10-month-old-sleep-schedule).

## What can make an 11 month schedule harder

- Switching to one nap at the first sign of nap refusal.
- A milk feed as the very last step of falling asleep.
- Settling your baby with a bottle in bed; HealthyChildren.org connects it to cavities and ear infections.
- Juice, or too much milk, crowding out meals (HealthyChildren.org).

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask your doctor about feeding if your baby refuses most solids, gags or chokes often, isn't gaining weight, or has signs of a food allergy. For sleep, mention loud snoring, pauses in breathing, or night wakings that leave you unable to cope.

## Frequently asked questions

**How many naps does an 11 month old need?**  
Usually two. Most babies keep two naps until somewhere between 12 and 18 months.

**What is a good feeding schedule for an 11 month old?**  
Three meals and two snacks with breast milk or formula at most of them, about 24 ounces of milk a day in total (HealthyChildren.org sample menu).

**What are 11 month wake windows?**  
About 3–4 hours in app examples; Cleveland Clinic's 10–12 month range is 3–6 hours.

**Can my 11 month old drink cow's milk?**  
Not as a main drink yet. HealthyChildren.org advises waiting until 12 months.

**What time should an 11 month old go to bed?**  
Usually somewhere from 6:30 to 8 in the evening, roughly three and a half to four hours after the afternoon nap ends.

## Sleep and meals in one log (Yorix)

**Yorix** logs naps, night wakings, and feeds in one place, so you can see whether a later lunch or a shorter morning nap changes the afternoon. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [10 month old sleep schedule](/10-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [12 month old sleep schedule](/12-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Baby feeding schedule](/baby-feeding-schedule)
- [Baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age)
- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026. App pages are used only as labeled examples.

2. American Academy of Sleep Medicine. "Recharge with sleep: Pediatric sleep recommendations promoting optimal health." <https://aasm.org/recharge-with-sleep-pediatric-sleep-recommendations-promoting-optimal-health/>.

body:
# 12 Month Old Sleep Schedule: A Day in the Life of a One-Year-Old

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Happy first birthday. This page is for planning an **ordinary day** for a one-year-old: total sleep, nap times, wake windows, bedtime, and the practical changes that arrive at 12 months, like whole milk, cups, and a few things that are now allowed in the crib. If your child's sleep has recently gone off the rails, with new night wakings or a sudden refusal to nap, start with our [12 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/12-months) page instead; it also walks through the "two naps or one?" decision in detail.

## Short answer

Sleep guidance switches age bands at the first birthday. The **AASM** recommends **12–16 hours** for 4–12 months and **11–14 hours** for 1–2 years, naps included; the CDC uses the same ranges. Most 12-month-olds still take **two naps**: KidsHealth says most toddlers move to one nap **around 18 months or sometimes sooner**, and Boys Town Pediatrics puts the usual switch at **15–18 months**. Published wake windows for 10–12 months are **3–6 hours** (Cleveland Clinic). Bedtime in most examples falls between about **6:30 and 8 p.m.**

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total sleep | 12–16 h up to 12 months; 11–14 h from 1 to 2 years | AASM; CDC |
| Night | 9–12 hours (8–12 months) / 10–12 hours (after 12 months) | KidsHealth / Pregnancy, Birth and Baby |
| Naps | Usually 2 at 12 months; one nap most often by 15–18 months | KidsHealth; Boys Town Pediatrics |
| Wake windows (10–12 months) | 3–6 hours / 3–7.5 hours | Cleveland Clinic / Sleep Foundation |
| Milk from 12 months | Whole milk, about 16–24 oz (2–3 cups) a day | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |
| Bottle to cup | Finish between 12 and 18 months | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |

## How much should a 1 year old sleep?

On the first birthday the official range shifts from 12–16 hours (AASM, 4–12 months) to 11–14 hours (AASM, 1–2 years). Your child doesn't need an hour less overnight; the bands just overlap. KidsHealth describes 9–12 hours at night for 8–12 months, and Pregnancy, Birth and Baby gives 10–12 hours at night after 12 months.

**App examples (not clinical guidance):** Huckleberry aims for at least 13.25 hours, with 11–12 hours at night and 2–3 hours over 2 naps.

## 12 month old nap schedule

Plan on **two naps**. Huckleberry (app example) says 12 months is typically too early to drop to one nap, and both KidsHealth (about 18 months, sometimes sooner) and Boys Town (15–18 months) put the usual switch later. Mayo Clinic is the outlier: it says babies of 10–12 months often drop the morning nap.

What a two-nap day usually looks like at this age:

- A morning nap starting roughly 3–3.5 hours after waking *(our reading of the app examples)*.
- An early-afternoon nap after lunch.
- Each nap somewhere between 40 minutes and 2 hours. Boys Town describes two-nap days with naps of about 40 minutes to 2 hours each.

If your one-year-old has started fighting one nap, the full comparison of two-nap and one-nap days is on the [12 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/12-months) page. The [15 month old sleep schedule](/15-month-old-sleep-schedule) explains how the switch to one nap usually goes.

## 12 month wake windows

| Source | Age band | Wake window |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cleveland Clinic | 10–12 months | 3–6 hours |
| Sleep Foundation | 10–12 months | 3–7.5 hours |
| Huckleberry (app example) | 12 months | 3.25–4 hours |
| Napper (app example) | 11–14 months | 3–4 hours |

Most one-year-olds on two naps sit around **3.25–4 hours**, with the longest stretch before bed *(our reading of the app examples)*. These are not clinical figures; there is no AAP or AASM wake-window standard.

## Sample schedule for a 12 month old (example only)

**This is an example only.**

| Time | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| 6:45 a.m. | Wake; milk in a cup or breastfeed; breakfast soon after |
| 10:00–11:00 a.m. | Morning nap |
| 11:30 a.m. | Lunch |
| 12:00–2:15 p.m. | Play, outing, snack |
| 2:30–3:45 p.m. | Afternoon nap |
| 4:00 p.m. | Snack and water |
| 5:30 p.m. | Dinner |
| 6:45 p.m. | Bath, pajamas, teeth, books |
| 7:15–7:30 p.m. | Lights out |

**App example:** Huckleberry's 12-month sample: wake 6:30, naps 9:45–10:45 and 2:15–3:15, bedtime 7:15 p.m.

## Milk, cups, and bottles at one year

These changes don't decide sleep, but they shape the evening routine:

- **Cow's milk.** HealthyChildren.org says children of 12–24 months can drink whole milk, about 16–24 ounces (2–3 cups) a day, plus 8–32 ounces of water. Breastfeeding can continue for as long as you both want.
- **Juice.** Not needed; the CDC says no more than 4 ounces of 100% juice a day if you give it.
- **Bottles.** The AAP suggests finishing the move from bottle to cup between 12 and 18 months and dropping the nap-time and bedtime bottles gradually. HealthyChildren.org warns that giving in to a bedtime bottle can turn a short protest into a longer struggle; offer extra cuddles, songs, or stories instead.
- **Teeth.** Brush, Book, Bed (AAP): the toothbrush should be the last thing to touch the teeth before bed.

## The crib after the first birthday

- **Blanket and lovey.** KidsHealth says that after the first birthday a light blanket and a small "lovey" are OK in the crib, but not extra-large soft toys.
- **Comfort object.** Nationwide Children's Hospital suggests introducing a security object by 12 months and including it in the bedtime routine. The CDC's 1-year tips also suggest bringing a favorite toy or blanket when your child meets a new caregiver.
- **Bumpers.** Nationwide Children's advises removing crib bumpers by about 12 months, when babies can begin to climb.
- **Climbing.** KidsHealth suggests keeping the mattress on the lowest setting and not leaving toys that can be stacked to climb on.

## Bedtime routine for a one-year-old

The CDC's 1-year tips stress routines for sleeping and feeding. A one-year-old routine can be the AAP's Brush, Book, Bed in its simplest form: milk earlier in the evening, bath if it's a bath night, brush teeth, one or two books, the same goodnight phrase, lights out. KidsHealth suggests deciding how long the routine should be and keeping it from growing night by night. In a randomized trial of children aged 7–36 months, a consistent routine helped them fall asleep faster and wake less (Mindell et al., 2009).

## What can make a one-year-old's schedule harder

- Dropping to one nap before your child is ready, which can lead to an overtired evening.
- A bottle or cup of milk in the crib (HealthyChildren.org).
- Screens in the hour before bed (KidsHealth).
- A routine that keeps getting longer (KidsHealth).

## When to talk to your pediatrician

See your doctor if your child snores loudly or seems to pause breathing, is very hard to wake, isn't pulling up to stand, or has lost skills they had before. Mention ongoing night wakings or early waking if they're wearing you down.

## Frequently asked questions

**How many naps does a 12 month old need?**  
Usually two. Most children move to one nap between about 15 and 18 months (Boys Town; KidsHealth).

**How much sleep does a 1 year old need?**  
The AASM recommends 11–14 hours a day, naps included, for ages 1–2.

**What are 12 month wake windows?**  
Around 3.25–4 hours in app examples; Cleveland Clinic gives 3–6 hours for 10–12 months.

**What time should a 1 year old go to bed?**  
Most example schedules land between 6:30 and 8 p.m. Earlier after a short afternoon nap.

**Can my 1 year old have a blanket in the crib?**  
KidsHealth says a light blanket and a small lovey are OK after the first birthday.

## Watch the nap pattern before you change it (Yorix)

**Yorix** lets you look back over a week or two of naps at once. If the morning nap keeps getting shorter while the afternoon nap holds, that's a pattern worth seeing before you drop a nap. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [12 month milestones](/12-month-milestones)
- [12 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/12-months)

description: 15 month old sleep schedule: 11–14 hours of sleep, when and how to move from 2 naps to 1, sample one-nap and two-nap days, wake windows and a toddler bedtime.
body:
# 15 Month Old Sleep Schedule and the Switch From Two Naps to One

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Fifteen months is right in the middle of the most common window for the **2-to-1 nap transition**. Some toddlers have already settled into one long midday nap; others still need two; plenty bounce between the two patterns for weeks. This page explains how much sleep a 15-month-old needs, how to tell whether your toddler is ready for one nap, how to make the switch, and what the day can look like on either pattern.

## Short answer

The AASM recommends **11–14 hours of sleep a day, naps included, for children aged 1–2**, and the CDC repeats it on its 15-month milestone page. Boys Town Pediatrics says the move from two naps to one usually happens **between 15 and 18 months**, and KidsHealth says most toddlers have **one nap by about 18 months**, sometimes sooner. A meta-analysis found that **fewer than 2.5% of children stop napping altogether before age 2** (Staton et al., 2020), so this is a merge, not an end to naps. During the switch, plan on an **earlier bedtime** and some mixed days.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total sleep, ages 1–2 | 11–14 hours a day, naps included | AASM; CDC (15 months) |
| Night | 10–12 hours (after 12 months) | Pregnancy, Birth and Baby |
| 2-to-1 nap switch | Usually 15–18 months / most by 18 months | Boys Town Pediatrics / KidsHealth |
| One nap length | About 1–2 hours (after 12 months) | Pregnancy, Birth and Baby |
| Stopping naps completely before 2 | Fewer than 2.5% of children | Staton et al., 2020 (meta-analysis) |
| Wake windows | No clinical chart covers this age; apps suggest about 4–6 hours | Napper and Huckleberry (app examples) |

## How much sleep does a 15 month old need?

The AASM gives 11–14 hours for 1–2 years, and the CDC's 15-month page says the same. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby describes 10–12 hours at night after 12 months, plus one nap of 1–2 hours.

**App example (not clinical guidance):** Huckleberry aims for about 13 hours, usually at least 11 at night and 2–3 hours of day sleep over 1 or 2 naps.

## Is my toddler ready for one nap?

Boys Town Pediatrics calls 15–18 months the average age for the change and notes it may not line up with a daycare's schedule. KidsHealth gives one clear sign: **a toddler who fights the morning nap is probably ready for just an afternoon nap**. Huckleberry (app example) also lists naps that become very brief, fighting either nap, and nights that regularly come in below 10 hours.

**Probably ready** *(practical suggestion)*:

- The morning nap is refused or very short on most days for 1–2 weeks.
- When the morning nap does happen, the afternoon nap gets skipped or bedtime drifts late.
- Your toddler copes well until lunch without the morning nap.

**Probably not yet:**

- Your toddler is visibly exhausted by 10 a.m.
- Skipped morning naps lead to more night waking or early rising.
- It's a rough week for another reason (illness, teething, a new caregiver).

## How to move from two naps to one

Boys Town describes the usual pattern: families gradually trim the afternoon nap and keep the child up a little longer each morning, until the old 9:30 and 2:30 naps become one nap around midday. Lunch usually moves earlier too. A step-by-step version *(practical suggestion, based on that description)*:

1. **Push the morning nap later** by 15–30 minutes every few days.
2. **Cap the afternoon nap** if needed so bedtime doesn't drift (Huckleberry, app example, suggests capping each of two naps at 90 minutes).
3. **Move lunch earlier,** to around 11–11:30 a.m., so your toddler isn't hungry at nap time.
4. **When the morning nap reaches about 11:30–12:00,** it has become the single midday nap.
5. **Bring bedtime earlier** for a few weeks. Mayo Clinic suggests moving the afternoon nap and bedtime up by about half an hour once the morning nap is gone, and Boys Town notes your child may need an earlier night or a longer morning sleep to make up for it.
6. **Expect mixed days.** Huckleberry notes that the new single nap can need at least a week before it stretches out to 2–3 hours.

## 15 month old wake windows

Neither Cleveland Clinic nor Sleep Foundation publishes wake windows past 12 months. The only figures we found are from apps:

| Source | Age band | Wake window |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Napper (app example) | 14–24 months | 4–6 hours |
| Huckleberry (app example) | 15 months, one nap | 5–5.5 hours before the nap |

Treat these as loose guides. At this age, a steady nap time and bedtime usually matter more than counting minutes *(practical suggestion)*.

## Sample 15 month old schedules (examples only)

These are **examples only**.

| | Two-nap day | One-nap day |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wake | 6:45 a.m. | 6:45 a.m. |
| Breakfast | 7:15 a.m. | 7:15 a.m. |
| Morning nap | 10:00–10:45 a.m. | — |
| Lunch | 12:00 p.m. | 11:15 a.m. |
| Main nap | 2:30–3:45 p.m. | 12:00–2:15 p.m. |
| Snack | 4:00 p.m. | 3:00 p.m. |
| Dinner | 5:30 p.m. | 5:15 p.m. |
| Bedtime routine | 6:45 p.m. | 6:15 p.m. |
| Asleep | 7:15 p.m. | About 6:45 p.m. |

**App example:** Huckleberry's one-nap sample: wake 7:00, nap 12:00–2:30, bedtime 8:00 p.m.

## Bedtime for a 15 month old

The CDC's 15-month tips describe exactly what a toddler routine needs: **a calm, quiet bedtime — put on pajamas, brush teeth, and read 1 or 2 books**. A few more pointers:

- **Keep it the same length each night.** KidsHealth warns that extras like a long back rub can turn into nightly demands.
- **Screens off** in the hour before bed, and no devices in the bedroom (KidsHealth).
- **Comfort items are fine now.** KidsHealth says a light blanket and a small lovey can go in the crib after the first birthday.
- **Expect protests when tired.** The CDC notes tantrums are more likely when toddlers are tired or hungry, which is one reason an earlier bedtime helps during the nap switch.

## Milk, bottles, and night sleep

HealthyChildren.org (AAP) recommends whole milk for 12–24 months, about 16–24 ounces a day, and suggests finishing the move from bottle to cup between 12 and 18 months, dropping the nap and bedtime bottles gradually. The CDC's 15-month tips also encourage letting your child drink from a cup without a lid. If your toddler still has a bottle to fall asleep, replace it step by step with cuddles and a story; HealthyChildren.org says giving in at bedtime can make a short problem last longer.

## Crib safety for climbers

KidsHealth suggests keeping the crib mattress at its lowest setting and not leaving toys that could be stacked to climb. If your toddler keeps climbing out even then, it may be time to think about a bed; our [2 year old sleep regression](/sleep-regression/2-years) page covers the crib-to-bed move.

## What can make the 15 month schedule harder

- Dropping the morning nap abruptly without an earlier bedtime.
- A late, long afternoon nap that pushes bedtime past 8:30 p.m. *(practical suggestion)*.
- A bottle as the last step of falling asleep (HealthyChildren.org).
- Screens close to bedtime (KidsHealth).

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Talk to your doctor if your toddler snores most nights, has pauses in breathing, seems very sleepy during the day despite enough sleep, isn't taking any steps alone, or has lost words or skills. Also mention it if night wakings have gone on for weeks.

## Frequently asked questions

**How many naps should a 15 month old take?**  
One or two. Boys Town says the switch to one usually happens between 15 and 18 months.

**How do I know my toddler is ready for one nap?**  
KidsHealth: a toddler who fights the morning nap is probably ready for just an afternoon nap. Look for a pattern over 1–2 weeks.

**What time should a 15 month old go to bed?**  
Usually between about 6:30 and 8 p.m.; earlier during the nap transition.

**How long should a 15 month old's single nap be?**  
About 1–2 hours (Pregnancy, Birth and Baby), sometimes longer once the transition settles.

**How much sleep does a 15 month old need?**  
11–14 hours a day including naps (AASM; CDC).

## See the transition in your data (Yorix)

**Yorix** shows one-nap and two-nap days in the same weekly view, so you can see whether the switch is working: steady naps, calm evenings, and a night that isn't shrinking. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [18 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/18-months)
- [Baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age)
- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)
- [2 year old sleep regression](/sleep-regression/2-years)

heading: 2 Month Old Sleep Schedule: What an 8- to 11-Week Day Can Look Like
description: 2 month old sleep schedule: 14–17 hours, 4–5 short naps, wake windows of about 1–1.5 hours, a sample 8-week day and a simple bedtime routine, with sources.
body:
# 2 Month Old Sleep Schedule: What an 8- to 11-Week Day Can Look Like

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Something often shifts around eight weeks. Your baby is smiling back at you, stays alert a little longer, and you may notice the first hints of a pattern: a nap that keeps landing at about the same time, or a night stretch that's suddenly longer. This guide is for babies from about **8 to 11 weeks**. It covers sleep totals, nap count, wake windows, a sample day, and a first real bedtime routine. Younger baby? See the [1 month old sleep schedule](/1-month-old-sleep-schedule). Nearer 12 weeks? The [3 month old sleep schedule](/3-month-old-sleep-schedule) picks up from here.

## Short answer

A 2-month-old typically sleeps **14–17 hours in 24 hours** (National Sleep Foundation panel, quoted by KidsHealth) in **several naps plus a longer night stretch**. Sleep Foundation says the sleep hormones melatonin and cortisol start following a daily rhythm at about **8–9 weeks**, which is when sleep may start becoming more predictable. Wake windows are usually about **1 to 1.5 hours** (Cleveland Clinic gives 1–2 hours for 1–3 months). Bedtime is often still late. A strict clock schedule isn't needed yet; the CDC's advice for this age is simply to **have routines for sleeping and feeding**.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total sleep | 14–17 hours per 24 hours (0–3 months) | National Sleep Foundation panel; KidsHealth |
| Body clock | Melatonin and cortisol start following a circadian rhythm at about 8–9 weeks | Sleep Foundation |
| Naps | 2–4 at 2 months / 2–3 for 1–3 months | Nationwide Children's / KidsHealth |
| Wake windows | 1–2 hours (1–3 months) / 1–3 hours (1–4 months) | Cleveland Clinic / Sleep Foundation |
| "Sleeping through" at this age | A stretch of only 5–6 hours | KidsHealth (1–3 months) |
| Night feeds (formula) | Most formula-fed babies stop needing a middle-of-the-night feed between 2 and 4 months, or when they weigh more than 12 pounds | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |

## How much sleep at 2 months?

KidsHealth, quoting the National Sleep Foundation, recommends 14–17 hours over 24 hours for babies up to 3 months, and says the range of normal is still very wide. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby notes that from about 8 weeks babies might start sleeping for longer periods.

**App examples (not clinical guidance):** Napper describes 14–17 hours at 2 months, with about 8–9 hours at night and 6–8 hours across several short naps. Huckleberry suggests aiming for 5–6 hours of daytime sleep.

## How many naps does a 2 month old take?

Counts vary because naps are still short and uneven:

- **Nationwide Children's Hospital:** 2–4 naps a day at 2 months.
- **KidsHealth:** many 1- to 3-month-olds settle into 2–3 naps followed by a longer night stretch after a late-night feed.
- **App examples:** Huckleberry and Napper both describe 4–5 naps; Napper says each can last from 30 minutes to 2 hours.

The number matters less than the total and how your baby seems. A day of five 40-minute naps and a day of three long ones can both be fine. Short naps at this age are common and usually nothing to fix. If you like, our [contact naps guide](/contact-naps) covers what to do when the only long nap is on you.

## 2 month wake windows

| Source | Age band | Wake window |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cleveland Clinic | 1–3 months | 1–2 hours |
| Sleep Foundation | 1–4 months | 1–3 hours |
| Huckleberry (app example) | 2 months | 45 minutes–1.75 hours |
| Napper (app example) | 4–12 weeks | 60–90 minutes |

Most 8- to 11-week-olds sit around **60–90 minutes**, feed and diaper change included *(our reading of where the sources overlap)*. The first window after the morning wake-up is often the shortest *(practical suggestion)*. Look for yawning, eye rubbing, faster blinking, or staring to the side (Sleep Foundation) and start the next sleep then, rather than holding out for a number.

## A sample 2 month old schedule (example only)

**This is an example only.** Feeds come on demand, and the times will drift from day to day.

| Time | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| 7:00 a.m. | Wake, feed, daylight |
| 8:15–9:15 a.m. | Nap 1 |
| 9:15 a.m. | Feed, tummy time on your chest or the floor |
| 10:30–11:45 a.m. | Nap 2 |
| 11:45 a.m. | Feed, outing or play |
| 1:15–2:30 p.m. | Nap 3 |
| 2:30 p.m. | Feed |
| 4:00–4:45 p.m. | Nap 4 |
| 6:00–6:30 p.m. | Short nap 5 if needed; feed |
| About 8:30–9:30 p.m. | Bedtime routine, feed, down for the night |
| Night | Feeds as needed, lights low, little talk |

**Why might bedtime be late?** Huckleberry (app example) says bedtimes after 9 p.m. are common at 2 months and tend to move earlier between 3 and 4 months, as the body clock matures. Napper (app example) says many parents put a 2-month-old down between 7 and 9 p.m. Both can work.

## Bedtime routine for a 2 month old

KidsHealth says this is a good time to start a familiar, relaxing bedtime routine: bathing, reading, and singing can signal the end of the day, and "be consistent" is the key. The NHS lists a bath, night clothes and a fresh diaper, a story, dim lights, a lullaby, and a cuddle as ideas. Cleveland Clinic suggests a routine of about 20–30 minutes, with the feed near the start.

A 2-month-old version takes about 20 minutes:

1. **Dim the room** and close the curtains.
2. **Quick wash or bath** (a bath doesn't have to be nightly).
3. **Fresh diaper, sleepsuit or sleep sack.**
4. **Feed** in low light.
5. **One short book or song,** the same each night.
6. **Into the crib or bassinet on the back,** ideally a little drowsy but still awake.

KidsHealth explains why the last step helps: if you rock your baby fully to sleep at bedtime, they may expect rocking after every night waking. It also suggests that if your baby squirms or fusses a little, you can wait a few minutes to see whether they settle, unless you think they're hungry or unwell. Don't worry if this doesn't work yet. Cleveland Clinic says babies under 3 months still rely on you to help them back to sleep.

## Night sleep at 2 months

- **Longer stretches start for some.** KidsHealth says some babies sleep 5–6 hours at a time by 2–3 months, but some don't.
- **Moving a feed.** KidsHealth suggests that if your baby eats at 7 p.m. and wakes at 2 a.m., you could try waking them for a feed at about 11 p.m., to line up their long stretch with yours. That's a version of a [dream feed](/dream-feed).
- **Formula-fed babies.** HealthyChildren.org says most formula-fed babies no longer need a middle-of-the-night feed between 2 and 4 months or once they weigh over 12 pounds. Breastfed babies may feed more often; check with your pediatrician before cutting feeds.
- **Night vs day.** Keep night wakings dark and dull: change or feed, then straight back down (KidsHealth).

## Comfort, crying, and pacifiers

The CDC's 2-month tips say you can't spoil a baby by holding or responding to them, that infant crying is often worse in the first few months but gets better, and that sucking on fingers or a pacifier can help a baby learn to self-soothe. KidsHealth says you can offer a pacifier at sleep time without forcing it, and that if you're breastfeeding you should wait until feeding is well established.

## Safe sleep at this age

KidsHealth notes that swaddling is OK until a baby starts trying to roll, typically at 3–4 months, and warns against weighted blankets, sleepers, or swaddles. It also says not to let a baby sleep in a car seat, on a feeding pillow, or in an infant lounger. Nationwide Children's suggests deciding where your baby will sleep long term by about 3 months. The AAP recommends room-sharing without bed-sharing for at least 6 months.

## What can make it harder

- **Long stretches awake** to tire your baby out. KidsHealth's newborn guide says overly tired infants often have more trouble sleeping at night.
- **A bright, social night.**
- **Expecting the same schedule every day.** Huckleberry (app example) also advises against a fixed clock schedule at 2 months because nap lengths are still unpredictable.
- **Product shortcuts** like inclined sleepers or loungers (KidsHealth).

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Speak to your doctor if your baby is feeding poorly or has fewer wet diapers, has a fever (any fever under 12 weeks needs a call right away), has noisy or labored breathing in sleep, is unusually hard to wake, or doesn't smile at people or hold up their head on their tummy by around 2 months (CDC milestones).

## Frequently asked questions

**What should a 2 month old sleep schedule look like?**  
Feeds, short wake windows of about 60–90 minutes, and several naps across the day, then a longer night stretch. Times will vary day to day.

**How many naps should a 2 month old take?**  
Anywhere from 2 to 5. Nationwide Children's says 2–4; apps often describe 4–5.

**What time should a 2 month old go to bed?**  
Between about 7 and 10 p.m. is common. Many babies move to an earlier bedtime between 3 and 4 months.

**When does a 2 month old sleep longer at night?**  
Some sleep 5–6 hours at a time by 2–3 months (KidsHealth), many not until later.

**Is it too early for a bedtime routine at 2 months?**  
No. KidsHealth recommends starting one now if you haven't already.

## See the pattern emerge (Yorix)

At 2 months the pattern is easier to see in a log than in your head. **Yorix** turns tapped naps, feeds, and night wakings into a simple daily view and suggests the next nap time from the last wake-up. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [3 month old sleep schedule](/3-month-old-sleep-schedule)

description: 6 month old sleep schedule: how much sleep, 3-nap and 2-nap example days, wake windows, a bedtime routine and a simple sleep plan, all with sources checked.
body:
# 6 Month Old Sleep Schedule: Naps, Wake Windows, Bedtime Routine, and a Simple Plan

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Six months is often the first age at which a day starts to feel plannable. Naps become more predictable, the longest night stretch is usually longer than it was at 3 or 4 months, and solid foods begin to appear on the menu. This page puts everything a parent searches for at this age in one place: how much sleep is typical, how many naps, wake windows, example days, a bedtime routine, and a step-by-step sleep plan. If sleep has suddenly got worse, read our separate [6 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/6-months) page instead.

## Short answer

Babies from 4 to 12 months need **12–16 hours of sleep in 24 hours, naps included** (American Academy of Sleep Medicine, endorsed by the AAP). KidsHealth says that by 6 months most babies sleep **9 hours or longer at night**, with brief wakings, and get about **3–4 hours of daytime sleep** in **at least two naps**. Many 6-month-olds still take **three naps**, with the third usually short; Mayo Clinic suggests dropping a late-afternoon third nap at about **9 months**. Published **wake windows** for this age run from about **2 to 4 hours** (Cleveland Clinic, 5–7 months). A **20- to 30-minute bedtime routine** in the same order each night is one of the best-supported things you can do (Cleveland Clinic; Mindell et al., 2009).

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total sleep per 24 hours | 12–16 hours, naps included | AASM (endorsed by the AAP) |
| Night sleep by 6 months | 9 hours or longer, with brief wakings | KidsHealth (4–7 months) |
| Daytime sleep | About 3–4 hours (4–7 months); 2–4 hours (6–12 months) | KidsHealth; Pregnancy, Birth and Baby |
| Naps | At least 2; many take 3 until about 9 months | KidsHealth; Mayo Clinic |
| Wake windows | 2–4 hours (5–7 months) / 1.5–4.5 hours (5–7 months) | Cleveland Clinic / Sleep Foundation |
| Night feeds | Most no longer need a middle-of-the-night feed, though some (often breastfed) babies still wake | KidsHealth; Nationwide Children's |
| Bedtime routine length | About 20–30 minutes | Cleveland Clinic |

## How much should a 6 month old sleep?

The official range is wide on purpose. The **AASM recommends 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours** for 4–12 months. Within that, the sources describe a typical shape:

- **Night:** KidsHealth says most babies sleep 9 hours or longer at night by 6 months. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby gives 10–14 hours of night sleep for 6–12 months.
- **Day:** about 3–4 hours across naps (KidsHealth, 4–7 months), or 2–4 hours (Pregnancy, Birth and Baby, 6–12 months).

**App examples (not clinical guidance):** Huckleberry suggests about 14 hours in total, split into 11–12 hours at night and 2.5–3.5 hours over 3 naps. Napper describes 12–15 hours, with 10–11 at night and 2–5 hours over 2–3 naps.

A baby who is growing well, feeding well, and mostly content when awake is getting enough sleep, even if the numbers don't match a chart exactly.

## 6 month old nap schedule: how many naps?

Most 6-month-olds take **three naps**, while some are already managing on two longer ones:

- **KidsHealth** says babies of 4–7 months take at least two naps a day.
- **Mayo Clinic** says babies from 4 months to 1 year nap at least twice a day, morning and early afternoon, and some also need a late-afternoon nap. It suggests cutting out that third nap at about 9 months, which helps move bedtime earlier.
- **App example:** Huckleberry says most babies aren't ready to drop the third nap until 7–9 months and suggests the first two naps last 60–90 minutes each, with the third around 30–45 minutes.

**How long should naps be?** There's no clinical target. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby describes naps of up to 2 hours at 3–6 months. Mayo Clinic suggests letting babies nap as long as they want unless they then struggle to fall asleep at night. A short third nap is normal: its job is to bridge the gap to bedtime.

**Three naps or two?** If your baby fights the third nap most days and copes well without it, try a two-nap day with an earlier bedtime. If two-nap days end in an exhausted, crying baby by 5 p.m., go back to three for now *(practical suggestion)*. Our [baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age) explains the 3-to-2 transition in more detail.

## 6 month wake windows

A wake window is the time from waking up until falling asleep again, feeds included. There is no official AAP or AASM figure. The published ranges are:

| Source | Age band | Wake window |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cleveland Clinic | 5–7 months | 2–4 hours |
| Sleep Foundation | 5–7 months | 1.5–4.5 hours |
| Huckleberry (app example) | 6 months | 2–3 hours, longest before bed |
| Napper (app example) | 6 months | 2.5–3.5 hours |

**How to use them:** start the first window of the day near the lower end (about 2 hours), lengthen slightly through the day, and make the stretch before bedtime the longest, as Huckleberry suggests. Then let your baby's cues correct the numbers. Nationwide Children's Hospital lists fussing or crying, eye rubbing, staring into space, and pulling on the ears as common sleepy signs, and says babies fall asleep more easily if you put them down as soon as they show them.

## Example 6 month old schedules (examples only)

These are **examples only**. Shift every time to match your baby's real wake-up time and cues.

**Example A: three-nap day**

| Time | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| 6:45 a.m. | Wake, milk feed, curtains open |
| 8:45–10:00 a.m. | Nap 1 |
| 10:00 a.m. | Milk feed; solids practice if you've started |
| 12:30–1:45 p.m. | Nap 2 |
| 2:00 p.m. | Milk feed, floor play, outdoor time |
| 4:15–4:45 p.m. | Nap 3 (short) |
| 6:50 p.m. | Bedtime routine starts with a milk feed |
| About 7:30 p.m. | Down for the night; feeds if your baby still needs them |

**Example B: two-nap day (for a baby who is resisting nap 3)**

| Time | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| 6:45 a.m. | Wake, milk feed |
| 9:00–10:30 a.m. | Nap 1 |
| 1:30–3:00 p.m. | Nap 2 |
| 6:00 p.m. | Bedtime routine |
| About 6:30–6:45 p.m. | Asleep (earlier, to cover the longer afternoon) |

**App examples:** Huckleberry's sample starts at 6:30 a.m. with naps at 8:30, 12:00, and 4:00 and sleep at 7:15 p.m. Napper's sample starts at 7:00 a.m. with naps at 9:30, 1:00, and an optional 4:30 nap and bedtime at 7:30–8:00 p.m.

## Night sleep and night feeds at 6 months

- **Feeds.** KidsHealth says most babies of 4–7 months no longer need a middle-of-the-night feed, though some, particularly breastfed babies, still wake for one. Nationwide Children's Hospital says that by 6 months most babies are physiologically able to sleep through the night without feeding, yet 25–50% still wake at night. Ask your pediatrician before dropping night feeds, especially if weight gain has been slow.
- **Formula amounts.** HealthyChildren.org (AAP) says that by 6 months a formula-fed baby typically takes 6–8 ounces at each of 4 or 5 feeds in 24 hours.
- **"Sleeping through" isn't universal.** In a study of 388 infants, 27.9% to 57.0% of babies at 6 and 12 months were not sleeping through the night, depending on whether the definition was 6 or 8 hours, and this was not linked to development (Pennestri et al., 2018).
- **All babies wake.** Nationwide Children's explains that all babies wake briefly 4–6 times a night. The difference is whether they can settle back without help.

## Bedtime routine for a 6 month old

A routine is the one sleep habit with direct trial evidence at this age. In a randomized study of 405 families with children aged 7–36 months (slightly older than 6 months), a consistent nightly routine improved how quickly children fell asleep and reduced the number and length of night wakings within weeks, and mothers' mood improved too (Mindell et al., 2009).

A simple 20–30 minute routine, built from what the sources suggest:

1. **Milk feed first, or just before the routine.** Cleveland Clinic suggests feeding at the *start* of the routine so your baby doesn't rely on feeding to fall asleep. Nationwide Children's goes a step further and advises keeping bedtime feeds out of the bedtime routine after 6 months, so some families offer the last feed before the bath.
2. **Bath or wash and clean pajamas.** KidsHealth describes a warm bath followed by stories or singing as a good end-of-day signal.
3. **Brush the first teeth.** The AAP's Brush, Book, Bed program suggests brushing with a smear of fluoride toothpaste once a tooth appears. Don't put your baby to bed with a bottle (HealthyChildren.org).
4. **A short book or song.** Brush, Book, Bed suggests reading aloud together every day, even for 15 minutes.
5. **Into the crib drowsy but awake.** Finish in the room where your baby sleeps, with the lights low (Nationwide Children's).

Keep the steps in the same order every night, including weekends.

## A simple sleep plan for a 6 month old

If you want to improve sleep rather than just track it, here is a gentle plan using only what the sources support:

1. **Fix the wake-up time.** Start the day at about the same time each morning. Newcastle Hospitals NHS says this, with daylight, helps set your baby's body clock.
2. **Offer naps by cues and windows.** Use the windows above as a guide and put your baby down at the first sleepy signs.
3. **Protect the routine.** Same steps, same order, same place, every night.
4. **Practice falling asleep in the crib.** KidsHealth suggests putting your baby down drowsy but awake. If they cry, wait a few minutes, then soothe briefly without picking them up, and repeat as needed, as long as you know they are safe, fed, and well.
5. **Keep night visits brief.** KidsHealth notes that cuddling, feeding, or talking at every waking can teach a baby to wake for that attention.
6. **Give it about two weeks before judging** *(practical suggestion)*. In the Mindell trial, routine effects were measured over two weeks.

If you are considering a more structured method, our [sleep training methods guide](/sleep-training-methods-explained) compares the options.

## What else is changing at 6 months

- **Movement.** CDC says that by 6 months most babies roll from tummy to back, push up on straight arms, and lean on their hands to sit. KidsHealth says that once your baby rolls both ways consistently, they can stay in the position they choose, but always place them on their back to start. Nationwide Children's advises removing mobiles and hanging crib toys by about 5 months.
- **Solids.** The AAP supports starting solid foods at about 6 months alongside breast milk or formula (HealthyChildren.org). We found no evidence that starting solids improves sleep.
- **Cup.** HealthyChildren.org says you can offer a cup when solids start and a little water (4–8 ounces a day) from about 6 months.
- **Where baby sleeps.** The AAP recommends room-sharing without bed-sharing for at least the first 6 months (KidsHealth).

## What can make a 6 month schedule harder

- **Dropping the third nap too early** and ending up with an overtired baby at bedtime.
- **Feeding to sleep at every sleep,** which can make night wakings harder to settle (Cleveland Clinic; Nationwide Children's).
- **Keeping your baby up to "sleep better tonight."** Nationwide Children's warns that cutting naps leads to overtiredness and a worse night.
- **Changing the sleep setup** often, or keeping lighting different at bedtime from the rest of the night (Nationwide Children's).
- **A bottle in the crib** (HealthyChildren.org).

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Talk to your pediatrician if your baby snores loudly or seems to pause breathing in sleep, is unusually hard to wake, is feeding poorly or gaining weight slowly, or if broken nights continue for weeks. CDC also suggests telling your doctor if your baby has lost skills they once had or isn't meeting milestones.

## Frequently asked questions

**How many naps does a 6 month old need?**  
Usually three, sometimes two. KidsHealth says at least two; Mayo Clinic suggests dropping the late-afternoon third nap at about 9 months.

**What are normal 6 month wake windows?**  
About 2–4 hours (Cleveland Clinic, 5–7 months), shortest in the morning and longest before bed.

**What time should a 6 month old go to bed?**  
There is no official bedtime. Choose a time that follows the last nap by a full wake window, often between about 6:30 and 8 p.m. in the examples above, and earlier on days with short naps.

**Should a 6 month old sleep through the night?**  
Many can, but many don't. Nationwide Children's says 25–50% still wake at night at this age.

**What is a good sleep routine for a 6 month old?**  
A 20–30 minute routine in the same order every night: feed, bath or wash, teeth, a book or song, and into the crib drowsy but awake.

**Is 6 months a good age for a sleep plan?**  
Yes, many families start one now. KidsHealth describes a gentle drowsy-but-awake approach for 4–7 months.

## Let the schedule adjust itself (Yorix)

**Yorix** suggests the next nap from your baby's real day: log a short nap and it moves the rest of the day's windows and bedtime. You can see whether three or two naps is working better across the week. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [6 month milestones](/6-month-milestones)
- [6 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/6-months)
- [5 month old sleep schedule](/5-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [7 month old sleep schedule](/7-month-old-sleep-schedule)

- [Baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age)
- [Dream feed](/dream-feed)

body:
# 7 Month Old Sleep Schedule: Keeping Three Naps or Moving to Two

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

The question most parents of a 7-month-old are really asking is: *is it time for two naps?* At this age some babies are still happily on three, some are fighting the late-afternoon catnap, and some swing between the two from one day to the next. Below you'll find the sleep totals, how to tell which nap pattern fits, wake windows for 7 months, two example days, and a bedtime routine that holds up when the day has gone sideways.

## Short answer

Seven-month-olds need the same **12–16 hours a day** (naps counted) as every baby between 4 and 12 months, per the AASM, which the AAP endorses. Most are on **two or three naps**. Mayo Clinic expects a morning and an early-afternoon nap through the first year and only recommends phasing out an extra late-day nap at around **9 months**. Wake windows in the published charts are **2–4 hours** for 5–7 months and **2.5–4.5 hours** for 7–10 months (Cleveland Clinic). If the third nap keeps failing, try two naps with an **earlier bedtime** rather than pushing your baby to stay awake.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Topic | Figure | Where it comes from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sleep per day, counting naps | 12 to 16 hours | AASM (endorsed by the AAP) |
| Overnight | Usually a 9+ hour stretch by half a year, with short wake-ups | KidsHealth (4–7 months) |
| Daytime total | Roughly 3–4 hours; Australia's government site gives 2–4 hours for 6–12 months | KidsHealth; Pregnancy, Birth and Baby |
| Nap count | Two or three; the late catnap tends to go around 9 months | Mayo Clinic |
| Awake time between sleeps | Cleveland Clinic: 2–4 h up to 7 months, then 2.5–4.5 h. Sleep Foundation: 1.5–4.5 h, then 1.5–6 h | Cleveland Clinic; Sleep Foundation |
| Night waking past 6 months | Still happens for a quarter to half of babies | Nationwide Children's Hospital |

## How much sleep does a 7 month old need?

Nothing changes officially at 7 months: the AASM's 12-to-16-hour band covers every baby from 4 months up to the first birthday. For the split between night and day, Australia's Pregnancy, Birth and Baby site suggests nights of 10 to 14 hours for babies between 6 and 12 months, with naps adding up to 2 to 4 hours.

**App examples (not clinical guidance):** Huckleberry's target for this month is roughly 14 hours a day, of which 2.5–3 hours are naps. Napper's range is 12–15 hours, and it pictures two naps lasting between one and two hours apiece.

## Three naps or two at 7 months?

There's no age at which a baby must drop the third nap. The two app examples even disagree: Huckleberry says most 7-month-olds still need three naps "for another month or so," while Napper describes most babies of this age on two. Mayo Clinic's 9-month suggestion for losing the extra nap is a reasonable outer marker.

**Signs two naps might suit your baby now** *(practical suggestion)*:

- The third nap takes 20+ minutes to start, or doesn't happen, most days for a week or more.
- The first two naps are each about an hour or longer.
- Your baby is still in a good mood by late afternoon on days without the third nap.
- Bedtime keeps getting pushed late because of the third nap.

**Signs to stay on three for now:** short first naps, a baby who melts down by 4 p.m., or night wakings that increase when you try two naps.

**Making the switch.** Move bedtime earlier on two-nap days. Losing daytime sleep without making it up at night tends to backfire: Nationwide Children's Hospital links fewer naps to an overtired baby and a rougher night. Expect some mixed weeks with two naps on some days and three on others. For the bigger picture, see how nap counts shift month by month in our [baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age).

## 7 month wake windows

Seven months falls right where two chart bands meet, so it helps to see both:

| | Band ending at 7 months | Band starting at 7 months |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cleveland Clinic | 2 to 4 h | 2.5 to 4.5 h |
| Sleep Foundation | 1.5 to 4.5 h | 1.5 to 6 h |

The apps give narrower targets for this exact month (app examples, not clinical guidance): Huckleberry 2.25 to 3.5 h, Napper 2.5 to 3.5 h.

On a three-nap day the windows sit at the lower end, often around 2.25–2.5 hours. On a two-nap day they need to stretch to about 3–3.5 hours, especially before bedtime *(our reading of the ranges above)*. No organization like the AAP or AASM publishes wake windows; treat every row as a starting point and adjust by your baby's signs.

## Example 7 month old schedules (examples only)

These are **examples only**. Start from your baby's real wake-up time.

**Three naps**

| Time | Plan |
| --- | --- |
| 6:30 a.m. | Up, milk feed |
| 8:45–9:45 a.m. | Nap 1 |
| 10:00 a.m. | Solids practice, then play |
| 12:15–1:30 p.m. | Nap 2 |
| 1:30 p.m. | Milk feed, walk outdoors |
| 4:00–4:30 p.m. | Nap 3 (catnap) |
| 5:00 p.m. | Family dinner: solids |
| 6:30 p.m. | Bedtime routine |
| 7:00 p.m. | Asleep |

**Two naps**

| Time | Plan |
| --- | --- |
| 6:30 a.m. | Up, milk feed |
| 9:15–10:30 a.m. | Nap 1 |
| 11:00 a.m. | Solids, play |
| 1:45–3:15 p.m. | Nap 2 |
| 3:15 p.m. | Milk feed |
| 5:00 p.m. | Solids dinner |
| 6:00 p.m. | Bedtime routine |
| 6:30–6:45 p.m. | Asleep |

**App examples:** Huckleberry's 7-month sample uses three naps (9:15, 12:45, and 4:15) with bedtime at 7:30 p.m. Napper's uses two naps (9:30–11:00 and 1:30–3:00) with bedtime at 7:30–8:00 p.m.

## Bedtime routine for a 7 month old

The strongest evidence for any bedtime habit comes from a randomized trial of 405 mothers whose children were 7–36 months old. After a baseline week, families who followed a set nightly routine for two weeks saw children fall asleep faster and wake less often and for shorter periods than the control group (Mindell et al., 2009). Seven months was the youngest age in the infant arm (7–18 months).

To build a 7-month routine:

- **Keep it short.** Cleveland Clinic suggests about 20–30 minutes.
- **Finish where the night happens.** Nationwide Children's Hospital wants the final steps done in your baby's sleep room, with lighting that stays the same until morning.
- **Separate milk from sleep.** After six months, the same hospital suggests the bedtime feed shouldn't be a routine step. Offer milk first, then move on to the bath and the rest.
- **Brush the first tooth.** Once a tooth shows, the AAP's Brush, Book, Bed campaign recommends a rice-grain smear of fluoride toothpaste, and it rules out bottles in bed.
- **Let your baby finish falling asleep.** KidsHealth's approach for this age is to put your baby down still a little awake; if there's crying, give it a few minutes, then comfort without lifting them out.

## Night wakings and feeds at 7 months

By this age, KidsHealth says, a feed in the middle of the night is usually no longer a need, although plenty of breastfed babies still ask for one. Brief rousing is universal: Nationwide Children's Hospital counts four to six short wake-ups a night for every baby and separates "self-soothers," who drift off again unaided, from "signalers," who call out. It also notes that somewhere between a quarter and half of babies keep waking past six months. If your baby still has night feeds and you want to reduce them, talk to your pediatrician first, and see our [dream feed](/dream-feed) page for one gentle option.

Separation worries can start to appear in this window too (KidsHealth). The same source points out that if each wake-up earns a cuddle, a feed, or a chat, a baby may learn to wake for it.

## Daytime development that affects sleep

- **Solids.** HealthyChildren.org suggests solids from about 6 months, alongside breast milk or formula. Plan solid meals during wake windows, not right before a nap *(practical suggestion)*.
- **Rolling and sitting.** A baby who rolls front-to-back and back-to-front reliably may sleep in whatever position they end up in, KidsHealth says, but should still be put down on their back. Anything hanging over the crib should already be gone; Nationwide Children's sets that at around 5 months.
- **Room-sharing.** The AAP's advice (via KidsHealth) is a separate sleep space in the parents' room for six months at minimum, and ideally until age one.

## What can make a 7 month schedule harder

- Dropping the third nap without moving bedtime earlier.
- A long, stimulating routine that keeps stretching *(practical suggestion)*.
- Leaving a bottle with your baby in the crib (HealthyChildren.org warns of tooth decay and ear infections).
- Big changes to the nap place or bedtime from day to day.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Talk to your doctor if your baby snores loudly or has pauses in breathing, isn't feeding well or gaining weight, seems unusually sleepy or hard to wake, has lost skills, or if night wakings are leaving you unable to cope.

## Frequently asked questions

**How many naps should a 7 month old take?**  
Two or three. Plenty of babies keep a short late-day nap until around 9 months.

**What are 7 month wake windows?**  
Usually about 2.25–3.5 hours. Cleveland Clinic's charts give 2–4 hours (5–7 months) and 2.5–4.5 hours (7–10 months).

**What time should a 7 month old go to bed?**  
Example schedules mostly put it between 6:30 and 8 p.m. On two-nap days, go early.

**What's a good bedtime routine for a 7 month old?**  
Something short and repeatable: milk before the routine, then washing, sleepwear, brushing any teeth, a song, and down awake. Around 20–30 minutes is plenty.

**Why is my 7 month old fighting the third nap?**  
Often because they're ready to stay awake longer. Try a two-nap day with an earlier bedtime and see how the night goes.

## Track the 3-to-2 switch (Yorix)

**Yorix** shows three-nap and two-nap days side by side in a weekly view, so you can see which pattern gives a calmer evening and a better night. It also suggests an earlier bedtime when a nap is skipped. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.
