description: 8 month old sleep schedule: a typical 2-nap day, 8 month wake windows, bedtime, meals and milk around sleep, and how a schedule differs from a regression.
body:
# 8 Month Old Sleep Schedule: A Typical Two-Nap Day

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

This page is about the **ordinary day** of an 8-month-old: when naps usually fall, how long your baby can stay awake, where meals and milk fit, and what time bedtime tends to land. If your baby's sleep has suddenly fallen apart (new night wakings, nap strikes, standing up in the crib at 2 a.m.), that's a different question, answered on our [8 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/8-months) page. Many families need both: a sensible plan for the day, and patience for the weeks when a new skill disrupts it.

## Short answer

KidsHealth says babies of 8–12 months need **12–16 hours of sleep a day, including 9–12 hours at night**, and will likely still take **two naps** lasting anywhere from 30 minutes to 2 hours. Some 8-month-olds still have a short third nap; Mayo Clinic suggests phasing it out at about **9 months**. Published wake windows for 7–10 months are **2.5–4.5 hours** (Cleveland Clinic). Most example schedules put bedtime somewhere between **6:30 and 8 p.m.**, earlier after short naps.

### Key numbers at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total sleep | 12–16 hours per 24 hours | KidsHealth (8–12 months); AASM |
| Night stretch | 9–12 hours | KidsHealth |
| Naps | Likely 2, each 30 minutes to 2 hours | KidsHealth |
| Third nap | Usually phased out around 9 months | Mayo Clinic |
| Wake windows (7–10 months) | 2.5–4.5 hours / 1.5–6 hours | Cleveland Clinic / Sleep Foundation |
| Milk | About 24 ounces (720 mL) of breast milk or formula a day, alongside solids | HealthyChildren.org (AAP), 8–12 months |

## Schedule or regression? A quick check

| If you're seeing... | It's probably... | Where to read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A fairly steady day; you want times for naps and bedtime | A schedule question | This page |
| The third nap getting harder, bedtime drifting later | A nap transition | This page, "Two naps or three" |
| Sudden new night wakings, standing or crawling in the crib, crying when you leave | A developmental disruption, often called the 8-month regression | [8 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/8-months) |

Newcastle Hospitals NHS says it's normal for some babies to begin waking more often at night again at 8–9 months, so a steady schedule and a rough patch can overlap.

## How much sleep at 8 months?

The 12–16 hour range (KidsHealth; AASM) holds all the way to the first birthday. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby gives a similar picture for 6–12 months: 10–14 hours at night and 2–4 hours of naps.

**App examples (not clinical guidance):** Huckleberry aims for about 14 hours, with 11–12 at night and 2–3 hours over 2–3 naps. Napper describes 12–15 hours, with 10–12 at night and 2–3 hours in two naps of 1–1.5 hours each.

## Two naps or three at 8 months?

Most 8-month-olds are on two naps or moving there. KidsHealth says babies of this age will likely still take two naps, and Mayo Clinic recommends a morning and early-afternoon nap (it suggests trying 9 a.m. and 1 p.m.), with any late-afternoon third nap cut at about 9 months.

Huckleberry (app example) describes 8 months as a common time for the switch and says it's normal to have a mix of two-nap and three-nap days while it happens. If the morning and afternoon naps are each an hour or more, two naps usually cover the day; if one is short, a 20–30 minute catnap in late afternoon can still rescue bedtime *(practical suggestion)*.

## 8 month wake windows

| Source | Age band | Wake window |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cleveland Clinic | 7–10 months | 2.5–4.5 hours |
| Sleep Foundation | 7–10 months | 1.5–6 hours |
| Huckleberry (app example) | 8 months | 2.25–3.5 hours |
| Napper (app example) | 8 months | 3–4 hours between naps |

On a two-nap day, a common shape is a shorter morning window (about 2.5–3 hours), a longer midday one, and the longest before bed *(our reading of the app examples)*. Sleep Foundation suggests watching for your baby's own "tell": the sign that, when you act on it, lets your baby fall asleep within about 15 minutes of being put down.

## A typical 8 month old day (example only)

This is **an example only**, built around two naps, three meals, and milk feeds. Move the whole day earlier or later to match your baby's wake-up time.

| Time | Sleep | Food and activity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 6:45 a.m. | Wake | Milk feed |
| 7:45 a.m. | | Breakfast (solids) |
| 9:30–10:45 a.m. | Nap 1 | |
| 11:00 a.m. | | Milk feed, floor play |
| 12:00 p.m. | | Lunch |
| 2:15–3:30 p.m. | Nap 2 | |
| 3:30 p.m. | | Milk feed and a snack, outdoor time |
| 5:30 p.m. | | Dinner |
| 6:30 p.m. | Bedtime routine | Last milk feed before the bath |
| 7:00 p.m. | Asleep | |

**App examples:** Huckleberry's 8-month sample: wake 7:00, naps 9:45–11:15 and 2:30–4:00, bedtime 7:30 p.m. Napper's: wake 7:00, naps 9:30–11:00 and 1:30–3:00, bedtime 7:30–8:00 p.m.

## Meals, milk, and sleep

HealthyChildren.org (AAP) says babies of 8–12 months still need about 400–500 calories a day from breast milk or formula, roughly 24 ounces, and that around 8 months you can offer slightly coarser foods. Its sample menu includes milk with each meal and a last breast milk or formula feed before bed, followed by water or toothbrushing.

Two sleep-related points from the same source and its sister pages:

- **No bottle in the crib.** HealthyChildren.org warns this can lead to tooth decay and ear infections.
- **Cup practice** can start now. The AAP suggests offering a cup around 6 months and finishing the move off bottles between 12 and 18 months.

We found no evidence that more solids at dinner make a baby sleep longer.

## Bedtime at 8 months

KidsHealth suggests a soothing routine, such as a warm bath followed by stories or singing, and says the same activities can carry on for years. Then put your baby in the crib drowsy but still awake. If your baby cries, KidsHealth suggests staying away for a few minutes, then soothing briefly without picking them up, as long as you know they're safe, fed, dry, and well.

Keep the routine short (Cleveland Clinic suggests 20–30 minutes), and keep the last steps in the bedroom (Nationwide Children's Hospital).

## A safer crib for a mover

Many 8-month-olds crawl, sit up by themselves, and start pulling up (the CDC's 9-month milestones include getting to a sitting position without help). KidsHealth suggests checking what your baby can reach from a sitting or standing position in the crib, such as cords, curtains, or wall hangings. Nationwide Children's Hospital says to take down mobiles by about 5 months, when babies begin pulling up. What to do when your baby stands up in the crib at night is covered on our [10 month old sleep schedule](/10-month-old-sleep-schedule) page.

## What can make an 8 month schedule harder

- Holding on to three naps once the third one pushes bedtime past 8 p.m.
- Dropping the third nap without an earlier bedtime (Nationwide Children's: cutting naps leads to overtiredness).
- A bottle or nursing session as the very last step every night, if your baby then needs it at every waking (KidsHealth; Cleveland Clinic).
- Big weekend swings in nap times *(practical suggestion)*.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Talk to your doctor about loud snoring, pauses in breathing, poor feeding or weight gain, a baby who is hard to wake, loss of skills they used to have, or broken nights that leave you unable to cope.

## Frequently asked questions

**How many naps does an 8 month old need?**  
Usually two, sometimes a third short one while transitioning. KidsHealth says babies of 8–12 months likely take two.

**What are 8 month wake windows?**  
About 2.5–4.5 hours in Cleveland Clinic's 7–10 month range; app examples cluster around 2.25–4 hours.

**What time should an 8 month old go to bed?**  
Often 6:30–8 p.m. Aim for a full wake window after the last nap.

**Is my 8 month old's bad sleep a regression or the wrong schedule?**  
If the day is steady and bedtime is late, adjust the schedule. If sleep changed suddenly with new skills or separation worries, read our [8 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/8-months) page.

**How much milk does an 8 month old need?**  
About 24 ounces a day of breast milk or formula, according to HealthyChildren.org.

## Plan the day around two naps (Yorix)

**Yorix** predicts the next nap from your baby's last wake-up and moves bedtime when a nap runs short. Meals and milk feeds can sit in the same log. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

- [9 month old sleep schedule](/9-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age)
- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)

body:
# 9 Month Old Sleep Schedule: Settling Into Two Naps

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Nine months is when most schedules shrink to **two naps**. The third, late-afternoon catnap is usually gone or on its way out, wake windows stretch toward three hours or more, and bedtime often moves a little earlier to make up for it. At the same time, many 9-month-olds become clingy and wary of strangers, which can show up at bedtime. This page gives you the numbers, a sample day, and a calm way to handle the evening.

## Short answer

A 9-month-old still needs **12–16 hours of sleep in every 24**, and KidsHealth expects **9–12 of them overnight**, with the rest in **two naps**. Mayo Clinic suggests cutting out a late-afternoon third nap at about **9 months**, which lets bedtime move earlier. Cleveland Clinic's wake-window chart gives **2.5 to 4.5 hours** for this age band. The CDC's 9-month advice is short and practical: **have routines for sleeping and feeding**, because consistent sleep times make it easier.

### Key numbers at a glance

| At 9 months | Range | Based on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Daily sleep with naps | 12 to 16 h | CDC 9-month page; KidsHealth |
| Overnight stretch | 9 to 12 h | KidsHealth |
| How many naps | Two for most; the third goes around now | KidsHealth; Mayo Clinic |
| Each nap | Half an hour up to two hours | KidsHealth |
| Time awake between sleeps | Cleveland Clinic 2.5 to 4.5 h; Sleep Foundation 1.5 to 6 h (both for 7–10 months) | Cleveland Clinic; Sleep Foundation |
| Social milestones | Shy, clingy, or fearful with strangers; reacts when you leave | CDC (9 months) |

## How much sleep does a 9 month old need?

The CDC's 9-month milestone page repeats the AASM range: **12 to 16 hours a day for 4- to 12-month-olds, including naps**. KidsHealth puts 9–12 of those hours at night. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby describes 2–4 hours of naps for 6–12 months.

**App examples (not clinical guidance):** Huckleberry's 9-month target is close to 14 hours a day, two of them or a little more in naps. Napper's page pictures two naps of roughly an hour to an hour and a half.

## Saying goodbye to the third nap

Mayo Clinic recommends a morning and an early-afternoon nap from 4 months to 1 year and suggests cutting a late-afternoon third nap at about 9 months. Huckleberry (app example) says most babies are ready to drop it by 9 months and lists signs like shorter naps, resisting one nap (often the last), and resisting bedtime.

**How to drop it** *(practical suggestion)*:

1. Push the morning nap 15–30 minutes later over a few days.
2. Let the afternoon nap start after lunch rather than straight after the morning one.
3. On days when the afternoon nap ends early, bring bedtime forward. Nationwide Children's Hospital warns that cutting naps without replacing the sleep leads to overtiredness and a worse night.
4. If your baby is falling apart by 5 p.m. most days, a 15–20 minute catnap is still fine for a week or two.

## 9 month wake windows

- **Clinical charts (7–10 months):** Cleveland Clinic says 2.5 to 4.5 hours; Sleep Foundation's band is wider, 1.5 to 6 hours.
- **App examples for 9 months:** Huckleberry uses 2.75 to 3.5 hours; Napper says 3 to 4.

That works out to roughly **3 hours before the first nap, a bit more before the second, and 3.5 hours or so before bed** for many babies *(our reading of the app examples, not a clinical figure)*. The two apps even disagree about which window is longer: Napper says babies often stay awake longer in the morning, while Huckleberry's sample has the shortest window first. Follow your baby's signs.

## Sample 9 month old schedule (example only)

**Example only.** Adjust every time to your baby's morning wake-up.

| Time | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| 6:30 a.m. | Wake, milk |
| 7:30 a.m. | Breakfast |
| 9:30–10:45 a.m. | Morning nap |
| 11:00 a.m. | Milk, play, outing |
| 12:00 p.m. | Lunch |
| 2:00–3:30 p.m. | Afternoon nap |
| 3:30 p.m. | Milk and snack |
| 5:15 p.m. | Family dinner |
| 6:30 p.m. | Bath, pajamas, teeth, book |
| 7:00 p.m. | Asleep |

**App examples:** Huckleberry's 9-month day starts at 6:30 a.m., puts naps at 9:15 and 2:15 (90 minutes each) and has the baby asleep by 7:15 p.m. Napper's starts at 7, with naps at 10 and 2:30 and a 7:30–8 p.m. bedtime.

## Clinginess at bedtime: what helps

The CDC lists being **shy, clingy, or fearful around strangers** and **reacting when you leave** as 9-month milestones. KidsHealth says separation anxiety commonly appears between 8 months and 1 year. That can make the moment you walk out of the bedroom the hardest part of the day.

- **Say goodnight, don't sneak out.** The CDC's 9-month tip is to say a quick, cheerful goodbye instead of sneaking away, even if your baby cries.
- **Short, loving check-ins.** KidsHealth describes a few calm words from the bedroom door and a quick exit, lengthening the time between visits.
- **Don't add new comfort habits at night.** KidsHealth notes that cuddling, feeding, or talking at each waking can encourage regular waking for that attention.
- **A comfort object later.** Nationwide Children's Hospital suggests introducing a security object, like a small stuffed animal or blanket, by 12 months. Until the first birthday, KidsHealth advises keeping soft objects and blankets out of the crib.

Our [8 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/8-months) page covers the wider 8–10 month dip in more depth.

## Night feeds at 9 months

Nationwide Children's Hospital says that by 6 months most babies are physiologically able to sleep through the night without feeding, but 25–50% still wake. Newcastle Hospitals NHS adds that some babies start waking more often again at 8–9 months, and that most babies are at least a year old before they settle all night, every night. If your baby still feeds at night and you'd like to cut back, check with your pediatrician first, especially if weight gain is a concern. The [dream feed](/dream-feed) page explains one way some families shift a feed earlier.

## Getting ready for the first birthday

- **Pulling up and standing.** The CDC's 9-month tip is to put your baby close to things they can safely pull up on during the day.
- **Crib check.** KidsHealth advises looking for anything your baby can reach from sitting or standing, such as blind cords or curtains.
- **Cup practice.** HealthyChildren.org suggests reducing bottle feeds gradually and finishing the switch to a cup between 12 and 18 months, starting with bottles at naps and bedtime.

## What can make a 9 month schedule harder

- Keeping a late third nap that pushes bedtime toward 8:30 p.m. or later.
- Sneaking out at bedtime, which can make separation worries worse (CDC tip).
- Changing the bedtime routine on alternate nights.
- Handing over a bottle once your baby is lying in the crib, which HealthyChildren.org advises against.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Speak to your doctor if your baby snores loudly or seems to stop breathing in sleep, isn't gaining weight, seems unusually tired or hard to wake, isn't sitting without support, or has lost skills. The CDC's milestone checklist is a useful starting point for that conversation.

## Frequently asked questions

**How many naps should a 9 month old take?**  
Usually two. Mayo Clinic suggests cutting the late-afternoon third nap at about 9 months.

**What are 9 month wake windows?**  
Apps suggest roughly 2.75 to 4 hours; the Cleveland Clinic band for 7–10 months is 2.5 to 4.5.

**What time should a 9 month old go to bed?**  
Anywhere from about half past six to eight is typical; short-nap days call for the earlier end.

**Why is my 9 month old suddenly clingy at bedtime?**  
Separation anxiety is common between 8 months and 1 year (KidsHealth). Keep goodbyes short and cheerful.

**Should a 9 month old still wake to feed?**  
Some do. Nationwide Children's says 25–50% of babies still wake after 6 months. Ask your pediatrician before night weaning.

## Two-nap days at a glance (Yorix)

**Yorix** shows how long each wake window actually ran, so you can see whether 3 hours or 3.5 hours before the afternoon nap gives a better sleep. It also flags days when bedtime should come earlier. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

heading: Baby Waking Every Hour at Night: Why It Happens and What Helps
description: Why babies wake every hour at night by age, what's normal and what isn't, the signs to call your pediatrician, and practical steps toward longer stretches.
body:
# Baby Waking Every Hour at Night: Why It Happens and What Helps

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Few things are as draining as a baby who wakes every hour. By the third night you're counting cycles, and by the fifth you're wondering whether something is wrong. Frequent waking is common in babies, and some of it is protective. Hourly waking *all night, every night*, though, usually has a cause worth looking for. Below we explain what's normal at each age, the most common reasons for hourly waking, when to call the doctor, and what helps.

## Short answer

Waking often is **normal for young babies**, especially under 6 months, and many still wake at night well beyond that. Waking **every hour for part of the night** is common during the newborn months, the 4-month sleep changes, illness, or teething. Waking **every hour all night with no longer stretches** isn't typical: Huckleberry (app example) suggests checking in with your pediatrician, because reflux, feeding problems, or another medical issue may be involved. When health checks out, the most common causes are **needing the same help to fall back asleep at each cycle**, **overtiredness**, **hunger**, and **discomfort**. A steady routine, the right daytime schedule, and (when your baby is old enough) practice falling asleep independently usually help.

### Key facts at a glance

| Question | What we found | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Night wakings in young infants | 0–3.4 per night (0–2 months) in pooled studies | Galland et al., 2012 |
| Under 6 months | Waking regularly is normal; behavioral programs not shown to help | Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne |
| Waking 1–3 times a night | Not unusual for the first 6 months | Texas Children's |
| Longer stretches at 3–4 months | Only about 1 in 3 babies, per NCT | NCT |
| A "good sleeper" | Wakes often but can get back to sleep | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |
| Hourly waking all night | Not typical; talk to your pediatrician | Huckleberry (app example) |

## Why babies wake between sleep cycles

Everyone surfaces briefly at the end of each sleep cycle. Adults rarely remember it. Babies' cycles are shorter, so the surfacing happens more often, and if something is different from when they fell asleep, they call out. The Royal Children's Hospital (RCH) Melbourne explains that babies who fall asleep with help (being fed, patted, rocked, or held) may need that same help every time they wake between cycles. The UK charity NCT adds that night waking is a normal part of development and is thought to be protective against SIDS, so the goal isn't to stop all waking.

## What's normal at each age

| Age | What's typical | Is hourly waking expected? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0–2 months | Frequent feeds day and night; days and nights may be mixed up | For part of the night, yes; but most newborns have some longer stretches |
| 3–4 months | Sleep becomes more adult-like; the [4 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/4-months) | Common for a few weeks |
| 5–6 months | Many still wake 1–3 times; some begin linking cycles | Not usually all night |
| 6–12 months | Object permanence; sleep associations matter more | Possible in phases; usually a cause to find |
| 12 months + | Most babies have long night stretches, but some still wake | Not typical; look for causes |

Sources for this table: Huckleberry (app example), RCH Melbourne, Texas Children's, and Henderson et al. (2010).

### Newborns

Hunger is the main reason newborns wake often, especially during growth spurts and cluster feeding. Huckleberry (app example) notes that even newborns usually manage some stretches longer than an hour. If yours seems to wake hourly around the clock, mixed-up days and nights may be part of it; capping daytime naps at about 2 hours and keeping nights dark can help.

### 4 month old waking every hour

Around 3–4 months, sleep matures and babies spend more time in lighter sleep. Babies who were fed or rocked all the way to sleep may now need that help at each cycle. Huckleberry (app example) calls this the most common reason for hourly waking in babies 3–4 months and older.

### 6 month old waking every hour

RCH Melbourne explains that from about 6 months, babies reach object permanence: they know you still exist when they can't see you, and they may cry at the end of each cycle to bring you back. Sleep associations can start causing more problems at this age.

### 8–12 months and beyond

The same causes apply, and by now most babies have at least one long night stretch. If hourly waking continues for weeks, look at the daytime schedule and at how your baby falls asleep at bedtime.

## Common causes of waking every hour

1. **Sleep associations.** Your baby needs the same help to fall back asleep at every cycle change (RCH Melbourne; Huckleberry, app example).
2. **Overtiredness.** Short naps or long wake windows make it harder to stay asleep. Napper (app example) points out that a newborn's wake window can be as short as 30–50 minutes, so overtiredness can creep up quickly.
3. **Hunger.** Especially in young babies, during growth spurts, or if daytime intake has dropped.
4. **Day/night confusion.** Long daytime naps and stimulating nights.
5. **Illness and discomfort.** A cold, teething, a wet diaper, or feeling too hot or cold (NCT; Huckleberry, app example).
6. **Reflux or feeding problems.** Frequent spit-up, arching, or coughing during feeds (Huckleberry, app example).
7. **Breathing problems during sleep.** Snoring, pauses in breathing, or struggling to breathe (RCH Melbourne).
8. **Changes in routine.** Travel, a new caregiver, a move.

## When to call your pediatrician

Talk to your doctor or child health nurse if your baby:

- wakes every hour **all night** with no longer stretches;
- snores, seems to pause when breathing, or has trouble breathing at any age (RCH Melbourne);
- seems to be in pain, or shows reflux signs such as frequent spit-up, arching, or coughing during feeds;
- isn't gaining weight well;
- is feeding fewer than 8–12 times a day if breastfed or 5–8 times if bottle-fed, or has fewer than 4 wet diapers a day (HealthyChildren.org);
- has a fever, or you have any other worry. Trust your instincts.

RCH Melbourne also recommends speaking to your doctor or nurse if you're struggling to cope. Sleep deprivation is hard, and asking for support is part of looking after your baby.

## What helps: a practical plan

### 1. Rule out health problems first

Go through the list above. If something fits, start with your pediatrician.

### 2. Get the daytime schedule right

Overtired babies tend to sleep worse, not better. Check [wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age) and make sure naps add up to a reasonable total. If naps are very short, see [short naps](/short-naps).

### 3. Build a predictable bedtime routine

RCH Melbourne notes that by about 6 months, babies can predict and respond to positive routines. Keep the same few calm steps every evening.

### 4. Feed fully in the day and early evening

For babies who still need night feeds, keep them. For older babies, a full bedtime feed (not one where your baby falls asleep halfway) can reduce hunger wakings. Ask your pediatrician before dropping night feeds.

### 5. Separate feeding from falling asleep (when your baby is ready)

Moving the feed earlier in the bedtime routine helps break a feed-to-sleep link. RCH Melbourne says there's no evidence behavioral sleep interventions help babies **under 6 months**, so for young babies, respond to cues as best you can. From about 6 months, gentle approaches or structured sleep training are options. See [when to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training).

### 6. Respond consistently at night

Keep night interactions quiet, dim, and the same each time. Whatever approach you choose, consistency helps more than switching tactics every night.

### 7. Share the load

NCT suggests sharing night-time care where possible. If your baby is formula-fed, another caregiver can give some feeds; NCT also discusses how a breastfed baby's feeds can be shared once breastfeeding is established.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is it normal for my baby to wake every hour?**  
For part of the night, especially in young babies or during a regression, illness, or teething, yes. Every hour all night isn't typical and is worth discussing with your pediatrician.

**Why does my 4 month old wake every hour?**  
Usually because sleep has just matured and your baby needs help to link cycles, often the same help they had at bedtime.

**Why does my 6 month old wake every hour?**  
Common reasons are sleep associations, new skills, object permanence, and overtiredness. Hunger and teething can also play a part.

**Will my baby grow out of waking every hour?**  
Many babies' sleep consolidates over time; Henderson et al. found the fastest changes in the first 4 months. If the pattern lasts weeks, look for causes rather than waiting.

**Does feeding to sleep cause night waking?**  
It can contribute from about 3–4 months, because your baby may need a feed to fall back asleep at each cycle. It's not harmful, and you don't have to change it if it works for your family.

**What if my baby wakes every 30–45 minutes at night?**  
Huckleberry (app example) says waking every 30 minutes without longer stretches isn't typical and may point to extreme overtiredness or discomfort such as reflux or illness. Talk to your pediatrician.

## See the pattern behind the wakings (Yorix)

**Yorix** logs each night waking alongside naps and feeds, so after a week you can see whether wakings cluster after short-nap days or late bedtimes, and bring that log to your pediatrician. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [Surviving night wakings](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents)
- [Split nights](/split-nights)
- [False starts](/false-starts)
- [Sleep regression ages](/sleep-regression)
- [Cry it out method](/cry-it-out-method)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026. Study details come from the published abstracts. App pages are used only as labeled examples.

1. The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne. Kids Health Info: "Sleep problems – babies and toddlers." Reviewed February 2025. <https://www.rch.org.au/kidsinfo/fact_sheets/Sleep_problems_babies_and_toddlers/>.
2. NCT. "What to do when a baby or toddler keeps waking at night." <https://www.nct.org.uk/information/baby-toddler/caring-for-your-baby-or-toddler/what-do-when-baby-or-toddler-keeps-waking-night>.
3. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Sleeping Through the Night." <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/Sleeping-Through-the-Night.aspx>.
4. Texas Children's. "Tips for parents on infant sleep training and safety." <https://www.texaschildrens.org/content/wellness/tips-for-parents-infant-sleep-training-and-safety>.
5. Galland BC, et al. "Normal sleep patterns in infants and children: a systematic review of observational studies." *Sleep Medicine Reviews*, 2012. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21784676/> (abstract via Europe PMC).
6. Henderson JM, et al. "Sleeping through the night: the consolidation of self-regulated sleep across the first year of life." *Pediatrics*, 2010. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20974775/> (abstract via Europe PMC).
7. App example: Huckleberry. "Why your baby wakes up every hour and what to do about it." Updated 3 September 2026. <https://huckleberrycare.com/blog/baby-waking-up-every-hour>.
8. App example: Napper. "Why won't my baby sleep - common causes and tips." <https://napper.app/en/blog/baby-sleep/why-wont-my-baby-sleep/>.

heading: Contact Naps: Safety Rules, Benefits, and How to Transition to the Crib
description: Contact naps explained: why babies love sleeping on you, safety rules from AAP-based guidance, when they become a problem, and gentle ways to move to the crib.
body:
# Contact Naps: Safety Rules, Benefits, and How to Transition to the Crib

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

A contact nap is any nap your baby takes on or against you: on your chest, in your arms, or snuggled in a carrier. For many babies, especially in the early weeks, it's the only nap that seems to work. Contact naps are not a bad habit, and they can be lovely. But they come with one firm safety rule, and if they become the only way your baby sleeps, they can wear you down. This guide covers both.

## Short answer

**Contact naps** are fine as long as **you stay awake and alert** the whole time. U.S. safe sleep guidance from NICHD's Safe to Sleep campaign, based on AAP recommendations, says couches and armchairs are **never safe places for babies to sleep** and are **extremely dangerous** if an adult falls asleep while holding a baby. If you might doze off, put your baby on their back in their own crib or bassinet. If you do fall asleep, move your baby to their own sleep space **as soon as you wake**. Carriers and slings are not meant for routine naps; if your baby falls asleep in one, move them to their sleep space as soon as possible. In the early months, holding your baby a lot won't spoil them (KidsHealth).

### Key facts at a glance

| Question | Answer | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Are contact naps safe? | Only while the adult is fully awake | NICHD Safe to Sleep; HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |
| Can a baby nap with me on the couch? | No: couches and armchairs are never safe for baby sleep | NICHD Safe to Sleep |
| What if I fall asleep holding my baby? | Move them to their own sleep space as soon as you wake | NICHD; HealthyChildren.org |
| Naps in a carrier or sling? | Not for regular sleep; move baby when possible | NICHD Safe to Sleep |
| Will holding my newborn spoil them? | No: spoiling isn't a concern in the first months | KidsHealth |
| Benefits of carrying | Newborns held or carried more tend to have less colic and fussiness | KidsHealth |

## Why babies love contact naps

Being held is calming. Newcastle Hospitals NHS lists cuddling, skin-to-skin contact, and being carried among the activities that help babies relax enough to sleep. The NHS describes skin-to-skin time as comforting for both parent and baby in the early weeks. KidsHealth notes that newborns who are held or carried more during the day tend to have less colic and fussiness.

For many families, contact naps are also simply practical: a way to get a newborn to nap at all, or to rest during a growth spurt or illness.

## The safety rules for contact naps

These rules come from NICHD's Safe to Sleep campaign and HealthyChildren.org (AAP):

1. **Stay awake.** A contact nap is safe only while you are alert. If you feel drowsy, put your baby on their back in their crib, bassinet, or play yard.
2. **Never on a couch or armchair if you might fall asleep.** NICHD calls these surfaces extremely dangerous when an adult falls asleep while feeding, comforting, or snuggling a baby.
3. **If you fall asleep anyway,** move your baby to their own safe sleep space as soon as you wake (NICHD; HealthyChildren.org).
4. **Carriers and slings are not nap spaces.** NICHD says not to use carrying devices for regular sleep. If your baby falls asleep in one, move them to their sleep space as soon as you can. The NHS advises using slings safely.
5. **Clear the area** of pillows and loose bedding when you feed or cuddle while tired (HealthyChildren.org).

### Tips to stay awake during a contact nap

HealthyChildren.org suggests ideas for tired parents during feeds that work for contact naps too:

- have a snack and water within reach;
- listen to or watch something that keeps your attention;
- set a phone alarm to go off every few minutes;
- ask another adult to stay with you.

## When contact naps work well

Contact naps can be a good choice when:

- your baby is a newborn and still sorting out days and nights;
- your baby is unwell or going through a rough patch and needs extra comfort;
- you are awake, rested enough, and happy to sit for a while;
- it's one nap of the day, and others happen in the crib.

## When contact naps become a problem

They may be worth gently changing if:

- **you can't stay awake** reliably while holding your baby;
- **every nap depends on you**, so you can't eat, rest, or care for others;
- **your baby wakes as soon as you move,** leaving very short naps;
- **night wakings need the same help.** HealthyChildren.org explains that babies who are held or rocked all the way to sleep may struggle to get back to sleep when they wake at night.

## How to transition from contact naps to the crib

There's no single proven method for this. The steps below combine sourced principles (drowsy-but-awake practice, a consistent routine) with practical suggestions from us.

### 1. Start with one nap

Pick the nap that tends to go best and try that one in the crib first. Keep the others as contact naps for now. *(Practical suggestion.)*

### 2. Use a short, repeatable pre-nap routine

A few steps every time, such as a diaper change, a dim room, a sleep sack, and a song, help your baby predict sleep. KidsHealth recommends consistent, soothing routines.

### 3. Practice "drowsy but awake"

HealthyChildren.org and KidsHealth suggest putting babies down while they're drowsy but still a little awake, so they learn to fall asleep in their own bed. Don't worry if it doesn't work every time.

### 4. Transfer gently if your baby falls asleep on you

Wait until they seem settled, then lay them on their back in the crib. Keep a hand on their chest for a moment if that helps. *(Practical suggestion.)*

### 5. Watch the timing

A baby who is overtired or not tired enough fights any nap, including in the crib. Our [wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age) chart can help you pick the moment.

### 6. Be patient and consistent

Expect some resistance for a while. Keep offering the crib for the same nap each day.

## Contact naps at different ages

| Age | What to expect |
| --- | --- |
| Newborn | Contact naps are common and comforting. Spoiling isn't a concern (KidsHealth). Follow the stay-awake rule. |
| 2–4 months | A good time to start practicing one crib nap a day *(practical suggestion)*. |
| 4–6 months | Sleep Foundation says babies usually aren't ready for formal sleep training until 4–6 months; gentle crib practice can continue. |
| 6 months+ | If all naps still happen on a parent and you want change, see our [sleep training methods guide](/sleep-training-methods-explained). |

## What can make contact naps riskier

- **Being exhausted.** It's easy to drift off holding a warm, sleeping baby.
- **Reclining on a sofa, armchair, or adult bed** with your baby.
- **Pillows, blankets, or cushions** around you and the baby.
- **Using a carrier as the main nap space.**

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Talk to your pediatrician if your baby only sleeps when held and seems unusually unsettled, cries inconsolably, feeds poorly, or has reflux symptoms or breathing noises during sleep. And if you're so tired that you are falling asleep holding your baby, ask for help from a partner, family, or your healthcare provider.

## Frequently asked questions

**Are contact naps safe?**  
Yes, as long as you stay fully awake. If you might fall asleep, put your baby on their back in their own crib or bassinet (NICHD Safe to Sleep).

**Will contact naps spoil my baby?**  
Not in the first months. KidsHealth says spoiling isn't a concern for young babies.

**My baby only naps on me. Is that normal?**  
Very common, especially for newborns. If it becomes hard to sustain, try one crib nap a day.

**How do I stop contact naps?**  
Gradually: start with one crib nap, keep a short routine, practice drowsy-but-awake, and watch awake times.

**Can my baby nap in a carrier?**  
Carrying is soothing, but NICHD says carriers and slings shouldn't be used for regular sleep. Move your baby to a safe sleep space when you can.

## See how naps are going (Yorix)

**Yorix** lets you log each nap in one tap, so over a couple of weeks you can see how your baby's naps are changing. It also suggests the next sleep window from your baby's day. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule)
- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)
- [Baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age)
- [Surviving night wakings](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents)
- [Sleep regression ages](/sleep-regression)
- [Short naps](/short-naps)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. NICHD Safe to Sleep. "Ways to Reduce Baby's Risk." <https://safetosleep.nichd.nih.gov/reduce-risk/reduce>.
2. HealthyChildren.org / AAP. "Safe Sleep Tips for Sleep-Deprived New Parents." Last updated 13 September 2026. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/Safe-Sleep-Tips-for-Sleep-Deprived-Parents.aspx>.
3. HealthyChildren.org / AAP. "How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby Safe: AAP Policy Explained." Last updated 11 September 2026. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/A-Parents-Guide-to-Safe-Sleep.aspx>.
4. HealthyChildren.org / AAP. "Getting Your Baby to Sleep." Last updated 4 June 2024. <https://www.healthychildren.org/english/ages-stages/baby/sleep/pages/getting-your-baby-to-sleep.aspx>.
5. Nemours KidsHealth. "Sleep and Your Newborn." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleepnewborn.html>.
6. Nemours KidsHealth. "Infant Sleep: 1- to 3-Month-Olds." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sleep13m.html>.
7. Newcastle Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust. "Sleep (infants 0–12 months)." <https://www.newcastle-hospitals.nhs.uk/services/great-north-childrens-hospital/childrens-sleep-service/sleep-infants-0-12-months/>.
8. NHS. "Breastfeeding: the first few days." <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/breastfeeding-and-bottle-feeding/breastfeeding/the-first-few-days/>.
9. NHS. "Helping your baby to sleep." <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/caring-for-a-newborn/helping-your-baby-to-sleep/>.
10. Sleep Foundation. "Sleep Training: What It Is, When to Start, and How to Do It." Updated 21 July 2025. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/sleep-training>.

description: The cry it out method explained: what extinction means, why it's not for newborns, what research on crying and attachment shows, fuss it out, and no-cry options
body:
# The Cry It Out Method: What It Is, When It's Used, and What the Research Says

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

"Cry it out" (CIO) may be the most argued-about phrase in parenting. Some parents credit it with saving their sanity; others feel it goes against every instinct they have. The research is calmer than the online debate, but it also has real gaps, especially for young babies. This page focuses on CIO itself: what researchers mean by it, the age questions, what studies on crying, stress, and attachment actually found, the "fuss it out" middle ground, and options with less crying. For a side-by-side table of every method, see [sleep training methods explained](/sleep-training-methods-explained); for check-in schedules, see [the Ferber method](/ferber-method-baby-sleep).

## Short answer

In research, cry it out is called **unmodified extinction**: after a bedtime routine, a baby is put down awake and parents don't go back in until a set morning time, except to check for illness, injury, or danger. A 2006 review for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine found extinction-based methods effective, and later follow-ups found **no long-term harm** in healthy babies who were sleep trained. But **CIO is not for newborns**: experts quoted in the research say extinction shouldn't be used under **6 months**, and there are essentially no studies of full CIO in babies that young. If you'd rather avoid long crying, graduated check-ins, "fuss it out," the chair method, or bedtime fading are reasonable alternatives.

### Key facts at a glance

| Question | What we found | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Research name | Unmodified (full) extinction | Mindell et al., 2006 (AASM review) |
| How common in the evidence | 42 of the 52 studies in that review used some form of extinction; 19 used full extinction | Blunden et al., 2016 |
| Lowest age commonly advised | Not before 6 months; some experts suggest 8–12 months | Blunden et al., 2016 |
| Newborns | Not recommended; no studies of full extinction under 6 months | Huckleberry (app example); Gordon, 2025 |
| Main drawback | Stressful for parents; hard to stay consistent | Mindell et al., 2006; Cleveland Clinic |
| Long-term harm | None found at 18 months (observational) or at 5 years (sleep training trial) | Bilgin & Wolke, 2020; Korownyk & Lindblad, 2018 |

## What "cry it out" actually means

The term gets used loosely, so it helps to be precise. Researchers describe three related approaches:

| Name | What parents do | Crying |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Full extinction (classic CIO)** | Put baby down awake, leave, don't return until morning except for safety or illness | Usually the most at first, often for the shortest number of nights |
| **Graduated extinction (Ferber, "controlled crying")** | Leave, then return for brief checks at growing intervals | Moderate |
| **Extinction with parental presence** | Stay in the room but don't interact while the baby falls asleep | Varies; some parents find it easier to stay consistent |

Some websites call all three "cry it out." In this article, CIO means full extinction. Cleveland Clinic pediatrician Noah Schwartz, MD, describes it as "almost like going cold turkey": you put your baby down, say goodnight, and close the door, but you still pay close attention.

## Why CIO is not for newborns

Searches for "letting a newborn cry it out" are common, so to be clear: **the sources we checked don't recommend CIO in the newborn months.**

- **Newborns can't self-settle yet.** Huckleberry (app example) says sleep training is not recommended for newborns because they don't yet have the ability to self-soothe and need help to fall and stay asleep.
- **They still need night feeds.** Frequent waking in the first months is expected and protects feeding.
- **The evidence isn't there.** Writing in Psychology Today in 2025, Macall Gordon, M.A., who reviews infant sleep research, points out that there are no studies of full extinction in babies under 6 months, and few studies of any extinction method that report results for young infants separately.
- **Early behavioral programs haven't shown big benefits.** A 2013 systematic review by Douglas and Hill concluded that behavioral sleep interventions in the first 6 months had not been shown to reduce crying, prevent later sleep problems, or protect against postnatal depression, and could carry risks such as earlier weaning from breastfeeding and more maternal anxiety.

In the early weeks, responding to crying is part of the job. What you can do instead is build foundations: a predictable bedtime routine, a dark room at night, and sometimes putting your baby down drowsy. See [when to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training).

## What age is cry it out used?

There is no single official age, and sources disagree slightly:

- **Cleveland Clinic:** around **4–6 months**, when many babies can begin to fall asleep on their own.
- **Huckleberry (app example):** at least **5–6 months** for bedtime, and **6 months** before using it in the middle of the night, after checking with your pediatrician whether your baby still needs night feeds.
- **Blunden et al. (2016):** many professionals agree extinction shouldn't be used under **6 months**, and some argue for waiting until **8–12 months**.

A practical reading: not before 6 months for full CIO, only with a healthy, growing baby, and only after night feeds have been discussed with your pediatrician.

## What the research says

### Does CIO work?

Yes, for many children. The 2006 AASM review (Mindell and colleagues) concluded that extinction and related behavioral methods reliably improve bedtime problems and night waking. A 2018 evidence summary for family doctors (Korownyk and Lindblad) estimated that sleep training helps about **1 in 4 to 1 in 10** families compared with no sleep training, and noted that letting a baby cry it out was similarly effective, although parents often find it more stressful.

### Does it harm attachment or behavior?

- **Bilgin & Wolke, 2020 (UK, 178 infants):** parents reported how often they left their baby to cry it out at birth, 3, and 6 months. At **18 months**, there were **no adverse effects** on mother–infant attachment or behavioral development. Babies left to cry out a few times at birth and often at 3 months had *shorter* crying durations at 18 months. This was an observational study: it shows no link with harm, but it can't prove cause and effect, and it measured everyday parenting rather than a structured CIO program.
- **Sleep training trial with 5-year follow-up:** the family-doctor summary reports that a trial of a tailored sleep intervention that included sleep training, started at about 7 months, found **no differences in any of 20 outcomes** at age 5, including behavior, the parent–child relationship, and maternal mental health.

### What about stress hormones?

The most-quoted worry comes from **Middlemiss et al., 2012**. In a 5-day inpatient sleep program, 25 babies aged 4–10 months learned to settle through extinction. By day 3 the babies had stopped crying at bedtime, but their cortisol (a stress hormone) was still raised, while their mothers' cortisol had fallen. The authors described this as a mismatch between mother and baby. The study was small, its abstract describes no comparison group, and it measured only a few days, so it can't tell us about long-term effects. A 2016 trial by Gradisar and colleagues, testing graduated extinction rather than full CIO, found small *decreases* in babies' cortisol and no effect on attachment a year later.

### The honest summary

For healthy babies over 6 months, the studies we found show CIO and related methods improve sleep, and none found long-term harm. The evidence is thinner for full CIO than for graduated methods, and almost absent for young babies. Parents who decide against CIO aren't ignoring the science, and parents who use it at the right age aren't harming their child.

## If you choose CIO: a safety-first checklist

1. **Get the go-ahead.** Ask your pediatrician whether your baby is growing well and still needs night feeds.
2. **Pick a calm week.** Avoid starting during illness, teething flare-ups, travel, or a move.
3. **Agree as a team.** Cleveland Clinic stresses that everyone who does bedtime must follow the same plan.
4. **Meet every need first.** Fed, clean diaper, right temperature, a predictable routine, put down awake but sleepy.
5. **Keep sleep safe.** Back to sleep, on a firm, flat surface with nothing else in the crib. The AAP recommends room-sharing (without bed-sharing) for at least the first 6 months.
6. **Listen, even if you don't go in.** Dr. Schwartz advises checking on your child if the pitch of the crying changes or it goes on for a long time. Always go in for vomiting, illness, or anything that sounds different.
7. **Expect an "extinction burst."** The AASM review warns that crying can come back briefly after a few good nights. Responding inconsistently at this point teaches longer crying.
8. **Know your stopping point.** Child Mind Institute's expert suggests that if you see no progress after one to two weeks of consistent effort, take a break and try again later or choose a different approach.

How long will the crying last? Cleveland Clinic notes that some babies cry for a few minutes and others for hours. Huckleberry (app example) says some babies fuss for under 10 minutes, while persistent babies may cry for hours on the first nights, and most families see improvement within several days.

## "Fuss it out": the middle ground

"Fuss it out" (FIO) comes from Alexis Dubief's book *Precious Little Sleep*. You put your baby down awake and leave. Low-level fussing and protest are allowed; if the crying becomes intense, you go in and comfort briefly. The Swedish sleep resource Somnfakta notes that FIO hasn't been studied as a separate method and that the line between fussing and real crying is hard to define, but it shares principles with graduated extinction and is used as a compromise.

FIO tends to suit parents who:

- can tell their baby's "winding down" grumble from a distressed cry;
- want to give their baby a few minutes to try before stepping in;
- don't want to follow a fixed timer.

## Sleep training without cry it out

If CIO isn't right for your family, you have options:

- **Graduated check-ins (Ferber).** Brief visits at lengthening intervals. See [the Ferber method](/ferber-method-baby-sleep).
- **Chair method / camping out.** Sit by the crib and move a little farther away every few nights.
- **Pick up, put down.** Lift your baby to calm them, then lay them back down while still awake. Child Mind Institute lists this among the "no-cry" approaches and notes they can take longer.
- **Bedtime fading.** Temporarily move bedtime later so your baby falls asleep quickly, then bring it earlier in small steps. In the 2016 trial it shortened settling time without adverse effects.
- **Simply not sleep training.** Many babies consolidate sleep on their own with time; sleep training is a choice, not a requirement.

Child Mind Institute's expert points out that for some children, check-ins actually make them more worked up, while for others they're soothing. Your baby's temperament matters as much as the method's name.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is the cry it out method harmful?**  
In the studies we found of healthy babies over 6 months, no long-term harm to attachment, behavior, or mental health was seen. One small study found babies' stress hormones stayed raised for a few days while learning to settle.

**At what age can you let a baby cry it out?**  
Not before 6 months for full extinction, according to the expert consensus quoted in Blunden et al. (2016). Some suggest waiting until 8–12 months. Talk to your pediatrician first.

**Can you let a newborn cry it out?**  
No. Newborns need help to settle and frequent night feeds, and full extinction hasn't been studied at that age.

**How long does cry it out take to work?**  
Often within several days to a week if you're consistent. If nothing improves after one to two weeks, pause and reassess.

**What's the difference between cry it out and Ferber?**  
With CIO you don't go back in until morning (except for safety). With Ferber you return for brief check-ins at set, growing intervals.

**What is the fuss it out method?**  
A looser approach: allow fussing, go in for real distress. It hasn't been studied on its own.

## Track the nights, not the feelings (Yorix)

**Yorix** logs how long settling takes and each night waking, so you can see the real trend over a week instead of judging by the hardest night. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [Sleep training methods explained](/sleep-training-methods-explained)
- [The Ferber method](/ferber-method-baby-sleep)
- [When to start sleep training](/when-to-start-sleep-training)
- [Baby waking every hour](/baby-waking-every-hour)
- [Surviving night wakings](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents)

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026. Study details come from the published abstracts or full texts. App pages are used only as labeled examples.

title: Dream Feed: What It Is, How to Do It & When to Stop | Yorix
heading: Dream Feed: What It Is, How to Do It Safely, and When to Stop
description: Dream feed guide: what a dream feed is, how to do it safely, when to start and stop, and what the research actually shows about whether dream feeding works.
body:
# Dream Feed: What It Is, How to Do It Safely, and When to Stop

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

A dream feed is one of the most popular baby sleep "hacks," and one of the least studied. The idea is simple: instead of waiting for your baby to wake you at 1 a.m., you offer a feed at around 10 or 11 p.m., while they are still mostly asleep, and then go to bed yourself. Some parents swear by it; for others it changes nothing. Below we explain what a dream feed is, how to do one safely, when to start and stop, and what the small amount of research really shows.

## Short answer

A **dream feed** is a late-evening breast or bottle feed given to a sleeping or very drowsy baby, usually just before the parents go to sleep, to line up the baby's longest stretch with theirs. The only randomized trial we found tested a **package**: a "focal feed" between 10 p.m. and midnight *plus* gradually stretching the gaps between night feeds and making nights clearly different from days. Breastfed babies in that program slept longer at night (Pinilla & Birch, 1993), and a Cochrane review called this "some evidence" based on that single small trial. Nobody has studied when to stop. If you try it, **hold your baby semi-upright for a bottle, never prop a bottle or feed lying flat, never leave a bottle in the crib, and lay your baby back down on their back.**

### Key facts at a glance

| Question | What we found | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A late-evening feed (often 10 p.m.–midnight) given to a sleeping or drowsy baby | Pinilla & Birch, 1993; Cochrane review |
| Evidence it works | 1 small randomized trial of a combined program (26 families); Cochrane: "some evidence" | Pinilla & Birch, 1993; Renfrew et al., 2000 |
| Observational signal | Bottle at bedtime at 1 month linked to a 62-minute longer longest night stretch at 6 months | Quante et al., 2022 |
| When to start | No official age; app examples describe use from about 6 weeks, often starting at 3–6 months | Huckleberry; Napper (app examples) |
| When to stop | Not studied; no official guidance | — |
| Safety basics | Semi-upright bottle feeding; no feeding lying down; no bottle in the crib; back to sleep | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |

## What is a dream feed?

A dream feed (also called a focal feed) is a feed you start rather than your baby. Typically your baby goes to bed at around 7–8 p.m., and a couple of hours later, before you go to bed, you lift them, feed them while they're drowsy, and lay them back down. The goal is that the next waking comes later, closer to the time you'd want to be up anyway.

The term isn't medical. Napper (app example) describes it as a method developed by sleep coaches rather than a standard recommendation. In research, the same idea appears as a "focal feed" between 10 p.m. and midnight.

## Do dream feeds work? What the research shows

The evidence is thin, and it's worth knowing exactly what it says:

- **One small trial of a whole program.** Pinilla and Birch (1993) randomly assigned 26 first-time parents of exclusively breastfed babies to a program or to usual care. The program had three parts: a focal feed between 10 p.m. and midnight, gradually lengthening the gaps between middle-of-the-night feeds with other care (re-swaddling, diapering, walking), and maximizing the difference between day and night. By 3 weeks the babies had longer night sleep episodes, and by 8 weeks all 13 program babies "slept through" from midnight to 5 a.m., compared with 23% of the control group. Their total 24-hour milk intake didn't differ; they simply drank more in the early morning.
- **What that does and doesn't prove.** Because the focal feed was tested together with the other two parts, the trial can't show how much the late feed alone contributed. "Sleeping through" was defined as midnight to 5 a.m., not the whole night.
- **Cochrane review.** Renfrew and colleagues (2000) found only one trial that met their criteria (33 couples) and concluded there is "some evidence" that a structured program can help first-time parents teach breastfed babies to sleep through the night by 8 weeks.
- **An observational study.** In the Rise & SHINE cohort of 313 infants, bottle feeding at bedtime at 1 month was associated with a 62-minute longer longest night stretch at 6 months (Quante et al., 2022). This was not a trial, and a bedtime bottle isn't exactly a dream feed, so it can't prove cause and effect.

**Bottom line:** a late feed may help some families shift the longest stretch to fit their own sleep, especially as part of a broader day-night routine. It's reasonable to try for a week or two; if it doesn't help, nothing is lost by stopping.

## When to start a dream feed (and dream feeds for newborns)

There's no official starting age. In the trial above, the program began in the first weeks after birth. The app examples (not clinical guidance) vary:

- **Huckleberry:** most commonly used for babies between about 6 weeks and 10 months, with 3–4 months a popular time to start.
- **Napper:** most babies develop a day-night rhythm between 3 and 6 months, a good time to try; earlier is fine too.

**Dream feeds for newborns.** In the first weeks, frequent feeding is normal: KidsHealth says breastfed newborns feed about every 2–3 hours and bottle-fed newborns every 3–4 hours, and that a baby should be woken to feed every 3–4 hours until they show good weight gain. A dream feed doesn't replace that. If your baby was born early, had slow weight gain, or has a medical condition, ask your pediatrician before planning night feeds around your own sleep.

## How to dream feed, step by step

1. **Pick a time.** Usually 2–3 hours after bedtime and just before you go to bed, often between about 9 and 11 p.m. (Napper, app example). Keep it the same each night for a week *(practical suggestion)*.
2. **Keep the room dark and quiet.** Lift your baby slowly. Change the diaper only if it's dirty or very wet.
3. **Feed in a safe position.**
   - **Bottle:** hold your baby in your arms, semi-upright, with their head in the crook of your arm. HealthyChildren.org warns that feeding a baby lying on their back increases the risk of choking and can let milk run into the ears' eustachian tubes, possibly causing ear infections. Never prop the bottle.
   - **Breast:** feed sitting up in a chair or bed where you're unlikely to doze off *(practical suggestion)*. If there's any chance you'll fall asleep with your baby in your bed, the AAP says to remove pillows and blankets first and move your baby back to their own sleep space as soon as you wake. Never feed on a couch or soft armchair if you might fall asleep: the AAP says the risk of sleep-related death is up to 67 times higher there.
4. **Make sure your baby is actually feeding.** Napper (app example) advises making sure your baby is awake enough to suck and swallow actively before bottle feeding.
5. **Burp if your baby usually needs it.**
6. **Lay your baby down on their back** in their own crib or bassinet, with nothing else in it (AAP).

## Is dream feeding safe?

Dream feeding is not dangerous in itself if the feed and the sleep space are safe. The main risks come from **how** it's done:

- **Bottle feeding lying flat** (choking and ear infection risk) — HealthyChildren.org.
- **A bottle left in the crib** — HealthyChildren.org says never to put your baby in the crib with a bottle for comfort, because of tooth decay and ear infections.
- **Falling asleep with your baby** on a couch, armchair, or in an adult bed — AAP.

One physician resource for breastfeeding (Physician Guide to Breastfeeding) goes further: it says giving a large bottle of expressed milk (for example 5–6 ounces) to a **sleeping** baby isn't medically recommended, because drinking reflexively from a bottle while asleep is different from breastfeeding. It suggests that a partner gives a bottle when the baby wakes naturally instead. That's one expert view rather than an AAP policy, but it's a good reason to make sure your baby is drowsy and actively feeding rather than fully asleep. (The same page mentions bed-sharing; the AAP recommends against it, and we follow the AAP.)

## Example evening with a dream feed (example only)

**Example only.** Times will be different for your family.

| Time | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| 6:45 p.m. | Bedtime feed, then bath, pajamas, book |
| 7:15 p.m. | Baby asleep |
| 10:15 p.m. | Dream feed in a dim room, then back down on their back |
| 10:45 p.m. | Parents go to sleep |
| 2:30–4:00 a.m. | Next waking (if any), handled as usual |
| 6:30–7:00 a.m. | Morning wake-up |

If your baby starts waking *earlier* after the dream feed than before, or is very hard to settle afterwards, the feed may be breaking up their sleep rather than extending it.

## When to stop or drop the dream feed

No study has looked at this, so there's no evidence-based age. Practical signs it may be time *(practical suggestions)*:

- Your baby takes very little at the dream feed.
- Your baby is hard to settle afterwards or wakes more often in the second half of the night.
- Your baby already sleeps a long stretch without it, or has started sleeping through.
- Your pediatrician says night feeds are no longer needed.

**How to drop it.** Huckleberry (app example) describes two options: stop waking your baby and let them wake when hungry, or gradually offer less milk or time at the breast each night. Napper (app example) says there's no particular reason to stop as long as it works for you. Happiest Baby (a third-party baby sleep brand) suggests stopping 2–4 weeks after your baby has been sleeping well from the dream feed through to the morning.

## When can babies drop night feeds altogether?

A dream feed is often the last night feed to go, so this question comes up alongside it:

- **Formula-fed babies:** HealthyChildren.org says most can make it through the night without a feed sometime between 2 and 4 months, or once they weigh more than about 12 pounds.
- **4–7 months:** KidsHealth says most babies no longer need a middle-of-the-night feed, though some, often breastfed babies, still wake to feed.
- **By 6 months:** Nationwide Children's Hospital says most babies can physically sleep through the night without feeding, yet 25–50% continue to wake.

Before you drop night feeds, check with your pediatrician, especially if your baby was premature, had slow weight gain, or has a medical condition.

## Dream feeds and "drowsy but awake"

A dream feed doesn't conflict with teaching your baby to fall asleep on their own at bedtime. Cleveland Clinic suggests feeding at the start of a 20–30 minute bedtime routine so your baby doesn't rely on feeding to fall asleep, and KidsHealth suggests putting your baby down drowsy but still awake. The dream feed happens hours later, once your baby is already asleep. If your baby can only fall asleep while feeding at every waking, a dream feed won't change that on its own; see our [sleep training methods](/sleep-training-methods-explained) page.

## What can make dream feeding backfire

- Fully waking your baby with bright lights, talking, or play.
- Feeding a baby who is too deeply asleep to suck and swallow properly.
- Timing it too late, so it cuts into your baby's natural longest stretch (Napper, app example).
- Adding a dream feed to replace night feeds your baby still needs.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Talk to your doctor before planning night feeds around your own sleep if your baby was born early, isn't gaining weight well, has reflux, or has fewer wet diapers. HealthyChildren.org suggests contacting your pediatrician if a breastfed baby feeds fewer than 8–12 times a day, a bottle-fed baby fewer than 5–8 times, or there are fewer than 4 wet diapers a day.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is a dream feed?**  
A late-evening feed given to a sleeping or drowsy baby, usually just before parents go to bed, to try to push the next waking later.

**How do you dream feed safely?**  
Keep the room dim, hold your baby semi-upright for a bottle, never prop the bottle or feed lying flat, and lay your baby back down on their back in their own sleep space.

**Do dream feeds work?**  
Sometimes. One small trial of a combined program (including a 10 p.m.–midnight feed) found longer night sleep in breastfed babies; nobody has tested the dream feed on its own.

**When should I start a dream feed?**  
There's no official age. Many families try it from about 6 weeks to 4 months.

**When should I stop the dream feed?**  
There's no research on this. Drop it when your baby takes little at the feed, sleeps well without it, or the feed seems to cause extra wakings.

**Can I dream feed a newborn?**  
Newborns need frequent feeds anyway. A dream feed can fit into that, but it shouldn't replace feeds your newborn needs.

## Find your dream-feed time (Yorix)

**Yorix** logs each feed and night waking, so after a week you can see whether a dream feed at 10 p.m. actually moved the next waking later. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [2 month old sleep schedule](/2-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [6 month old sleep schedule](/6-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [Baby feeding schedule](/baby-feeding-schedule)
- [Survive night wakings as new parents](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents)
- [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026. App pages are used only as labeled examples.

2. Renfrew MJ, et al. "Interventions for influencing sleep patterns in exclusively breastfed infants." *Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews*, 2000. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10796136/> (abstract via Europe PMC).
3. Quante M, et al. "Associations of sleep-related behaviors and the sleep environment at infant age one month with sleep patterns in infants five months later." *Sleep Medicine*, 2022. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35489116/> (abstract via Europe PMC).
4. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Bottle Feeding Basics." Last updated 21 May 2012. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/feeding-nutrition/Pages/Bottle-Feeding-How-Its-Done.aspx>.
5. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Sleeping Through the Night." Last updated 5 September 2013. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/sleeping-through-the-night.aspx>.
6. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby Safe: AAP Policy Explained." Last updated 11 September 2026. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/A-Parents-Guide-to-Safe-Sleep.aspx>.
