description: The 2 year old sleep regression: nap strikes, bedtime stalling, early waking and the move from crib to bed. What the evidence says and calm, practical fixes.
body:
# 2 Year Old Sleep Regression: Nap Strikes, Bedtime Stalling, and the Big-Kid Bed

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Two-year-olds can talk, climb, negotiate, and remember that you gave in last night. So when sleep goes wrong at this age, it often looks less like a baby waking for comfort and more like a small person with a plan. They skip the nap, ask for "one more" everything at bedtime, appear at your door at 5 a.m., or escape the crib. Here is what is really known about the "2 year old sleep regression" and what tends to help.

## Short answer

There is **no research showing a regression that arrives at the second birthday**. Sleep Foundation says sleep regressions can happen at any age. When sleep slips around age 2, common reasons include **testing limits, separation anxiety, fears and dreams, too much stimulation before bed, changes in the family's schedule, and teething**. Most 2-year-olds still need a nap. Fewer than 2.5% of children stop napping before age 2, so a nap strike is rarely the end of naps. Toddlers need about **11–14 hours of sleep in 24 hours** (AASM; KidsHealth). Most families get through this with a predictable routine, a clear and kind limit, and a well-timed bedtime.

### Key facts at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sleep need at 2 | About 11–14 hours per 24 hours, including a nap | AASM; KidsHealth |
| Typical nap at 2 | About 1–3 hours, early in the afternoon | Sleep Foundation |
| Nap end to bedtime | At least 3–4.5 hours | Sleep Foundation |
| Children who stop napping before 2 | Fewer than 2.5% (94% stop by age 5) | Staton et al., 2020 |
| Typical toddler bedtime | Around 6:30–7:30 p.m. | KidsHealth NZ |
| Crib-to-bed age | Usually between 18 months and 3 years; KidsHealth says most are ready at 2–3 years | Cleveland Clinic; KidsHealth |
| Outgrown the crib | Taller than 35 inches, or the rail is at mid-chest when standing | AAP, via Cleveland Clinic |

## How strong is the evidence for a 2-year regression?

Weak for a fixed date. Reasonable for the idea that toddler development and routines affect sleep.

- **Sleep Foundation** describes a sleep regression as a setback that can occur at any age, sometimes around certain stages of development.
- **"Sleep regression"** is described as a popular term that is not used in the scientific literature (Keys, Public Health Ontario webinar slides).
- **App example (not clinical guidance):** Huckleberry calls the idea that a regression starts the moment a child turns 2 a myth. It says some toddlers sail through this year with few changes, while others have more ups and downs.
- **What research does support** is that toddler bedtime problems respond to behavioral approaches. An American Academy of Sleep Medicine task force reviewed 52 treatment studies. It found that 94% reported behavioral interventions worked, with over 80% of children showing clear improvement that lasted 3 to 6 months (Mindell et al., 2006).

## Signs and likely causes

Signs parents describe include nap refusal, long bedtime stalling, calling out or leaving the room after lights-out, new night waking, and very early mornings.

| What might be behind it | What it can look like | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Independence and testing limits | Saying no to nap or bed, negotiating | Sleep Foundation |
| Separation anxiety | Clinginess at lights-out, calling for a parent | Sleep Foundation |
| Not yet able to resettle alone | Needing a parent after every night waking | Sleep Foundation |
| Nightmares or dreams | Waking upset, fear of the dark | Sleep Foundation |
| Too much stimulation before bed | Wound up and "not tired" at bedtime | Sleep Foundation; KidsHealth NZ |
| Family schedule changes | Travel, new childcare, a new sibling | Sleep Foundation |
| Teething | Discomfort and night waking | Sleep Foundation |
| Potty training, moving to a bed too early | Extra toilet requests, leaving the bed | Huckleberry (app example) |

## When your 2 year old refuses to nap

A string of skipped naps does not usually mean your child has outgrown them. A meta-analysis by Staton and colleagues found that fewer than 2.5% of children stop napping before their second birthday. Sleep Foundation adds that about half of children stop napping by age 3, and that refusing a nap doesn't necessarily mean a child is ready to give it up.

What helps:

- **Keep offering the nap at the same time each day.** Sleep Foundation recommends a regular nap time, bedtime, and wake time, with a short calming pre-nap routine.
- **Check the timing.** Sleep Foundation suggests the nap end at least 3 to 4.5 hours before bedtime. A nap that runs too late can push bedtime back.
- **Make it quiet time if sleep doesn't come.** Huckleberry (app example) suggests that even if your child doesn't sleep, quiet rest in their room is worth keeping.
- **Don't force it if the nap is truly gone.** Sleep Foundation says that once a child has clearly given up napping, forcing a nap can disrupt night sleep.

For daycare kids, Sleep Foundation quotes pediatrician Nilong Vyas: if your child's nap is short at daycare and they seem sleepy on weekends, a weekend nap of 1.5 to 3 hours is fine.

## Bedtime stalling and calling out

Bedtime stalling is one of the most common complaints at this age. KidsHealth New Zealand suggests:

- turning off TVs, tablets, and computers at least an hour before bed;
- avoiding lively play just before bed;
- a calming routine in the same order every night, even on weekends;
- checking your child has everything they need before you leave, and gently reminding them to stay in bed.

Two ideas that can take the fight out of bedtime:

- **Offer small choices.** KidsHealth's 30-month checkup guide suggests giving toddlers a sense of independence by offering a choice between two acceptable options, such as which pajamas or which book. More than two can be overwhelming.
- **Watch the clock, not just the child.** In app data from 841 children, later bedtimes went with shorter night sleep at every age (Mindell et al., 2016). Huckleberry (app example) adds the opposite risk: a bedtime set too soon after a late nap can meet resistance because the child isn't tired yet.

## Early morning waking

KidsHealth New Zealand notes that some toddlers wake early and need an earlier bedtime. It also explains that children sleep most deeply in the first hours of the night and are more likely to wake in the second half, when sleep is lighter. Keep early-morning contact quiet and dim until your chosen wake-up time *(practical suggestion)*.

## Moving from crib to bed

Crib-to-bed questions peak around age 2, and a move at the wrong moment is a common trigger for new sleep problems.

**Signs it may be time** (Cleveland Clinic, citing the AAP for the size limits):

- your child keeps climbing out, even with the mattress at its lowest;
- they are taller than 35 inches, or the rail is at about mid-chest when they stand;
- they can fall asleep on their own and follow other house rules.

HealthyChildren.org (AAP) also says that once a toddler can climb out of the crib, it may be time for a bed.

**Signs it may be too soon** (Cleveland Clinic): your child is still content in the crib, isn't sleeping through the night, or is having a hard time with limits. A sleep sack can make climbing harder for a while, though some children get out of those too.

**How to make the switch:**

1. **Talk about it ahead of time** and explain what you expect, including the morning routine (Cleveland Clinic).
2. **Let your child choose something,** such as the sheets, a night light, or a small comfort item (Cleveland Clinic).
3. **Start with naps** in the new bed, if you can (Cleveland Clinic).
4. **Keep the bedtime routine exactly the same** (HealthyChildren.org; Cleveland Clinic).
5. **Make one big change at a time.** Avoid moving to a bed during potty training, a house move, a new daycare, or a vacation (Cleveland Clinic).
6. **Walk them back, calmly, every time.** HealthyChildren.org suggests telling your child to stay in bed until you come for them. If they get up, lead them back quietly, briefly praise them for being in bed, and leave. It warns that 20 returns in an evening is not unusual at first.
7. **Praise or reward the morning after.** Cleveland Clinic suggests a sticker chart with small rewards.

**Make the room safe.** HealthyChildren.org advises clearing away furniture and large toys that could hurt a child who climbs or falls, anchoring dressers and other furniture so they can't tip, and gating the top of the stairs. A gate at the bedroom door may be needed. Cleveland Clinic adds checking cords, unlocked windows, outlets, and access to the kitchen, bathroom, garage, or outside.

## An example day for a 2 year old

**Example only.** This is adapted from Sleep Foundation's sample schedule. Your child's best times may differ.

| Time | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| 6:00–7:00 a.m. | Wake up |
| 12:30–1:00 p.m. | Nap after lunch |
| 1:30–3:00 p.m. | Wake from nap |
| 6:15–7:15 p.m. | Start the bedtime routine |
| 7:00–8:00 p.m. | Lights out |

## What can make it worse

- **Dropping the nap at the first refusal.**
- **Giving in to bedroom "breakouts."** HealthyChildren.org advises against rewarding them, for example by letting your child into your bed or back with the family.
- **Changing the rules night to night,** or stacking several big changes at once.
- **Screens and rough play** in the hour before bed.
- **Switching to a bed too early** for a child who isn't ready.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Talk to your child's doctor if sleep problems last more than a few weeks or are getting worse, if your child snores loudly, gasps, or seems to stop breathing during sleep, if nightmares are frequent, if sleep problems come with pain, fever, or other signs of illness, or if daytime behavior is changing a lot. Also reach out if you are exhausted or struggling.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is the 2 year old sleep regression real?**  
Sleep problems around age 2 are common, but there is no evidence for a regression that every child goes through at a set age. Sleep Foundation says regressions can happen at any age.

**How long does the 2 year sleep regression last?**  
There is no study-based answer. Huckleberry (app example) says some regressions pass in a week or two and nap strikes often last a couple of weeks. Longer stretches usually point to a habit or schedule that needs adjusting.

**My 2 year old won't nap. Should I drop the nap?**  
Usually not yet. Fewer than 2.5% of children stop napping before age 2 (Staton et al., 2020), and Sleep Foundation says about half of children have stopped napping by age 3. Keep offering the nap or quiet time.

**When should my toddler move from a crib to a bed?**  
When they can climb out, are taller than 35 inches, or the rail is at mid-chest (AAP, via Cleveland Clinic). Otherwise there's no rush. Many children move between 2 and 3 years.

**How much sleep does a 2 year old need?**  
About 11–14 hours in 24 hours, including a nap (AASM; KidsHealth).

## See the whole week, not just last night (Yorix)

**Yorix** logs naps and bedtimes, so on a bad week you can see whether skipped naps or later bedtimes line up with the rough nights. It updates the day's sleep plan as things change. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [Sleep regression ages](/sleep-regression)
- [18 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/18-months)
- [Baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age)
- [Sleep training methods explained](/sleep-training-methods-explained)
- [Surviving night wakings](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026. App pages are used only as labeled examples.

1. Sleep Foundation. "How Long Should a 2-Year-Old Nap?" Updated 27 May 2026. Medically reviewed by Nilong Vyas, MD, MPH. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/napping/how-long-should-a-2-year-old-nap>.
2. Staton S, et al. "Many naps, one nap, none: A systematic review and meta-analysis of napping patterns in children 0–12 years." *Sleep Medicine Reviews*, 2020. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31862445/> (abstract via Europe PMC).
3. American Academy of Sleep Medicine. "Recharge with sleep: Pediatric sleep recommendations promoting optimal health." <https://aasm.org/recharge-with-sleep-pediatric-sleep-recommendations-promoting-optimal-health/>.
4. Nemours KidsHealth. "2 Years (24 Months) Well-Child Checkup." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/checkup-2yrs.html>.
5. Nemours KidsHealth. "2.5 Years (30 Months) Well-Child Checkup." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/checkup-30mos.html>.
6. KidsHealth (New Zealand). "Normal Sleep: Toddlers 1 to 3 Years." <https://www.kidshealth.org.nz/normal-sleep-toddlers-1-to-3-years>.
7. Cleveland Clinic. "Signs Your Child Is Ready To Transition to a Toddler Bed." 1 October 2025. <https://health.clevelandclinic.org/from-crib-to-toddler-bed>.
8. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Big Kid Beds: When to Switch From a Crib." Last updated 1 August 2022. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/healthy-living/sleep/Pages/Big-Kid-Beds-When-To-Make-the-Switch.aspx>.
9. Mindell JA, et al. "Behavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children." *Sleep*, 2006. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17068979/> (abstract via Europe PMC).
10. Mindell JA, et al. "Development of infant and toddler sleep patterns: real-world data from a mobile application." *Journal of Sleep Research*, 2016. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27252030/> (abstract via Europe PMC).
11. Keys E. "Promoting and Supporting Sleep Health in Families of Infants." Webinar slides published by Public Health Ontario. <https://www.publichealthontario.ca/-/media/Event-Presentations/24/02/sleep-health-families-of-infants.pdf>.
12. App example: Huckleberry. "2 year old sleep regression: What causes it and what to do." Updated 3 September 2026. <https://huckleberrycare.com/blog/expert-advice-for-handling-the-two-year-sleep-regression>.

description: Is the 3 month sleep regression real? How it relates to the 4 month shift, how to tell it from normal 3-month sleep, what to rule out first, and what helps.
body:
# 3 Month Sleep Regression: Is It Real, and What Is Actually Going On?

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Your baby was finally giving you a longer stretch at night, and then, at around 12 weeks, the night falls apart again. Searching for answers turns up the "3 month sleep regression." This page doesn't repeat our full [4 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/4-months) guide or the [3 month old sleep schedule](/3-month-old-sleep-schedule). It answers three narrower questions: is a 3-month regression a real thing, how does it relate to the better-known 4-month one, and what should you do this week?

## Short answer

There is **no research describing a separate "3 month sleep regression."** What parents notice at 12–14 weeks is most likely the **early start of the same sleep change usually called the 4 month regression**. Sleep Foundation says babies begin to have four sleep stages at around three months, and that some babies have trouble sleeping a little earlier or later than 4 months, or have no noticeable regression at all. Before calling it a regression, check two things. Was sleep really better before? Is something else going on, such as illness, hunger, or a baby who is starting to roll? Then keep nights calm and offer some chances to fall asleep in the crib. Hold off on formal sleep training for now.

### Key facts at a glance

| Question | What the sources say | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Is "3 month regression" a scientific term? | No. "Sleep regression" is a popular term, not one used in the research literature | Keys, Public Health Ontario webinar |
| What changes around 3 months? | Babies begin to have four sleep stages instead of two | Sleep Foundation |
| Can the 4-month change start early? | Yes. Some babies struggle a few months earlier or later, and some not at all | Sleep Foundation |
| Typical sleep blocks in the first 3 months | Mostly under 3.5 hours at a time, day and night | Mindell et al., 2016 |
| "Sleeping through the night" at 1–3 months | A stretch of only 5–6 hours | KidsHealth |
| Fever before 12 weeks | Call your doctor now; give no fever medicine before your baby is seen | HealthyChildren.org (AAP) |

## Is the 3 month sleep regression real?

The night waking is real. Whether it deserves its own label is a different question.

- **We found no study that defines a regression at 3 months.** In slides from a webinar published by Public Health Ontario, nursing researcher Elizabeth Keys (University of British Columbia Okanagan) lists "sleep regression" as a popularized term that does not exist in the scientific literature. Cleveland Clinic makes a similar point: research has not shown regressions arriving on a schedule at one age for every baby.
- **A biological shift is under way.** Sleep Foundation explains that newborns have two sleep stages (REM and non-REM), while babies over about three months begin to show the four stages adults have. Most babies move toward a more adult-like pattern somewhere between three months and one year.
- **The timing is loose.** Sleep Foundation's 4-month regression page says some babies have trouble a few months before or after 4 months, and some show no detectable regression at all.
- **App example (not clinical guidance):** Huckleberry describes the "3 month regression" as the same maturing of sleep that people call the 4 month regression, which can simply show up earlier.

So "3 month sleep regression" is best read as a **search term**, not a diagnosis. It describes a real, temporary rough patch that some babies hit as their sleep matures.

## 3 month vs 4 month regression: what's the difference?

| | "3 month regression" | "4 month regression" |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What is behind it | The same maturing of sleep stages, starting early | The maturing of sleep stages |
| Research behind the label | None for a separate event | Also no fixed-age evidence, but widely described by Sleep Foundation and Cleveland Clinic |
| What still counts as normal at this age | Short, uneven naps; one or more night feeds; "through the night" = 5–6 hours | Night waking that often returns around 4–5 months (NHS services) |
| Sleep training? | Too early: readiness is usually placed at 4–6 months (Sleep Foundation) | Some experts suggest waiting until 6 months (Sleep Foundation) |
| Main job for parents | Rule out other causes; protect the night; low-pressure practice | Same, plus a steadier daytime rhythm |

In short, they are not two regressions. If your baby has a rough patch at 3 months, you are unlikely to face a second, separate one a few weeks later. You may simply be in the same transition for a little longer.

## Regression, or just normal 3-month sleep?

Many "regressions" at this age turn out to be ordinary infant sleep. Ask yourself:

1. **Was sleep clearly better for a week or more before this?** If naps were always 30–45 minutes, short naps are not a new problem. In app data from 841 children, Mindell and colleagues found that in the first 3 months, sleep mostly came in blocks of less than 3.5 hours, around the clock. Huckleberry (app example) makes the same point: short naps that have always been short are not a regression.
2. **Is your expectation realistic?** KidsHealth says that at 1–3 months, "sleeping through the night" means only about 5 or 6 hours, and that the range of normal is still very wide.
3. **Is it sudden and broad?** A real shift tends to show up together as more night waking, shorter naps, and a fussier, more tired baby. Sleep Foundation describes this pattern for the 4-month change.

If you answered "yes, it was better", "yes, I expect 5–6 hours, not 11", and "yes, it's sudden", the early start of the 4-month shift is a reasonable explanation.

## Check these first

Cleveland Clinic's Dr. Heidi Szugye warns against assuming every bad night is a regression. A baby may wake for many reasons, including illness, a dirty diaper, or an upset stomach. Run through:

- **Illness.** A fever in a baby younger than 12 weeks needs a call to your doctor right away, and HealthyChildren.org says not to give fever medicine before your baby is seen. Also watch for poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, or unusual sleepiness.
- **Hunger.** Night feeds are still normal at this age. A baby who suddenly wants more feeds may simply need them.
- **Rolling.** KidsHealth notes that babies typically start trying to roll at about 3 to 4 months. A swaddled baby who is trying to roll is a safety issue, not just a sleep one: stop swaddling.
- **Temperature, a wet diaper, or a changed sleep space.** These are small things that wake light sleepers.

## What to do this week

**1. Keep nights boring and short.** Feed and comfort in low light, with little talk, and settle your baby back in their own sleep space. This does not mean leaving a 3-month-old to cry for long periods.

**2. Offer some sleeps "drowsy but awake."** KidsHealth explains that a baby rocked to sleep at bedtime may expect rocking after every night waking. Try putting your baby down sleepy but not fully asleep for one or two sleeps a day, often the first nap or bedtime. If it fails, help them to sleep and try again tomorrow.

**3. Consider moving the late feed.** If your baby wakes for a feed shortly after you have gone to bed, KidsHealth suggests waking them for the late-night feed at a time that fits your own sleep. It may take a few nights to settle in.

**4. Don't start formal sleep training yet.** Sleep Foundation explains that babies don't have a strong body clock at birth and that most families may not be able to sleep train until about six months.

**5. Share the night.** If there are two adults, split the night into shifts so each person gets one longer block of sleep *(practical suggestion)*.

## How long does it last?

No study has measured how long a "3 month regression" lasts, because none defines one. For the related 4-month shift, Sleep Foundation describes a few days to a few weeks, and Cleveland Clinic says regressions usually last a week or two. Huckleberry (app example) suggests that some babies need until about 5–6 months to get good at falling asleep on their own. If sleep is still very broken after several weeks, or is getting worse, talk to your pediatrician.

## What can make it worse

- **Treating a feed or illness as "just a regression"** and missing what your baby actually needs.
- **Switching strategies every night.** Babies cope better with a predictable response.
- **Continuing to swaddle** once your baby is trying to roll.
- **Unsafe sleep fixes:** a couch, an inclined sleeper, pillows, loose blankets, or weighted sleep products. KidsHealth warns against weighted blankets, sleepers, and swaddles.
- **Starting formal sleep training too early** out of exhaustion.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Call promptly for any fever before 12 weeks (HealthyChildren.org). Also call for poor feeding or fewer wet diapers, a baby who is unusually hard to wake, breathing that looks like hard work or sounds noisy during sleep, or crying that you cannot soothe and that seems different from usual. It's also worth raising if the disruption lasts for weeks, or if you are struggling to cope.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is there a 3 month sleep regression?**  
Not as a separate, research-defined event. Changes at 12–14 weeks are most likely the early start of the sleep maturing usually called the 4 month regression (Sleep Foundation).

**Will my baby have a 4 month regression too?**  
Probably not a second, separate one. It is the same transition, and some babies go through it earlier, later, or barely at all (Sleep Foundation).

**How long does the 3 month sleep regression last?**  
There is no data for 3 months specifically. For the 4-month change, sources describe a few days to a few weeks (Sleep Foundation) or usually a week or two (Cleveland Clinic).

**Why is my 3 month old suddenly waking every hour?**  
Rule out illness, hunger, and rolling while swaddled first. If none applies and sleep had been better, maturing sleep is a likely reason.

**Can I sleep train a 3 month old?**  
It's generally considered too early. Sleep Foundation places readiness later, around 4–6 months.

## Keep track of what changed (Yorix)

**Yorix** keeps naps, feeds, and night wakings in one log, so you can look back and see whether sleep really got worse or has always looked like this. It suggests the next sleep window from your baby's actual day. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

heading: 6 Month Sleep Regression: Is It Real, and What Can You Do?
description: Is the 6 month sleep regression real? Many babies don't have one. Signs, likely causes, how long it lasts, and calm ways to handle more night waking.
body:
# 6 Month Sleep Regression: Is It Real, and What Can You Do?

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

Around six months, plenty of families expect sleep to get easier. For some it does. For others, a baby who had started to string longer nights together begins waking again, protesting in the crib, or snacking at night. Is this a "6 month sleep regression"? Sometimes it is a passing phase linked to development. Often it is something more ordinary, such as a schedule that needs a tweak.

## Short answer

The evidence for a distinct **6 month sleep regression** is weak. Sleep Foundation says **some babies have one, but many do not**, and some parents see their baby's sleep **improve** at this age. When sleep does get worse, Sleep Foundation links it to greater awareness of surroundings and sounds, new physical skills like rolling and sitting, and changing schedules. It says symptoms usually pass **within a few days or weeks**. A steady routine, putting your baby down sleepy but awake, and a brief pause before responding at night are the core strategies.

### Key facts at a glance

| Question | Answer | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Does every baby have a 6 month regression? | No; many don't, and some sleep better | Sleep Foundation |
| How long does it last? | Usually a few days to weeks | Sleep Foundation |
| Total sleep at 6 months | 12–16 hours in 24 hours | AASM (4–12 months) |
| Night sleep by 6 months | Most sleep 9 hours or more, with brief awakenings | KidsHealth |
| Babies not sleeping through at 6–12 months | 27.9%–57.0%, depending on the 6- or 8-hour definition | Pennestri et al., 2018 |
| Awake time between sleeps | 2–4 hours (5–7 months) | Cleveland Clinic |

## Is the 6 month sleep regression real?

There is no study showing that babies, as a group, sleep worse at exactly six months. Sleep Foundation stresses how much infant sleep varies: a 6-month-old can regress, stay the same, or improve, and all three are normal. Huckleberry's guide (an app example) reaches a similar view and calls the idea of a fixed 6-month regression a myth, while acknowledging that sleep can get bumpy as new skills emerge.

It also helps to separate a **regression** (sleep that was good, then got worse) from sleep that **hasn't consolidated yet**. In a study of 388 infants, between 27.9% and 57.0% of babies at 6 and 12 months did not sleep through the night, depending on whether that meant 6 or 8 hours in a row. Not sleeping through was not linked to mental or psychomotor development, or to mothers' mood. Waking at night at six months is common, not a sign that something has gone wrong.

## Signs parents notice

Sleep Foundation lists these as typical:

- more night wakings, and more trouble getting back to sleep;
- difficulty falling asleep at bedtime;
- more crying at night;
- longer daytime naps, sometimes at the expense of night sleep.

Before calling it a regression, check for **illness, teething discomfort, hunger,** or a **change in routine** such as travel, starting childcare, or a parent returning to work.

## What may be behind it

Sleep Foundation describes several overlapping changes:

- **More awareness.** Six-month-olds respond more to sounds and their surroundings and can be easily overstimulated.
- **New skills.** Rolling over and sitting without support take practice, and some babies "rehearse" in the crib.
- **Separation anxiety.** Some babies start protesting when a parent walks away.
- **Schedule shifts.** As more sleep moves to the night, nap times and bedtime often need adjusting.

Tresillian adds that at around 6–7 months many babies start waking more because they are more aware as they move into light sleep phases.

## How long does it last?

Sleep Foundation says the symptoms are usually short-lived, often resolving within a few days or weeks, though a plateau in progress can last longer. If things are no better after several weeks, look at whether a new sleep association has formed (for example, being fed or rocked back to sleep every time) or whether the daytime schedule fits your baby's age.

## How to help a 6-month-old sleep better

### Keep the same bedtime steps

Sleep Foundation recommends the same sequence every night, with a feed and calm activities beforehand. Choose three or four steps you can repeat anywhere, such as bath, pajamas, feed, song.

### Put your baby down sleepy but awake

Sleep Foundation and Cleveland Clinic both say this helps your baby link the crib with falling asleep, which makes it easier to resettle during the night.

### Pause before going in

Sleep Foundation suggests waiting a minute or two at a night waking to see whether your baby settles alone. If you need to go in, keep the light low and the visit short.

### Comfort without lifting, if you can

For separation protests, Sleep Foundation suggests staying by the crib and comforting with a gentle touch or quiet voice rather than taking your baby out, then moving away once they are calm. Tresillian describes a similar sequence: cuddle until calm, place on the back drowsy, then soothe with "shh" sounds and rhythmic patting, and return if distress builds.

### Check the day

At this age, Cleveland Clinic gives 2–4 hours of awake time between sleeps for 5–7 months, and Mayo Clinic suggests at least two naps, often around 9 a.m. and 1 p.m., with a third short nap for some babies. Our [wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age) chart and [nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age) can help you adjust.

### Daylight and activity

Sleep Foundation notes that active, light-filled days help babies learn that daytime is for play and night is for sleep.

## Night feeds, solids, and sleep at 6 months

- **Night feeds.** Whether your 6-month-old still needs a night feed depends on growth and feeding. Ask your pediatrician before you drop one.
- **Solids.** The AAP recommends introducing solid foods at about 6 months, when your baby shows signs of readiness. We found no evidence in the sources we checked that starting solids improves sleep, so treat it as a nutrition milestone rather than a sleep fix. See our [baby feeding schedule](/baby-feeding-schedule).

## Safe sleep reminders at 6 months

- Always place your baby on their back. Once they roll both ways on their own, you can leave them in the position they choose (NICHD Safe to Sleep; HealthyChildren.org).
- Keep the crib free of pillows, blankets, bumpers, and soft toys.
- Swaddling should have stopped once your baby started trying to roll (KidsHealth).

## Should you sleep train during a 6 month regression?

Sleep Foundation suggests that around 6 months many babies can self-soothe, making it a common time to start methods such as the Ferber method. Choose a calm week without illness or travel. Our [sleep training methods guide](/sleep-training-methods-explained) compares the options.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Sleep Foundation says sleep problems at 6 months don't usually need medical attention, but you can raise them at any checkup. Call sooner if poor sleep comes with fever, pain, breathing pauses or loud snoring, poor feeding, or fewer wet diapers, or if you feel you can't cope.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is the 6 month sleep regression real?**  
Some babies have a rough patch at around six months, but many don't (Sleep Foundation). The evidence for a fixed 6-month regression is weak.

**How long does the 6 month sleep regression last?**  
Usually a few days to a few weeks (Sleep Foundation).

**Why is my 6 month old suddenly waking at night?**  
Common reasons include more awareness of surroundings, practicing rolling or sitting, separation anxiety, illness, teething, or a schedule that needs updating.

**Should I feed my 6 month old every time they wake?**  
Not necessarily. Some wakings are for comfort. Ask your pediatrician whether your baby still needs a night feed.

**Can I sleep train at 6 months?**  
Many families do. Sleep Foundation describes 6 months as a common starting point.

## See whether it's a phase or a pattern (Yorix)

**Yorix** charts night wakings and naps day by day, so after a week or two you can see whether things are settling or whether the schedule needs adjusting. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

description: The 8, 9 or 10 month sleep regression: why crawling, pulling to stand, teething and separation anxiety can disrupt sleep, how long it lasts, and what helps.
body:
# 8 Month Sleep Regression: Why Sleep Gets Bumpy Between 8 and 10 Months

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

If your baby has just learned to crawl or haul themselves up on the furniture, and nights have suddenly fallen apart, you are in good company. The second half of the first year is a busy time for the brain and body, and sleep often takes a temporary hit. Parents call it the 8 month, 9 month, or 10 month sleep regression. They are usually describing the same window.

Looking for a normal day plan rather than help with a rough patch? Our [8 month old sleep schedule](/8-month-old-sleep-schedule) and [9 month old sleep schedule](/9-month-old-sleep-schedule) cover naps, wake windows, and bedtimes.

## Short answer

The so-called **8 month sleep regression** usually shows up somewhere between **8 and 10 months**. Of all the "regression ages", this one has some of the better evidence: small studies using sleep trackers found **disrupted sleep around the onset of crawling** and, in early achievers, **around pulling to stand**. Sleep Foundation adds **teething, separation anxiety, and overstimulation** as contributors, and notes that **not every baby goes through it**. Two NHS services describe night waking often returning at **8–9 months**. It is usually temporary, and calm consistency helps most.

### Key facts at a glance

| Question | Answer | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Typical window | Around 8–9 months (NHS services); disturbances more common around 9 months | Newcastle and Derbyshire NHS; Sleep Foundation |
| Does every baby have one? | No | Sleep Foundation |
| Linked milestones | Crawling onset; pulling to stand in early achievers | Scher & Cohen, 2015; Atun-Einy & Scher, 2016 |
| Separation anxiety | Usually appears between 8 months and 1 year | KidsHealth |
| Third nap usually dropped | Around 9 months | Mayo Clinic |
| Total sleep | 12–16 hours in 24 hours | AASM |

## 8, 9, or 10 month regression: same thing?

Mostly, yes. Development doesn't follow birthdays. Newcastle Hospitals NHS says some babies begin waking more often again at 8–9 months, and Sleep Foundation's wake-windows page says disturbances may be more common around 9 months. A baby who crawls at 7 months may have a bumpy patch then; a baby who pulls to stand at 10 months may hit it later. Huckleberry (app example) frames the whole stretch as 7–10 months.

## What the research says

This is one of the few "regressions" with direct research behind it, although the studies are small:

- **Crawling.** Scher and Cohen followed 28 infants from 5 to 11 months with actigraphy. While sleep generally improved over that time, periods with more long night wakings lined up with the onset of crawling.
- **Pulling to stand.** Atun-Einy and Scher followed 20 infants from 7 to 11–12 months. Among babies who pulled to stand early (by 8 months), the milestone was time-linked to disrupted sleep.
- **Walking and language.** A 2026 study by Waugh and Berger found sleep disruptions around several locomotor and language milestones, and suggests skill learning can affect sleep even before the new skill shows.

These findings support the idea of a **developmental** sleep disruption, linked to skills rather than to an exact age.

## Common signs

Sleep Foundation describes:

- trouble falling asleep, and more fussing or agitation around bedtime;
- more night wakings;
- longer naps during the day with less sleep at night.

Parents also often notice a baby who pops up to sitting or standing as soon as they are laid down, or who cries the moment a parent leaves.

## Why it happens

| Factor | What it looks like | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New motor skills | Crawling, sitting up, pulling to stand in the crib | Sleep Foundation; Scher studies |
| Separation anxiety | Crying when a parent leaves; calling out at night | KidsHealth; Sleep Foundation |
| Teething | Gum discomfort that wakes the baby | Sleep Foundation |
| Overstimulation | A busy, exciting day that makes winding down hard | Sleep Foundation |
| Nap transition | Third nap disappearing; awake periods lengthening | Mayo Clinic; Huckleberry (app example) |

## How long does it last?

Sleep Foundation describes regressions at this age as normally short-lived, and Cleveland Clinic says regressions in general typically last a week or two. Because the trigger is often a new skill, things tend to settle as the skill becomes routine. If disrupted sleep goes on for weeks, check whether new habits have formed during the rough patch.

## What helps

### Give new skills plenty of daytime practice

Lots of floor time for crawling, standing, and cruising means the crib is less of a training ground. Sleep Foundation also recommends daytime activity with natural light to support the body clock.

### Keep the routine predictable

Sleep Foundation suggests a consistent schedule, including naps, and the same bedtime steps every night, with a well-fed baby and a calm wind-down without too much stimulation.

### Lay your baby down drowsy

Putting your baby in the crib while drowsy, rather than already asleep, helps them associate the crib with falling asleep (Sleep Foundation).

### Handle separation protests calmly

Sleep Foundation advises comforting your baby without lifting them out of the crib when they cry because you are leaving. KidsHealth suggests reassuring quietly, a soothing pat, and a quick exit. Long cuddles, feeding, or chatting at night may encourage more waking.

### Ease teething discomfort

For teething pain, Sleep Foundation suggests gently rubbing the gums with a clean finger or offering a teething toy before bed. Ask your pediatrician before using any pain relief.

### Watch the nap transition

Mayo Clinic says most babies drop the third nap at about 9 months. If late-afternoon naps are pushing bedtime later, or your baby fights the third nap, a two-nap day may help. Cleveland Clinic suggests 2.5–4.5 hours of awake time between sleeps at 7–10 months.

For standing in the crib, our [10 month old sleep schedule](/10-month-old-sleep-schedule) has a step-by-step approach. Our [nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age) shows how the switch from three naps to two usually goes.

## What can make it worse

- **Starting new habits you don't want to keep,** such as feeding to sleep at every waking.
- **Dropping the third nap before your baby can manage longer awake periods.**
- **Stimulating play close to bedtime.**
- **Lifting your baby out at every protest,** which can turn bedtime into a game.

## Safe sleep at 8–10 months

- Remove anything reachable from sitting or standing, such as mobiles, cords, and wall hangings (KidsHealth).
- Keep the crib bare: no pillows, bumpers, or blankets in the first year (HealthyChildren.org / AAP).

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Sleep Foundation advises talking to your child's doctor if sleep problems continue. Call sooner if your baby has a fever, pulls at an ear and seems in pain, snores loudly or pauses in breathing, or is eating much less.

## Frequently asked questions

**When does the 8 month sleep regression start?**  
Usually somewhere between 8 and 10 months, often around a new skill such as crawling or pulling to stand.

**Is there a 9 month sleep regression?**  
It is usually the same developmental window. NHS services describe more waking at 8–9 months, and Sleep Foundation notes disturbances around 9 months.

**How long does the 8 month sleep regression last?**  
Typically one to a few weeks (Cleveland Clinic; Sleep Foundation).

**Should I drop to two naps during the 8 month regression?**  
Possibly. Mayo Clinic says the third nap usually goes around 9 months. Look for a fought or skipped late nap.

**Does every baby have an 8 month sleep regression?**  
No. Sleep Foundation says not all babies do.

## Match the bad nights to the milestones (Yorix)

**Yorix** logs night wakings and naps and suggests the next nap window as awake periods lengthen, which can make the 3-to-2 nap switch easier to see. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

heading: Sleep Regression Ages: A Stage-by-Stage Guide From Birth to Age 2
description: Sleep regression ages explained: what the evidence says about 3–4, 6, 8, 12 and 18 months and 2 years, whether newborns have one, signs and how long it lasts.
body:
# Sleep Regression Ages: A Stage-by-Stage Guide From Birth to Age 2

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

"Sleep regression" is not a medical diagnosis. It is a parenting term for a stretch of worse sleep that follows a better one. Online charts often list neat ages (4, 6, 8, 12, 18 months, 2 years), as if every baby passes through each one on schedule. The research is less tidy than that. This page is the overview: what each commonly named age is about, how strong the evidence is, and which page to read next.

## Short answer

The most commonly named **sleep regression ages** are around **3–4 months, 6 months, 8–10 months, 12 months, 18 months, and 2 years**. Only some have reasonable evidence behind them. Cleveland Clinic notes that research hasn't shown regressions arriving like clockwork at a set age for every baby, and Sleep Foundation describes them as phases that *can* happen during development rather than events every child is destined to have. Studies do link disrupted sleep to **new motor and language skills**, such as crawling, pulling to stand, walking, and first words, which helps explain why many babies have rough patches at roughly similar ages. Most episodes last **a week or two to a few weeks** (Cleveland Clinic; Sleep Foundation).

### Sleep regression ages at a glance

| Age often named | What is usually going on | Strength of evidence for a distinct "regression" | Read more |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Newborn (0–8 weeks) | Sleep is irregular from the start; not a regression | No source we checked describes one | [Newborn sleep schedule](/newborn-sleep-schedule) |
| 3–4 months | Sleep architecture matures into adult-like cycles; a "3 month regression" is usually the early start of the same change | Moderate: a well-described developmental change, but no separate 3-month event | [3 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/3-months); [4 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/4-months) |
| 6 months | Greater awareness, rolling, sitting; schedule shifts | Weak: Sleep Foundation says many babies don't have one | [6 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/6-months) |
| 8–10 months | Crawling, pulling to stand, separation anxiety, 3-to-2 naps | Moderate: small studies tie disrupted sleep to crawling and pulling to stand | [8 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/8-months) |
| 12 months | Walking, separation anxiety, nap timing | Weak to moderate: linked to walking milestones, not to the birthday itself | [12 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/12-months) |
| 18 months | Independence, language burst, 2-to-1 naps | Weak: mostly clinical experience and parent reports | [18 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/18-months) |
| 2 years | Nap refusal, bedtime stalling, fears, crib-to-bed moves | Weak: no study of a 2-year dip; Sleep Foundation says regressions can happen at any age | [2 year old sleep regression](/sleep-regression/2-years) |

## What "sleep regression" means

Sleep Foundation describes a sleep regression as a pause or a step backward in a baby's progress toward consistent sleep. Cleveland Clinic calls it a common phase in which a child slides backward after a period of steadier sleep. In practice, parents usually notice some mix of:

- more night waking, or wakings that are harder to settle;
- a baby who fights sleep at bedtime or naps;
- shorter or skipped naps;
- more fussiness during the day.

None of these is specific. The same signs appear with illness, teething, hunger, a schedule that no longer fits, or a change at home. Cleveland Clinic advises not to assume that every bad patch is a regression. One nursing researcher's webinar slides, published by Public Health Ontario, go further and list "sleep regression" as a popularized term that does not exist in the scientific literature.

## What the research actually shows

The evidence for **age-specific** regressions is thin. The evidence that **development and sleep interact** is stronger:

| Study | Who was studied | Finding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scher & Cohen, 2015 | 28 infants followed from 5 to 11 months with actigraphy | Alongside overall sleep improvement, periods of more long night wakings were linked in time to the onset of crawling |
| Atun-Einy & Scher, 2016 | 20 infants followed from 7 to 11–12 months | In babies who pulled to stand early (by 8 months), the milestone coincided with a period of disrupted sleep |
| Waugh & Berger, 2026 | Two cohorts tracked with an app and baby monitor | Sleep disruptions occurred around first crawling, first walking steps, walking mastery, and several language milestones |
| Mindell et al., 2016 | 841 children aged 0–36 months, app data | Sleep patterns changed constantly in the first three years, with wide individual variability |
| Pennestri et al., 2018 | 388 infants at 6 and 12 months | 27.9% to 57.0% did not sleep through the night (6- or 8-hour definitions), with no link to development or maternal mood |

Two practical conclusions follow. First, disrupted sleep tends to follow **your baby's developmental timetable**, not the calendar. An early crawler may have a "regression" at 7 months, a late one at 10. Second, many babies who wake at night are not regressing. They simply haven't consolidated their sleep yet, and that is within the normal range.

## Is there a newborn sleep regression?

We found no health source that describes a newborn sleep regression. Newborn sleep is irregular from the start. HealthyChildren.org (AAP) says newborns sleep about 16–17 hours a day but often only 1–2 hours at a time, and regular sleep cycles don't appear until about 4 months. Sleep Foundation notes that schedules tend to become more predictable from around 2 months.

What parents sometimes call a "newborn regression" is usually one of these:

- **Day and night still mixed up.** The NHS suggests teaching the difference from the start with light, play, and everyday noise by day, and dim, quiet feeds at night.
- **Hunger.** Breastfed newborns usually feed about every 2 hours (HealthyChildren.org), so a "bad night" may simply be a hungry one.
- **Overtiredness.** KidsHealth notes that overtired infants often have more trouble sleeping at night.

If a newborn is suddenly sleepier than usual, harder to wake, or feeding poorly, that is not a regression. Call your pediatrician (HealthyChildren.org).

## How long does a sleep regression last?

- **Cleveland Clinic:** typically a week or two.
- **Sleep Foundation:** 12- and 18-month regressions rarely last more than a few weeks, and 6-month problems often resolve within days or weeks.

Patterns that **outlast a few weeks** usually have another cause, such as a habit that formed during the rough patch (for example, being rocked to sleep at every waking), a schedule that needs adjusting, or a health issue. Then it is worth looking at routines, and talking to your pediatrician if you are unsure.

## What helps at any age

The specific pages cover age-appropriate details. The principles are the same across all of them:

1. **Rule out the basics:** illness, ear pain, teething discomfort, hunger, a room that is too hot or cold.
2. **Keep the routine steady.** Sleep Foundation's regression pages all stress a consistent bedtime routine and schedule.
3. **Make room for new skills in the day.** Lots of floor time to practice rolling, crawling, standing, or walking.
4. **Check the timing.** A nap that ends too late, or awake periods that no longer match your baby's age, can look like a regression. See [wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age) and our [nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age).
5. **Respond calmly and consistently** to night wakings, without introducing new habits you don't want to keep.
6. **Look after yourself.** Our guide to [night wakings](/survive-night-wakings-new-parents) covers sharing nights and getting help.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Contact your pediatrician if poor sleep comes with fever or other signs of illness, pain, breathing pauses or loud snoring, poor feeding, or fewer wet diapers. Also call if sleep problems last more than a few weeks or leave you struggling to cope.

## Frequently asked questions

**What are the sleep regression ages?**  
The ages most often named are about 3–4, 6, 8–10, 12, and 18 months, plus 2 years. Evidence is strongest for the changes around 3–4 months and around crawling and standing (often 8–10 months).

**Are sleep regressions real?**  
Bad patches are real and common. The idea that every baby has one at fixed ages is not supported: Cleveland Clinic says research hasn't shown them happening like clockwork for every baby.

**Can a newborn have a sleep regression?**  
We found no source describing one. Newborn sleep is irregular by nature.

**How long do sleep regressions last?**  
Usually one to a few weeks (Cleveland Clinic; Sleep Foundation).

**Do all babies go through sleep regressions?**  
No. Sleep Foundation notes that many babies don't have a 6-, 8-, 12-, or 18-month regression, and some sleep better at those ages.

## Spot the pattern behind the rough patch (Yorix)

**Yorix** logs naps and night wakings and follows your baby's development month by month, so you can see whether a bad week lines up with a new skill or a schedule that needs adjusting. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [3 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/3-months)
- [4 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/4-months)
- [6 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/6-months)
- [8 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/8-months)
- [12 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/12-months)
- [18 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/18-months)
- [2 year old sleep regression](/sleep-regression/2-years)
- [Contact naps](/contact-naps)
- [Baby waking every hour](/baby-waking-every-hour)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026. App pages are used only as labeled examples.

2. Sleep Foundation. "6-Month Infant Sleep Regression." Updated 15 July 2025. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/6-month-sleep-regression>.
3. Sleep Foundation. "8-Month Infant Sleep Regression." Updated 15 July 2025. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/8-month-sleep-regression>.
4. Sleep Foundation. "12-Month Infant Sleep Regression." Updated 15 July 2025. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/12-month-sleep-regression>.
5. Sleep Foundation. "18-Month Infant Sleep Regression." Updated 15 July 2025. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/18-month-sleep-regression>.
6. Sleep Foundation. "Newborn Sleep Schedule: What Parents Should Expect." Updated 15 September 2026. <https://www.sleepfoundation.org/baby-sleep/newborn-sleep-schedule>.
7. Scher A, Cohen D. "Sleep as a mirror of developmental transitions in infancy: the case of crawling." *Monographs of the Society for Research in Child Development*, 2015. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25704736/> (abstract via Europe PMC).
8. Atun-Einy O, Scher A. "Sleep disruption and motor development: Does pulling-to-stand impacts sleep-wake regulation?" *Infant Behavior & Development*, 2016. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26704990/> (abstract via Europe PMC).
9. Waugh M, Berger SE. "Infants' Sleep Supports the Emergence and Mastery of Locomotor and Linguistic Skills." *Developmental Psychobiology*, 2026. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42528314/> (abstract via Europe PMC).

13. NHS. "Helping your baby to sleep." <https://www.nhs.uk/baby/caring-for-a-newborn/helping-your-baby-to-sleep/>.
14. HealthyChildren.org / AAP. "How Often and How Much Should Your Baby Eat?" Last updated 2 April 2024. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/feeding-nutrition/Pages/How-Often-and-How-Much-Should-Your-Baby-Eat.aspx>.

description: Baby wide awake and happy for 1–3 hours at 2am? What split nights are, why too much time in bed causes them, and a schedule fix that usually works in a week.
body:
# Split Nights: Why Your Baby Is Wide Awake for Hours in the Middle of the Night

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

It's 2 a.m. and your baby isn't crying. They're babbling, rolling around, maybe laughing, and nothing you try puts them back to sleep for an hour or two. Then, just as suddenly, they doze off until morning. This pattern has a name among sleep specialists: a **split night**. Unlike most night wakings, it usually isn't about hunger or comfort. It's a timing problem, and the fix often runs against instinct: less time in bed, not more.

## Short answer

A split night is a **long, alert waking of about 1–3 hours** in the middle of the night, often in a good mood, that repeats every night or every few nights. Baby Sleep Science explains it as the two sleep drives coming apart: your baby has used up their **sleep pressure** before the **body clock** is ready for morning. The most common cause is **too many hours in bed**, usually from an **extra-early bedtime** after short naps, or **too much daytime sleep**. The usual fix is to match time in bed to the hours your baby can actually sleep: a **slightly later bedtime**, a **consistent morning wake time with daylight**, and **steady naps**. Expect a few rough nights, then improvement within about **4–7 days**.

### Key facts at a glance

| Question | What we found | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it looks like | One long waking, often 1–3 hours, baby alert or content | Pediatric Sleep Company; Baby Sleep Science |
| Root cause | Sleep pressure runs out before the body clock says "morning" | Baby Sleep Science |
| Most common trigger | Poor naps plus repeated extra-early bedtimes; too much day sleep | Baby Sleep Science; Pediatric Sleep Company |
| Will sleep training fix it? | Not on its own; it's a timing issue | Baby Sleep Science |
| Typical recovery | About 4–7 days with a consistent schedule | Baby Sleep Science |
| Total sleep, 4–12 months | 12–16 hours in 24 hours, naps included | AASM |

## How to tell a split night from other wakings

| Feature | Split night | Hunger or comfort waking | [Waking every hour](/baby-waking-every-hour) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Length | 1–3 hours | Minutes | Short, but many |
| Mood | Calm, chatty, playful | Crying, rooting | Fussy |
| Responds to feeding or rocking? | Not for long | Usually yes | Briefly |
| Pattern | One long gap, often after midnight | Around feed times | All night |

Baby Sleep Science adds that many babies having split nights actively *try* to sleep: changing position, sucking fingers, snuggling. The issue isn't that they don't know how to sleep; it's that they can't yet.

## Why split nights happen

Two systems work together at night:

1. **Sleep pressure** builds during the day and drains during sleep.
2. **The body clock** keeps your baby asleep until their usual wake time.

Every baby can only sleep so many hours at night. If your baby is in bed longer than that, the pressure can run out in the middle of the night, leaving them refreshed at 2 a.m. They stay up until a little pressure builds again and the body clock pulls them back to sleep.

### Cause 1: Short naps and early bedtimes, night after night

Baby Sleep Science calls this the most common cause. One early bedtime after a bad nap day usually works well: your baby catches up and still wakes at the normal time. The trouble comes when it repeats. After a few days of early bedtimes, either the morning starts creeping earlier or a long awake gap appears in the middle of the night.

### Cause 2: Too much daytime sleep

Long or extra naps leave less sleep need for the night. Pediatric Sleep Company lists this first among split-night causes.

### Cause 3: An inconsistent schedule

Pediatric Sleep Company notes that when naps and bedtime vary by more than about 30–45 minutes from day to day, the body clock gets mixed signals.

### Cause 4: Night disruption

Baby Sleep Science describes split nights that start after a disrupted night: practicing new motor skills like crawling or standing, illness (for example an hour in a steamy bathroom for congestion), or a feed or soothing session that turns into play.

## Split nights by age

Pediatric Sleep Company summarizes typical triggers by age:

| Age | Common trigger |
| --- | --- |
| 0–3 months | Immature sleep; long night wakings are common and normal |
| 4–7 months | Nap transitions and longer wake windows |
| 8–12 months | Crawling and standing |
| Toddlers | Too much or too late napping, inconsistent bedtime |

## How to fix split nights: step by step

### Step 1: Add up time in bed

Log a week: bedtime, morning wake time, every nap, and the length of the middle-of-the-night gap. Then compare total sleep with typical needs. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 12–16 hours in 24 hours for babies 4–12 months and 11–14 hours for 1–2 year olds, naps included.

### Step 2: Shorten the night slightly

This feels backwards, but it's the core of the fix. Baby Sleep Science gives an example: an 11-month-old with two 45-minute daycare naps goes to bed at 6:30 p.m., wakes at 2 a.m. for an hour and a half, and sleeps until 7 a.m., which is 12.5 hours in bed. At that age, the article says, many babies need about 3 hours of naps and 10.5–11 hours at night. Their suggested fix: bedtime around 7:15 p.m. and a wake-up around 6:15 a.m.

Your numbers will differ. The principle is to make the time in bed close to what your baby can actually sleep.

### Step 3: Wake at the same time every morning, with light

Baby Sleep Science explains that morning light "locks in" the body clock, so a consistent wake time, even if you have to wake your baby, helps the sleep drives line up again. Pediatric Sleep Company also recommends active, engaging awake time and natural daylight.

### Step 4: Rebuild the naps

To reach a slightly later bedtime, naps need to be decent. Baby Sleep Science suggests rocking, holding, extra soothing, and feeding are all fair tools while you fix a split night. See [short naps](/short-naps) for ways to lengthen them, and cap any very long naps to age-appropriate totals, as Pediatric Sleep Company recommends.

### Step 5: Keep the middle of the night boring

During the long waking, keep lights dim, voices quiet, and interaction minimal. Don't turn it into playtime. Pediatric Sleep Company gives this as part of its fix; Baby Sleep Science notes that if your baby still needs a night feed, feed in the dark and keep it brief.

### Step 6: Use early bedtimes sparingly

If short naps are unavoidable (for example at daycare), Baby Sleep Science suggests an early bedtime about twice a week, such as 1 hour early on two set nights, rather than every night. This limits sleep debt without bringing the split night back.

### Step 7: Be patient for about a week

Baby Sleep Science says your baby will probably still have long wakings for a few days after the schedule change, with things back to normal in about 4–7 days. Pediatric Sleep Company expects most split nights to settle within one to two weeks once the schedule is balanced.

## What not to do

- **Don't keep moving bedtime earlier** to make up for the lost night sleep. That's often what caused the problem.
- **Don't let your baby sleep in** to "catch up." It moves the body clock later and keeps the cycle going.
- **Don't expect sleep training to fix it alone.** Baby Sleep Science points out that a baby who simply isn't sleepy can't be trained to sleep. Sleep associations can still cause shorter wakings every 60–90 minutes, which is a separate issue.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

- The long waking comes with crying in pain, fever, ear tugging, or signs of reflux.
- Your baby snores loudly, gasps, or pauses in breathing during sleep.
- Your baby seems very sleepy or unwell during the day.
- You want to drop a night feed: Baby Sleep Science recommends asking your pediatrician first whether your baby (over 6 months) is ready.
- Nothing has changed after two weeks of consistent schedule changes.

## Frequently asked questions

**Why is my baby awake and happy at 2am?**  
Most likely a split night: your baby has had enough sleep for now, and their body clock isn't ready for the second part of the night yet.

**How long do split nights last?**  
With a consistent schedule change, often about 4–7 days. Without changes, the pattern tends to stick.

**Is a split night a sleep regression?**  
Not usually. Regressions involve more frequent, fussy wakings. A split night is one long, calm waking caused by timing.

**Should I put my baby to bed earlier after a split night?**  
Only occasionally. Repeated early bedtimes are a common cause of split nights.

**Can new skills cause split nights?**  
Yes. Practicing crawling or standing can disrupt a night. Give plenty of practice time during the day.

## See the hours in bed at a glance (Yorix)

**Yorix** shows naps, bedtime, and night wakings on one daily timeline and recalculates the next sleep window after each nap, so you can see how many hours your baby is spending in bed and whether a later bedtime closes the 2 a.m. gap. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [Early morning waking](/early-morning-waking)
- [Baby waking every hour](/baby-waking-every-hour)
- [Short naps](/short-naps)
- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)
- [Baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026.

1. Baby Sleep Science. "The 'Split' Night: Why some babies are awake for hours in the middle of the night and how to fix it." <https://www.babysleepscience.com/single-post/2014/09/09/the-split-night-why-some-babies-are-awake-for-hours-in-the-middle-of-the-night-and-how>.
2. Pediatric Sleep Company (Charlotte Chudy). "Split Nights: Why Your Baby Is Awake for Hours in the Middle of the Night (and How to Fix It)." <https://www.pediatricsleepcompany.com/blog-/split-nights-why-your-baby-is-awake-for-hours-in-the-middle-of-the-night-and-how-to-fix-it>.
3. American Academy of Sleep Medicine. "Recharge with sleep: Pediatric sleep recommendations promoting optimal health." <https://aasm.org/recharge-with-sleep-pediatric-sleep-recommendations-promoting-optimal-health/>.

description: What age to start sleep training, signs your baby is ready, when babies can self-soothe, and why there's no rush: guidance from pediatricians and research.
body:
# When to Start Sleep Training: Age, Readiness Signs, and Self-Soothing

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

"When should we start?" is often the first sleep training question, and it gets very different answers: 3 months, 4 months, 6 months, "whenever you're ready," or "never." The spread isn't just opinion. It reflects how quickly babies' sleep changes in the first year, and how little research there is on the youngest ages. This guide collects what pediatricians and studies say about the right age, the signs that a baby is ready, and when babies can actually self-soothe. It doesn't cover how each method works; for that, see [sleep training methods explained](/sleep-training-methods-explained).

## Short answer

Most pediatric sources put the **earliest start at about 4–6 months**, with **around 6 months** the most common choice. Cleveland Clinic says many babies are ready at about 4 months, Sleep Foundation says babies aren't ready before 4–6 months, and the Child Mind Institute calls about 6 months typical. **Newborns shouldn't be sleep trained.** Before you start, ask your pediatrician whether your baby is growing well and still needs night feeds. There is **no proven deadline**: older babies and toddlers can learn too, so start when your baby is ready *and* your family can be consistent.

### Key facts at a glance

| Question | What we found | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Earliest usual age | About 4–6 months | Cleveland Clinic; Sleep Foundation; Dartmouth Health |
| Most common start | Around 6 months | Child Mind Institute |
| Newborns | Not recommended | Cleveland Clinic; Huckleberry (app example) |
| When babies begin to self-soothe | Early signs in the first months; more reliable around 3–6 months | Texas Children's; Huckleberry (app example) |
| Fastest change in self-regulated sleep | From 1 to 4 months | Henderson et al., 2010 |
| Evidence before 6 months | Behavioral programs not shown to improve outcomes for mothers or babies | Douglas & Hill, 2013 |

## Recommended age by source

| Source | Suggested age | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cleveland Clinic (Noah Schwartz, MD) | About 4 months | Some babies a little earlier, others closer to 6 months |
| Sleep Foundation | 4–6 months | Before then, circadian rhythms that support longer sleep haven't developed |
| Dartmouth Health Children's | 4–6 months to encourage self-soothing | Before separation anxiety develops |
| Texas Children's | 3–6 months for self-soothing | Waking 1–3 times a night is common in the first 6 months |
| Child Mind Institute | Around 6 months typical | Recommendations range from 3 months to over a year |
| Huckleberry (app example) | Gentle practice from 3–4 months; most babies more capable around 6 months | Sleep training not recommended for newborns |

The pattern is clear: nobody we found recommends sleep training before about 3–4 months, and most land between 4 and 6 months.

## Signs your baby may be ready

You don't need every sign, but most of them should apply:

- **Age:** at least 4 months (adjusted age if your baby was born early), ideally closer to 6.
- **Healthy growth:** your pediatrician is happy with weight gain and feeding.
- **Night feeds discussed:** you know which feeds, if any, your baby still needs.
- **Some independent sleep:** Sleep Foundation notes that a baby who sometimes falls asleep on their own at night is likely ready.
- **Longer night stretches already appearing:** a sign the body clock is maturing.
- **A predictable routine:** a regular bedtime and similar steps each night.
- **You're ready:** all caregivers agree on a plan and can stick with it for one to two weeks.

## Signs to wait a little longer

- Your baby is unwell, teething hard, or recently vaccinated and uncomfortable.
- You're about to travel, move house, change childcare, or return to work.
- Your baby has reflux, feeding difficulties, or slow weight gain.
- Your baby snores loudly or seems to struggle to breathe during sleep. Sleep Foundation's Ferber guide notes that behavioral methods alone aren't enough when excessive snoring may point to a breathing disorder such as sleep apnea.
- You're not sure you can stay consistent right now. A half-done plan can make crying last longer.

## When can babies self-soothe?

Self-soothing is a baby's growing ability to calm down and settle without immediate help. It develops **after** babies have had lots of experience being soothed by a caregiver.

- **First months:** Huckleberry (app example) says some babies show early signs, such as bringing hands to the mouth or sucking a pacifier, but not consistently.
- **3–6 months:** Texas Children's says babies aren't cognitively ready to self-soothe until 3 to 6 months; from then, families can give them a chance to settle when they wake.
- **Around 6 months:** Huckleberry (app example) describes most babies as developmentally capable of falling and staying asleep more independently, as long as hunger and other needs are met.

Two clarifications help:

1. **Self-soothing isn't the same as sleeping through the night.** Dr. Schwartz at Cleveland Clinic points out that a sleep-trained baby has learned to settle but may still wake; a baby who sleeps through without training hasn't necessarily learned to settle.
2. **Waking is normal.** HealthyChildren.org (AAP) describes a good sleeper at this age as a baby who wakes often but gets back to sleep, not one who never wakes.

Comfort objects should wait: the AAP advises keeping soft toys and loose items out of the crib for the first year, as Huckleberry (app example) also notes.

## Sleep training by age: what to expect

### Before 4 months: build foundations instead

Babies' self-regulated sleep changes fastest in this period. In a study of 75 infants, Henderson and colleagues found the biggest increase in self-regulated night sleep between **1 and 4 months**. Many babies lengthen their night stretch on their own. Instead of training, focus on:

- dark, quiet nights and bright, social days;
- a short bedtime routine;
- sometimes putting your baby down drowsy but awake;
- responding to crying and feeding on demand.

A 2013 review by Douglas and Hill found that behavioral sleep programs in the first 6 months had not been shown to reduce crying, prevent later sleep problems, or protect against postnatal depression, and flagged risks such as earlier weaning from breastfeeding.

### 4–6 months: the earliest common window

Sleep becomes more adult-like around 4 months, which is also when many families meet the [4 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/4-months). Gentle approaches (bedtime fading, pick up/put down, chair method) are popular here. Check feeding plans with your pediatrician first, because many babies this age still feed at night.

### 6–12 months: the most studied window

The trials we checked enrolled babies from about 6 months up. A 2016 randomized trial included babies aged 6–16 months, and an Australian community trial (Hiscock et al., 2007) reached mothers of 7-month-olds with sleep problems; it reduced reported sleep problems and maternal depression symptoms at 10 and 12 months. Dartmouth Health suggests encouraging self-soothing a little earlier, between 4 and 6 months, before separation anxiety develops.

### After 12 months: still possible

Henderson's study found that at 12 months, 21 of 75 babies still weren't sleeping from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Toddlers can learn new sleep habits too. For toddlers who resist bedtime, Huckleberry (app example) describes pairing a warm, consistent routine with a temporarily later bedtime, then moving it earlier. Macall Gordon, writing in Psychology Today in 2025, notes there's no proof that waiting makes sleep training harder later.

## Is there a "best" age?

No study has identified one best age. A reasonable way to decide:

| If... | Consider... |
| --- | --- |
| Baby is under 4 months | Foundations only; no formal training |
| Baby is 4–6 months, healthy, and your pediatrician agrees | A gentle method, or wait |
| Baby is 6 months or older, and sleep problems are affecting the family | Any method you can follow consistently |
| You're happy with how things are | No need to train at all |

The Child Mind Institute's expert, Wendy Nash, MD, suggests looking for trends over weeks rather than reacting to single bad nights. Short disruptions from growth spurts or teething can pass on their own; if they last more than a week or two, sleep training becomes a reasonable option.

## Frequently asked questions

**What age is best to start sleep training?**  
Most sources point to 4–6 months at the earliest, and around 6 months is the most common choice. There's no single best age.

**Can you sleep train at 3 months?**  
Formal training isn't usually recommended this early. Gentle habits (routine, putting down drowsy) are fine.

**What age do babies self-soothe?**  
Early signs appear in the first months, but self-soothing becomes more reliable between about 3 and 6 months, and most babies are more capable by around 6 months.

**Is it too late to sleep train at 1 year or older?**  
No. There's no evidence of a closing window; toddlers can learn new sleep habits.

**Do I have to sleep train at all?**  
No. Sleep training is optional. Many babies consolidate sleep with time.

**How do I know it's working?**  
Track settling time and night wakings for a week. If there's no progress after one to two weeks of consistency, pause and reassess.

## Check readiness with real data (Yorix)

**Yorix** shows how your baby's longest night stretch and settling time are changing week by week, which can help you and your pediatrician judge whether the time is right. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

- [5 month old sleep schedule](/5-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [6 month old sleep schedule](/6-month-old-sleep-schedule)
