description: Huckleberry app vs Yorix: an honest look at nap predictions, AI help, free tiers, prices, languages, devices and privacy, to pick the baby app that fits you.
body:
# Huckleberry vs Yorix: A Fair Comparison of Two Baby Sleep Apps

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

*Disclosure: Yorix makes this page, so we have an interest in the outcome. To keep it fair, every Huckleberry detail below comes from Huckleberry's own website and App Store listing, and every Yorix detail from ours, all checked on 15 November 2026. Prices are U.S. App Store and website prices on that date and can change. If something is out of date, please tell us and we will correct it.*

Huckleberry is one of the best-known baby sleep apps. It is widely used, highly rated, and backed by a pediatric team. Yorix is a newer, iPhone-only app focused on predicting the next sleep and re-planning the day as it goes. Both log sleep and feeds and both predict nap times. The real differences are in pricing structure, devices, languages, extras such as expert sleep plans, and where your data lives.

## Short answer

Choose **Huckleberry** if you want an established app with **Android and Apple Watch** support, a **free tier** for logging all core activities, **SweetSpot®** nap predictions (Plus or Premium), and, in Premium, **expert-designed sleep plans** and the **Berry** AI chat. Huckleberry's listed prices are **$11.99/month or $68.99/year for Plus** and **$14.99/month or $119.99/year for Premium**.

Choose **Yorix** if you use an **iPhone or iPad** and want a next-sleep forecast that **recalculates the day after every logged nap**, an **AI coach** that answers from your own diary, **20 interface languages**, and a diary stored **on your device and in your own iCloud**. Sleep logging in Yorix is free; Premium is **$5.99/week (7-day free trial), $14.99/month, or $59.99/year**.

## Side-by-side comparison

| Feature | Huckleberry | Yorix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Devices | iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch (iOS 16+); also available on Android | iPhone and iPad (iOS 18+); no Android or web version |
| Interface languages (App Store) | English | 20 languages, including Spanish, German, French, Russian, Japanese, Arabic, and Hindi |
| Free tier | Track sleep, feeding, diapers, pumping, growth, and more; sleep summaries; multiple children; reminders; caregiver sync | Download and sleep logging free; other entry types (feeds, diapers, care, growth) limited in the free version |
| Nap and bedtime prediction | SweetSpot® (Plus and Premium, from 2 months) | Next-sleep forecast and a day plan that re-plans itself (Premium) |
| Schedule tools | Schedule Creator (Plus and Premium, from 2 months) | Adaptive day plan based on your baby's recent days (Premium) |
| AI chat | Berry, 24/7 (Premium only) | AI coach, 24/7, answering from your diary (Premium; extra AI credit packs sold separately) |
| Expert sleep plans | Custom sleep plans with regular check-ins (Premium) | Not offered |
| Data insights | Insights (tips and mini-plans) and Enhanced Reports (Plus and Premium) | Daily summaries, weekly reports, and analytics (Premium) |
| AI logging by text, voice, or photo | Yes (Plus and Premium) | Siri voice commands to log a sleep or a feed |
| Widgets and lock screen | Widgets, live lock screen updates, Apple Watch (Plus and Premium, iOS) | Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets, Live Activity, Dynamic Island |
| Partner sharing | Caregivers sign in to the same account on each device | Invite a partner via iCloud; no separate Yorix account needed |
| Solids | Solids tracking with allergens and reactions (free) | Starting Solids program with 272 foods (one-time purchase) |
| Sounds | Not listed on the pages we checked | White noise, rain, ocean sounds, and bedtime stories |
| Offline use | Not stated on the pages we checked | Diary, wake windows, and forecast work offline; AI coach and sync need internet |
| Free trial | Two weeks of free access (pricing page) | 7-day free trial on the weekly plan; annual plan has no trial |
| App Store rating (15 Nov 2026) | 4.9 from about 79,000 ratings; Editors' Choice | 5.0 from 4 ratings |

## Prices compared (U.S., checked 15 November 2026)

| Plan | Price | What it adds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Huckleberry Free | $0 | Logging, reports, caregiver sync |
| Huckleberry Plus | $11.99/month or $68.99/year (shown as $5.74/month billed yearly) | SweetSpot®, Schedule Creator, Insights, Enhanced Reports, AI logging, widgets/Watch |
| Huckleberry Premium | $14.99/month or $119.99/year (shown as $9.99/month billed yearly) | Everything in Plus, plus Berry AI chat and custom sleep plans |
| Yorix free | $0 | Sleep logging; limited other entry types |
| Yorix Premium | $5.99/week (7-day free trial), $14.99/month, or $59.99/year | Next-sleep forecast, self-adjusting day plan, AI coach, analytics, daily advice |
| Yorix add-ons | AI credits: 50 for $4.99, 200 for $14.99; programs: Starting Solids $19.99, Development leaps $24.99, both $31.99 (one-time) | Extra AI questions; lifetime access to programs |

Huckleberry's App Store listing also shows a one-time "Sleep Improvement Plan" purchase ($49.99). We didn't review what it includes.

## Where Huckleberry is stronger

- **Platforms.** Android, Apple Watch, and iPhone, which matters if your household mixes phones.
- **Track record and scale.** About 79,000 App Store ratings averaging 4.9, an Editors' Choice badge, and a company statement that it is trusted by over 5 million families.
- **Expert sleep plans.** Premium includes custom sleep plans with regular check-ins, designed by Huckleberry's experts. Huckleberry says its sleep guidance never requires "crying it out."
- **A generous free tier** for logging almost everything, including a contraction timer, a breastfeeding timer, and solids tracking.
- **Monthly flexibility** for Plus at $11.99.

## Where Yorix is different

- **The plan re-plans itself.** Log a short nap or a late wake-up and the rest of the day's windows are recalculated straight away.
- **Diary-aware AI coach.** Answers draw on your own entries, such as your baby's age and recent logs.
- **Languages.** 20 interface languages, useful for multilingual families and caregivers.
- **Data storage.** The diary lives on your iPhone and in your own iCloud. Yorix says it cannot read it, the AI coach receives only a short summary without names or contacts, and the app shows no ads.
- **Offline forecasts.** Forecasts are computed on the device, so they work without a signal.
- **Annual price.** $59.99 a year for Premium.

## Things to know before you choose

- **Yorix is newer.** It has far fewer ratings than Huckleberry, so there is less public feedback to go on.
- **Yorix is Apple-only.** If anyone in your family uses Android, Huckleberry is the more practical shared log.
- **Neither app replaces your pediatrician.** Both describe their guidance as informational.
- **Predictions are estimates.** Any nap prediction is a starting point. Your baby's cues come first. Our [wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age) guide explains the ranges that sleep apps build on.

## Looking for a Huckleberry alternative?

People usually look for an alternative for one of these reasons:

| If you want... | Consider |
| --- | --- |
| Lower annual cost for nap predictions and an AI chat | Compare Huckleberry Plus ($68.99/year, no AI chat) with Yorix Premium ($59.99/year, with AI coach) |
| An app in your own language | Yorix (20 languages) |
| A shared log across Android and iPhone | Huckleberry |
| Expert-designed sleep training plans | Huckleberry Premium |
| A diary that stays in your own iCloud | Yorix |
| A comparison with another popular nap app | Our [Napper vs Yorix](/yorix-vs-napper) page |

## Frequently asked questions

**Is the Huckleberry app free?**  
Huckleberry has a free tier with logging and reports. SweetSpot® predictions need Plus or Premium (Huckleberry pricing page).

**How much does Huckleberry cost?**  
Plus is $11.99/month or $68.99/year; Premium is $14.99/month or $119.99/year (U.S. prices on 15 November 2026).

**What is Huckleberry SweetSpot?**  
Huckleberry's feature that predicts nap and sleep times, available from 2 months on Plus and Premium.

**Is Yorix available on Android?**  
No. Yorix runs on iPhone and iPad (iOS 18 or later).

**Can two parents use the same log?**  
Yes, in both apps. Huckleberry caregivers sign in to the same account; Yorix partners join through an invite and see the same diary.

**Which app is better?**  
It depends on your devices, language, budget, and whether you want expert sleep plans (Huckleberry Premium) or a self-adjusting daily plan with on-device forecasts (Yorix).

## Try the next-nap forecast (Yorix)

**Yorix** is free to download, and sleep logging is free. Premium adds the next-sleep forecast, the self-adjusting day plan, and the AI coach. It is a support for tired parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.

## Related reading

- [Napper vs Yorix](/yorix-vs-napper)
- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)
- [Baby nap schedule by age](/baby-nap-schedule-by-age)
- [Sleep regression ages](/sleep-regression)
- [Sleep training methods explained](/sleep-training-methods-explained)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026. Prices are U.S. prices on that date.

1. Huckleberry. "Membership Pricing & Sign Up." <https://huckleberrycare.com/pricing>.
2. Huckleberry. Home page ("Also available on Android"; "trusted by over 5 million families"). <https://huckleberrycare.com/>.
3. Apple App Store. "Huckleberry: Baby Tracker" (Huckleberry Labs Inc.): description, compatibility, languages, ratings, in-app purchases. <https://apps.apple.com/us/app/huckleberry-baby-tracker/id1169136078>.
4. Yorix. Home page and FAQ (free vs subscription, data storage, devices, offline use, partner sharing). <https://yorix-app.com/>.
5. Apple App Store. "Yorix: Baby Sleep Tracker": description, compatibility, languages, ratings, in-app purchases. <https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id6788705252>.

# Napper vs Yorix: Which Baby Sleep App Fits Your Family?

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's sleep, feeding, growth, or breathing, contact your pediatrician.*

*Disclosure: this comparison is written by the team that makes Yorix, so read it with that in mind. We limited ourselves to what each company publishes: Napper facts come from napper.app, its App Store page, and its Google Play page; Yorix facts come from yorix-app.com and the Yorix App Store page. Everything was opened on 15 November 2026. Prices are U.S. store prices on that day and may change. Spot a mistake? Tell us and we'll fix it.*

Napper is a popular nap-scheduling app made by Napper AB. According to its App Store page, it was started by a dad on parental leave whose daughter wasn't a great sleeper. It builds a daily nap and bedtime plan from what you log, plays sleep sounds, and includes a short sleep course. Yorix, our app, also predicts the next sleep from your baby's real day, but it runs only on Apple devices and stores the diary in your own iCloud. This page sets out what each app offers, what each costs, and where Napper is the better choice.

## Short answer

**Napper suits you** if you need **Android** (or a mix of Android and iPhone in the family), want an **Apple Watch** app, or like the idea of a guided **sleep course** plus a large **sound library** (30+ sounds). It has a long public track record: **4.9 stars from about 4,700 ratings** on the U.S. App Store with an **Editors' Choice** badge, and **4.7 stars from about 17,300 reviews and 1M+ downloads** on Google Play. Napper's website lists **Napper Unlimited at $69.99 a year**.

**Yorix suits you** if your family is all on **iPhone or iPad**, you want the plan to **re-plan straight after each logged nap**, you'd like a **coach that answers from your own diary**, and you prefer a diary kept **on your device and in your iCloud**. Logging sleep in Yorix costs nothing; **Premium is $59.99 a year**, $14.99 a month, or $5.99 a week with a 7-day trial.

## Napper at a glance

| What | Napper (as published by Napper) |
| --- | --- |
| Developer | Napper AB |
| Platforms | iPhone (iOS 16.4+), Apple Watch (watchOS 26+), Apple Vision (visionOS 1.0+); Android (Google Play) |
| App languages | English plus 19 more, including Czech, Danish, Finnish, Greek, Hungarian, Romanian, Swedish, and Ukrainian (App Store list) |
| Ratings (15 Nov 2026) | App Store U.S.: 4.9, about 4.7K ratings, Editors' Choice. Google Play: 4.7, about 17.3K reviews, 1M+ downloads |
| Core idea | A daily nap chart that adjusts to your child's rhythm, built on wake windows and sleep pressure (Google Play description) |
| Extras | 30+ sleep sounds; a sleep and attachment-parenting course; a sleep guide called "Doulores" that answers questions; trends and statistics |
| Tracking | Sleep, breastfeeding, bottles, solids, medication, diapers; shareable with a partner and other caregivers |
| Newest addition | On iOS 27, the next nap and bedtime can appear in Spotlight search (App Store release notes) |

## Free vs paid: what Napper's pricing page shows

Napper's pricing page compares **Free** and **Unlimited**. In the free column, two features are available: **daily sleep tracking** and a **sleep schedule based on age**. Five more are shown with a lock in the free column and unlocked in Unlimited: **personalized sleep analysis, educational sleep courses, custom baby sleep sounds, trends and statistics,** and **"track everything."** The page gives Unlimited as **$69.99 a year**, and the gift page sells a one-year Unlimited gift for the same $69.99 that doesn't auto-renew.

**What we couldn't confirm.** The U.S. App Store lists several in-app purchases with different names: "Unlimited: Baby-Sleep Expert +" ($14.99, $29.99, $69.99), "Unlimited: Night Slumber +" ($49.99, $119.99), "Napper Sleep" ($14.99 monthly, $89.99 yearly), and "Napper Complete" ($19.99 monthly, $129.99 yearly). The listing doesn't say which of these are currently offered to new users or what separates "Sleep" from "Complete," and we didn't find a free-trial length on the pages we checked. Check the price inside the app before you subscribe.

## Yorix plans for comparison

| Yorix plan | U.S. price (15 Nov 2026) | Includes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free | $0 | Download and unlimited sleep logging; feeds, diapers, care, and growth entries are limited |
| Premium | $5.99/week with a 7-day free trial, $14.99/month, or $59.99/year (no trial) | Next-sleep forecast, a day plan that adjusts itself, the AI coach, analytics, daily tips |
| One-time add-ons | AI credits ($4.99 for 50, $14.99 for 200); Starting Solids $19.99; Development leaps $24.99; both $31.99 | Extra coach questions; programs you keep for life |

## Feature by feature

| Need | Napper | Yorix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Predicting the next nap and bedtime | Personalized schedule that adjusts as you log (Unlimited unlocks personalized analysis; free shows an age-based schedule) | Next-sleep forecast recalculated after every logged nap (Premium) |
| Asking questions at 3 a.m. | "Doulores," Napper's sleep guide, answers sleep questions for your baby's age | AI coach that reads a short summary of your diary (Premium, plus optional credit packs) |
| Learning about sleep | Sleep and attachment-parenting course written with sleep experts, presented as a 14-day program | Free sleep guides on yorix-app.com; Development and Starting Solids programs sold separately |
| Sleep sounds | 30+ sounds, including white noise, pink noise, heartbeat, womb sounds, and lullabies | White noise, rain, ocean, and bedtime stories with a sleep timer |
| Logging beyond sleep | Breastfeeding, bottles, solids, medication, diapers | Breastfeeding, bottles, pumping, diapers, growth with WHO percentiles, symptoms, mood, vaccinations |
| Quick logging | Apple Watch app; Spotlight on iOS 27 | Home and Lock Screen widgets, Live Activities, Dynamic Island, Siri voice commands |
| Sharing with a partner | Share profiles with another parent or caregiver | Partner invited through iCloud, no separate account |
| Devices | iPhone, Apple Watch, Apple Vision, Android | iPhone and iPad (iOS 18+); no Android, no web |
| Where the diary is kept | Not described on the pages we checked | On the device and in your own iCloud; Yorix says it can't read it |
| App Store privacy label (self-reported) | Lists identifiers as possibly used for tracking; purchases, coarse location, email, identifiers, usage, and diagnostics as data linked to you | Lists purchases, contact info, identifiers, and usage data as possibly used for tracking |
| Offline | Not stated | Diary, wake windows, and forecast work offline; the coach and sync need a connection |

Both apps ship in about 20 languages, so language alone isn't a reason to pick one over the other. The lists differ, though: Napper covers more European languages (for example Swedish, Danish, Finnish, Czech, Greek, Hungarian, Romanian), while Yorix covers more Asian ones (for example Korean, Thai, Vietnamese, Hindi, Indonesian, and both Chinese scripts).

## Where Napper is stronger

- **Android and wearables.** Napper runs on Android, Apple Watch, and even Apple Vision. Yorix has no Android version, so Napper is the realistic option for a mixed-phone household.
- **Proven at scale.** Over a million Google Play downloads, thousands of ratings on both stores, and an Editors' Choice badge on the App Store. Yorix has only a handful of ratings so far.
- **A structured course.** Napper offers a sleep and attachment-parenting course that it says can improve your sleep situation in 14 days or less. Yorix doesn't offer a step-by-step sleep course.
- **A bigger sound library.** More than 30 sounds, made with a composer, versus a shorter list in Yorix.
- **A free age-based schedule.** Napper's free tier includes a schedule based on age; Yorix keeps its forecast in Premium.
- **Gifting.** A non-renewing one-year gift subscription is available on Napper's website.

## Where Yorix takes a different approach

- **Re-planning in real time.** When a nap is cut short, Yorix immediately moves the next windows and bedtime for the rest of that day.
- **Answers grounded in your log.** The coach sees your baby's age and latest entries (without names or contacts), so replies reflect the day you actually had.
- **Your diary, your iCloud.** Entries are stored on the phone and synced through your own iCloud rather than a Yorix account. There are no ads in the app.
- **No signal needed for forecasts.** Forecasts are calculated on the device, which helps on flights or in places with poor coverage.

heading: 12 Month Milestones: What Most 1-Year-Olds Can Do
description: 12 month milestones from CDC's 2022 checklist: waving, 'mama' or 'dada', pulling to stand, cruising, pincer grasp. When walking is expected and when to ask.
body:
# 12 Month Milestones: What Most 1-Year-Olds Can Do

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your child's development, hearing, vision, or feeding, contact your pediatrician.*

The first birthday brings a flood of comparisons: one cousin is walking, another is saying five words, yours is cruising along the sofa and saying "da" for everything. This page sets out what CDC expects most children to do by 12 months, separates that from what often comes a few months later (independent walking, more words), and explains when it is worth asking your pediatrician. For naps and bedtime, see our [12 month old sleep schedule](/12-month-old-sleep-schedule).

## Short answer

By their first birthday, most babies **play games like pat-a-cake, wave "bye-bye", call a parent "mama", "dada", or another special name, understand "no" (pause or stop when you say it), put an object into a container, look for something they saw you hide, pull up to stand, walk while holding on to furniture, drink from an open cup you hold, and pick up small things between thumb and pointer finger.** This is CDC's 2022 checklist, which includes skills that **at least 75% of children** have by 12 months. **Walking alone isn't on the 1-year list**; taking a few steps without help appears on the **15-month** list.

### Key facts at a glance

| Question | Answer | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Checklist | CDC "Milestones by 1 Year" (2022 revision with the AAP) | CDC |
| Number of milestones | 10, in four areas | CDC |
| Threshold | Skills 75% or more of children have by this age | CDC; Zubler et al., 2022 |
| Walking alone | 15-month checklist ("takes a few steps on his own") | CDC |
| Words besides "mama"/"dada" | 15-month checklist (one or two words) | CDC |
| Baby walkers | Not recommended | CDC |
| First dental visit | Within 6 months of the first tooth and no later than 12 months | AAP (HealthyChildren.org) |

## 12 month milestones checklist (CDC, in our words)

| Area | Most children by 12 months… |
| --- | --- |
| Social and emotional | Join in simple games with you, such as pat-a-cake |
| Language and communication | Wave goodbye; use "mama", "dada", or another special name for a parent; understand "no" and briefly pause or stop |
| Thinking and learning | Drop an object into a container (a block into a cup); search for something they watched you hide (a toy under a blanket) |
| Movement and physical | Pull up to a standing position; "cruise" along furniture while holding on; sip from a lidless cup that you hold; pinch small items such as bits of food between thumb and index finger |

Source: CDC "Milestones by 1 Year" (updated May 2026).

## Walking: what's normal at 1 year

Most parents' first question at this age. On CDC's lists:

- **By 12 months:** pulls up to stand and walks holding on to furniture ("cruising").
- **By 15 months:** takes a few steps alone.

So a 1-year-old who cruises but doesn't yet walk alone is within the checklist. Reasonable ways to help, from CDC's tips: give your child safe furniture to pull up on, let them hold your hands to practice, and offer sturdy push toys or even an empty box to push. **Baby walkers aren't recommended** (CDC).

## Talking: first words and understanding

At 12 months the CDC list focuses on **communication**, not vocabulary:

- using "mama", "dada", or a special name for a specific parent;
- waving bye-bye;
- understanding "no".

One or two extra words (often half-words, like "ba" for ball) appear on the **15-month** list, along with pointing to ask for something and following a simple instruction given with a gesture. CDC's advice for building language: answer when your child points ("You want the cup? Here's your cup"), and expand what they say ("ta" → "Yes, a truck").

## Hands and eating

The neat pincer grasp (thumb and pointer finger) is a 1-year milestone, and it makes self-feeding much easier. CDC suggests:

- foods of different textures: smooth, mashed, or finely chopped, offered again and again, since many babies need several tries to accept a new food;
- letting your child feed themselves with their fingers while you sit with them, and practicing with a cup that has a little water in it;
- water, breast milk, or plain milk to drink; no juice is needed, and if you give it, no more than 4 ounces a day of 100% juice; no sodas, fruit drinks, or flavored milk.

Learn which foods are choking hazards before offering finger foods; see our [baby-led weaning](/baby-led-weaning) guide.

## Teeth and the first dental visit

Teeth aren't milestones, and the timing varies widely. The AAP says your child should see a dentist within 6 months of the first tooth appearing and **no later than 12 months**, whichever comes first, and that you should brush with a rice-grain-sized smear of fluoride toothpaste from the first tooth. If your child has no teeth yet at 1 year, the AAP says the timing can be hereditary and usually doesn't mean anything is wrong; ask at the checkup if you're unsure. More in our [teething symptoms](/teething-symptoms) guide.

## Play ideas for a 1-year-old

From CDC's tips for this age:

- **Narrate and sing** what you're doing: "We're washing your hands."
- **Point things out** (trucks, birds, the dog) so your child learns to follow your attention.
- **Books with flaps and textures**; "reading" can just mean talking about the pictures.
- **Blocks, cups, and containers** to fill, stack, and dump.
- **Pots, pans, and a drum** to make noise.
- **Teach wanted behaviors** with praise and hugs; redirect quickly instead of long explanations, and save a firm "no" for danger. CDC advises against spanking and yelling.
- **Comfort routines**: a familiar toy or blanket when meeting a new caregiver.

CDC continues to advise no screen time other than video calls before age 2.

## Babies born early

The AAP recommends using **corrected age** until age 2. A child who turns 1 but was born 6 weeks early is compared with what a baby about 10½ months old would do.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Ask about developmental screening, or call your state's early intervention program (free evaluation for children under 3 in the U.S.; cdc.gov/FindEI), if:

- by 12 months (corrected age) your child isn't doing one or more items on the checklist, for example **doesn't pull to stand, doesn't wave, doesn't use a name for a parent, or doesn't look for hidden objects**;
- by 15 months your child isn't taking a few steps alone (CDC 15-month checklist);
- your child **loses** words, gestures, or other skills they had;
- your child doesn't respond to their name or to sounds;
- you're worried for any reason. CDC's message is "don't wait".

The AAP recommends standardized developmental screening at 9, 18, and 30 months and autism screening at 18 and 24 months, but a screening can be done at any visit when there's a concern.

## Frequently asked questions

**What should a 1 year old be doing?**  
Most can pull up to stand, cruise along furniture, pick up small bits of food with a pincer grasp, wave bye-bye, use "mama" or "dada" for a parent, understand "no", play pat-a-cake, and find a toy you hid.

**Is it normal if my 1 year old isn't walking?**  
Yes, if they pull to stand and cruise. Walking a few steps alone is on CDC's 15-month checklist. Talk to your pediatrician if your child isn't pulling to stand by 12 months or isn't taking steps alone by 15 months.

**How many words should a 12 month old say?**  
CDC's 1-year list includes a special name for a parent ("mama", "dada"). One or two other words are expected by 15 months.

**Should my 1 year old use a walker?**  
CDC says baby walkers are not recommended. Push toys and holding hands are safer ways to practice.

**When should a baby have the first dental visit?**  
Within 6 months of the first tooth, and no later than the first birthday (AAP).

## Bring your notes to the 1-year checkup (Yorix)

**Yorix** lets you note the day of the first steps, a new word, or a worry next to the sleep and feeding log, so it is easy to answer your pediatrician's questions at the 12-month visit. It is a support for parents, not a medical device and not a developmental screening tool.

## Related reading

- [12 month old sleep schedule](/12-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [12 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/12-months)
- [15 month old sleep schedule](/15-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [9 month milestones](/9-month-milestones)
- [Teething symptoms](/teething-symptoms)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026. App pages are used only as labeled examples.

1. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "Milestones by 1 Year." Updated 16 May 2026. <https://www.cdc.gov/act-early/milestones/1-year.html>.
2. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "Milestones by 15 Months." Updated 16 May 2026. <https://www.cdc.gov/act-early/milestones/15-months.html>.
3. Zubler JM, et al. "Evidence-Informed Milestones for Developmental Surveillance Tools." *Pediatrics*, 2022. <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9680195/>.
4. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "When Does Teething Start?" Last updated 26 June 2024. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/teething-tooth-care/Pages/Teething-4-to-7-Months.aspx>.
5. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "American Academy of Pediatrics: Universal Screening Urged for Developmental Delays." Published 16 December 2019. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/news/Pages/Identifying-Developmental-Disorders-Through-Surveillance-and-Screening.aspx>.
6. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "What should I do if I am worried about my child's development?" Last updated 29 March 2019. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/tips-tools/ask-the-pediatrician/Pages/What-should-I-do-if-I-am-worried-about-my-childs-development.aspx>.
7. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Corrected Age For Preemies." Last updated 10 December 2018. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/preemie/Pages/Corrected-Age-For-Preemies.aspx>.

title: 4 Month Milestones: What Most Babies Do | Yorix
heading: 4 Month Milestones: What Most Babies Can Do and When to Talk to Your Doctor
description: 4 month milestones based on CDC's 2022 checklist: social, language, thinking, and movement skills most babies show by 4 months, play ideas, and when to ask.
body:
# 4 Month Milestones: What Most Babies Can Do and When to Talk to Your Doctor

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's development, hearing, vision, or feeding, contact your pediatrician.*

Around four months, many babies "wake up" socially: they hold your gaze longer, coo back at you, and start to giggle. This page lists the skills that most babies show by this age, explains where that list comes from and why it may differ from what you read elsewhere, and suggests simple everyday play. Looking for naps and bedtime instead? See our [4 month old sleep schedule](/4-month-old-sleep-schedule).

## Short answer

By 4 months, most babies **smile to get your attention, chuckle, coo ("ooo", "aah"), turn toward your voice, hold their head steady while held, bring their hands to the mouth, swing at toys, and prop up on their forearms during tummy time.** This list follows the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) checklist revised with the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) in 2022, which includes skills that **at least 75% of babies** have by this age. So if your baby is missing one, it is worth raising with your pediatrician rather than waiting. Rolling over is **not** on the 4-month list; CDC places rolling from tummy to back at 6 months.

### Key facts at a glance

| Question | Answer | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Whose checklist? | CDC "Learn the Signs. Act Early.", revised 2022 with an AAP expert group | CDC; Zubler et al., 2022 |
| What "milestone" means here | A skill 75% or more of babies have by this age | CDC; Zubler et al., 2022 |
| Number of 4-month milestones | 13 across four areas | CDC |
| Rolling over | Listed at 6 months (tummy to back), not 4 months | CDC |
| Born early? | Use corrected age until age 2 | AAP (HealthyChildren.org) |
| Next formal screening | Standardized developmental screening at the 9-month visit (also 18 and 30 months) | AAP |

## Why this list may look different from older lists

Before 2022, many milestone lists, including CDC's own, used ages at which about half of babies had a skill. The revision, described by Zubler and colleagues in *Pediatrics* (2022), moved to the **75th percentile**: a skill appears on the checklist at the age by which three out of four babies are expected to have it. The authors explain why: a 50% list sends too many healthy babies into "is something wrong?" territory, while also encouraging a wait-and-see habit. The total number of milestones shrank by about a quarter, roughly 4 in 10 of the final milestones were new, and a third of the milestones that were kept moved to a different age, most often an **older** one.

What this means for you: many babies do these things earlier than 4 months. A baby who does them by 4 months is on track. A baby who doesn't yet do one of them isn't necessarily delayed, but it is exactly the situation in which CDC and AAP want parents to speak up.

## 4 month milestones checklist (CDC, in our words)

| Area | Most babies by 4 months… |
| --- | --- |
| Social and emotional | Smile on their own to catch your attention; give a little chuckle (not yet a full laugh) when you play; look at you, wiggle, or make noises to get you to keep interacting |
| Language and communication | Coo with vowel-like sounds; answer your talking with sounds of their own; turn their head toward your voice |
| Thinking and learning | Open their mouth at the sight of breast or bottle when hungry; study their own hands with interest |
| Movement and physical | Keep their head steady without support while held; grasp a toy you place in their hand; swipe an arm at a toy; bring hands to the mouth; prop up on elbows or forearms on their tummy |

Source: CDC "Milestones by 4 Months" (updated May 2026). Nemours KidsHealth uses the same set.

## What these skills look like at home

- **The social smile becomes a tool.** At 2 months, CDC lists smiling *back* when you smile. By 4 months, babies start smiling first, to start the "conversation" themselves.
- **"Talking" back and forth.** Pause after you speak. Many 4-month-olds fill the gap with a coo, which is early turn-taking.
- **Hands are fascinating.** Long looks at their own fingers and bringing both hands to the mouth are normal and expected at this age, not a sign of hunger every time.
- **Stronger neck and upper body.** When you hold your baby upright, the head should no longer wobble much. On the floor, babies start resting on their forearms with the chest lifted. Regular [tummy time](/tummy-time) helps.
- **Batting at toys.** Babies swing at a hanging toy before they can grab it precisely. Grabbing on purpose (reaching for a toy they want) moves to the 6-month checklist.

## Skills that often come soon after 4 months

Some babies do these at 4 months and many don't; CDC places them at 6 months:

- rolling from tummy to back;
- pushing up on straight arms during tummy time;
- leaning on their hands while sitting with support;
- laughing out loud and blowing "raspberries".

The AAP's corrected-age article describes rolling from stomach to back as something that "often" appears around 4 months in term babies. That is not a contradiction: it describes a typical age, while CDC lists the age by which most babies (75%) do it.

## Play ideas for a 4 month old

These ideas are based on CDC's tips for this age:

1. **Answer every sound.** Smile, sound excited, and copy your baby's coos so they learn turn-taking.
2. **Floor time every day** on a blanket or mat, with a few safe toys within kicking and swiping distance.
3. **Mouthing is learning.** Let your baby explore safe objects with their mouth, as long as nothing is sharp, hot, or small enough to choke on.
4. **Track a toy.** With your baby on their back, move a bright toy slowly side to side and up and down.
5. **Read, sing, talk** about what you're doing during diaper changes and walks.
6. **Limit time in seats.** CDC suggests not keeping babies in swings, strollers, or bouncy seats for long stretches.
7. **No screens** except video calls with family; CDC does not recommend screen time under 2 years.

CDC also reminds parents that at this age babies need **only breast milk or formula**, with no other foods, water, or drinks, for about the first 6 months. If you're wondering about solids, see [when to start solids](/when-to-start-solids).

## How sleep and feeding fit in

Four months is also a time of big sleep changes for many families. That is a separate topic, covered in detail in our [4 month old sleep schedule](/4-month-old-sleep-schedule) and [4 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/4-months) pages. One link between the two: new motor skills such as rolling can temporarily disrupt sleep, and once a baby shows signs of starting to roll, swaddling needs to stop (see the safe-sleep notes on the schedule page).

## Babies born early: use corrected age

If your baby was born before 37 weeks, compare their skills with their **corrected age**, not their birthday. The AAP explains: take your baby's age in weeks and subtract how many weeks early they were born. Example: a baby born 8 weeks early who is now 16 weeks old has a corrected age of about 2 months, so the 2-month checklist is the fairer comparison. The AAP suggests using corrected age for the first 2 years.

## When to talk to your pediatrician

CDC's message is simple: **don't wait**. Contact your pediatrician and ask about developmental screening if:

- your baby isn't doing one or more of the skills above by 4 months (corrected age if born early);
- your baby has **lost** a skill they used to have;
- your baby doesn't react to loud sounds or doesn't seem to watch you as you move (both are already on CDC's 2-month list);
- your baby seems very floppy or very stiff, or uses one side of the body much more than the other;
- you simply have a gut feeling that something is off. The AAP notes that parents' concerns are often right.

If you and your doctor are still concerned, CDC suggests asking for a referral to a specialist and contacting your state's early intervention program (find it at cdc.gov/FindEI). In the U.S., an evaluation through early intervention is free for children under 3.

*Note: "very floppy or very stiff" is not a milestone. The 2022 review mentions "stiff or tight muscles" as an older CDC warning sign that is better picked up during a doctor's examination, so we list it as a reason to call, not as something to check off.*

## Frequently asked questions

**What should a 4 month old be doing?**  
Most babies this age smile to get attention, chuckle, coo, turn toward voices, hold their head steady when held, swing at toys, bring hands to the mouth, and push up on forearms on their tummy.

**Is it normal if my 4 month old isn't rolling over?**  
Yes. CDC lists rolling from tummy to back as a 6-month milestone. Keep up floor play and mention it at the 6-month visit if it hasn't happened.

**My baby doesn't laugh yet at 4 months. Should I worry?**  
A chuckle is on the 4-month list; a full laugh is on the 6-month list. If there's no chuckle or social smiling at all by 4 months, talk to your pediatrician.

**Should a 4 month old be sitting up?**  
Not independently. Sitting without support is on CDC's 9-month checklist.

**Do I use actual or corrected age for a premature baby?**  
Corrected age, for the first 2 years, according to the AAP.

## Keep notes for the next checkup (Yorix)

**Yorix** lets you add notes to your baby's day, so a first chuckle, a new sound, or a worry you want to mention is saved next to sleep and feeding data when you see your pediatrician. It is a support for parents, not a medical device and not a developmental screening tool.

## Related reading

- [4 month old sleep schedule](/4-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [4 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/4-months)
- [Tummy time by age](/tummy-time)
- [6 month milestones](/6-month-milestones)
- [Wake windows by age](/wake-windows-by-age)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026. App pages are used only as labeled examples.

1. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "Milestones by 4 Months." Updated 16 May 2026. <https://www.cdc.gov/act-early/milestones/4-months.html>.
2. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "Milestones by 2 Months." Updated 16 May 2026. <https://www.cdc.gov/act-early/milestones/2-months.html>.
3. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "Milestones by 6 Months." Updated 16 May 2026. <https://www.cdc.gov/act-early/milestones/6-months.html>.
4. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "About Learn the Signs. Act Early." Updated 16 February 2026. <https://www.cdc.gov/act-early/about/index.html>.
5. Zubler JM, et al. "Evidence-Informed Milestones for Developmental Surveillance Tools." *Pediatrics*, 2022. <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9680195/>.
6. Nemours KidsHealth. "Your Child's Development: 4 Months." Reviewed April 2022. <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/development-4mos.html>.
7. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Corrected Age For Preemies." Last updated 10 December 2018. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/preemie/Pages/Corrected-Age-For-Preemies.aspx>.
8. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "American Academy of Pediatrics: Universal Screening Urged for Developmental Delays." Published 16 December 2019. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/news/Pages/Identifying-Developmental-Disorders-Through-Surveillance-and-Screening.aspx>.
9. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "What should I do if I am worried about my child's development?" Last updated 29 March 2019. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/tips-tools/ask-the-pediatrician/Pages/What-should-I-do-if-I-am-worried-about-my-childs-development.aspx>.
10. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "Milestones by 9 Months." Updated 16 May 2026. <https://www.cdc.gov/act-early/milestones/9-months.html>.

heading: 6 Month Milestones: What Most Babies Do by Half a Year
description: 6 month milestones from CDC's 2022 checklist: rolling, pushing up, laughing, babbling, and reaching. What changes after 4 months, play ideas, and when to ask.
body:
# 6 Month Milestones: What Most Babies Do by Half a Year

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's development, hearing, vision, or feeding, contact your pediatrician.*

Half a year in, babies are busier and noisier: they roll, squeal, blow bubbles with their lips, grab whatever is within reach, and tell you with their whole face who they know. Below is the list of skills most babies have by 6 months, how it builds on the 4-month list, what is *not* expected yet, and when it is worth calling your pediatrician. For naps and bedtimes at this age, go to our [6 month old sleep schedule](/6-month-old-sleep-schedule).

## Short answer

By 6 months, most babies **recognize familiar people, enjoy their reflection, laugh, "talk" back and forth with you, blow raspberries, squeal, mouth objects, reach for a toy they want, close their lips when they've had enough food, roll from tummy to back, push up on straight arms, and lean on their hands while sitting with support.** That's the 2022 CDC checklist for this age, built so that **at least three out of four babies** can do each item. Sitting without support, crawling, and first words are **not** expected at 6 months.

### Key facts at a glance

| Question | Answer | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Checklist used | CDC "Learn the Signs. Act Early." (revised 2022 with the AAP) | CDC |
| Threshold | Skills 75% or more of babies have by 6 months | CDC; Zubler et al., 2022 |
| Number of 6-month milestones | 12, in four areas | CDC |
| Sitting without support | 9-month checklist | CDC |
| Crawling | Not on CDC's checklists up to 1 year; most crawl around 7–10 months | CDC; Cleveland Clinic |
| Food | Breast milk or formula is still the main source of nutrition | CDC |

## 6 month milestones checklist (CDC, in our words)

| Area | Most babies by 6 months… |
| --- | --- |
| Social and emotional | Recognize the people they see every day; like looking at themselves in a mirror; laugh |
| Language and communication | Trade sounds with you in turns; stick out the tongue and blow "raspberries"; make high squealing noises |
| Thinking and learning | Explore objects by putting them in the mouth; reach out to grab a toy they want; press their lips shut to show they don't want more food |
| Movement and physical | Roll from front to back; push the chest up on straight arms during tummy time; prop themselves on their hands when sitting with support |

Source: CDC "Milestones by 6 Months" (updated May 2026); the same set appears on Nemours KidsHealth.

## What's new compared with 4 months

The two checklists show how skills build on each other:

| Skill | By 4 months | By 6 months |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Laughing | Small chuckle when you play | Real laugh |
| Sounds | Coos and answers your voice | Takes turns, squeals, blows raspberries |
| Hands | Swipes at toys, holds a toy put in the hand | Reaches on purpose for a toy they want |
| Tummy | Props on forearms | Pushes up on straight arms |
| Body | Steady head when held | Rolls tummy to back; leans on hands when supported in sitting |
| Eating cues | Opens mouth for breast or bottle | Closes lips to say "no more" |

That last row matters if you're starting solids: a baby who presses their lips together or turns away is telling you they're done. CDC lists pushing food away, closing the mouth, and turning the head as signs of fullness, and pointing, opening the mouth for a spoon, and excitement at the sight of food as signs of hunger.

## Common questions at this age

**"My baby isn't sitting up on their own."** That's expected. CDC moved independent sitting to the 9-month checklist. At 6 months, sitting *with support* while leaning on the hands is the milestone.

**"My baby rolls only one way."** CDC lists rolling from tummy to back at 6 months. Rolling from back to tummy often comes around the same time or later; keep offering floor time on both front and back.

**"Everything goes in the mouth."** CDC counts mouthing as a thinking skill at 6 months: it's how babies learn about texture and shape. Keep small objects, coins, button batteries, and anything that fits through a toilet-paper tube out of reach *(the tube test is a common practical rule, not from CDC)*.

**"Is a first tooth a milestone?"** Teeth aren't on CDC's checklists. The AAP says most babies start teething between about 4 and 7 months, but later is common and usually normal. See our [teething symptoms](/teething-symptoms) guide.

**"Should my baby be eating solids?"** CDC suggests talking to your pediatrician about when to start; breast milk or formula remain the most important food. Read [when to start solids](/when-to-start-solids) for readiness signs.

## Play ideas for a 6 month old

Adapted from CDC's suggestions for this age:

- **Copy and reply.** When your baby smiles or makes a sound, answer the same way, then pause and let them have a turn.
- **Name the world.** On walks, point to dogs, trees, and buses and say what they are.
- **Toys just out of reach.** Put a toy a little beyond your baby's hands while they're on their tummy or back to tempt a roll.
- **Supported sitting practice.** Hold your baby sitting up and put toys in front of them so they practice balance.
- **Supported standing.** Hold your baby firmly under the arms and let them take weight on their feet for a moment while you look around together.
- **The drop game.** When a toy hits the floor, hand it back. It teaches cause and effect.
- **New sounds.** Whisper, clap, and make silly noises; notice which ones your baby turns to.
- **Calming skills.** When your baby is upset, help them settle with a soft voice, rocking, a song, or a pacifier.

CDC still advises no screen time before age 2 apart from video chats with family.

## Sleep at 6 months: where to read more

New motor skills and growing curiosity can make naps and bedtimes harder for a while. We cover sleep separately so that this page can stay focused on development: see the [6 month old sleep schedule](/6-month-old-sleep-schedule) and, if nights have suddenly changed, the [6 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/6-months) page.

## Premature babies

For a baby born early, compare skills with the checklist for their **corrected age** for the first 2 years, as the AAP recommends. For example, a 6-month-old born 2 months early is usually compared with the 4-month list.

## When to call your pediatrician

Talk to your baby's doctor and ask about developmental screening if:

- by 6 months (corrected age) your baby isn't doing one or more of the items on the checklist;
- your baby **loses** a skill they had, such as no longer babbling or no longer reaching;
- your baby doesn't respond to sounds or doesn't seem to see well;
- one side of the body moves much more than the other, or your baby feels very stiff or very floppy *(clinical warning signs, not CDC milestones)*;
- you're simply worried. CDC's advice is "don't wait".

You can also contact your state's early intervention program yourself; in the U.S., children under 3 can get a free evaluation (HealthyChildren.org). The AAP recommends formal developmental screening at the 9-month visit for every baby, but you don't have to wait for it if you have concerns.

## Frequently asked questions

**What should a 6 month old be doing?**  
Most 6-month-olds laugh, squeal, blow raspberries, take turns making sounds, recognize familiar people, reach for toys, roll from tummy to back, push up on straight arms, and lean on their hands when sitting with support.

**Should my 6 month old be sitting up alone?**  
No. Sitting without support is on CDC's 9-month checklist.

**Should a 6 month old crawl?**  
Not yet for most babies. Cleveland Clinic says most crawl between about 7 and 10 months; some start by rolling, belly-crawling, or scooting on their bottom first.

**Should a 6 month old say "mama"?**  
Not as a real word. Repeated syllables like "mamama" appear on the 9-month list; calling a parent "mama" or "dada" appears at 1 year.

**My 6 month old doesn't laugh. Is that a problem?**  
Laughing is on the 6-month checklist, so mention it to your pediatrician.

## Note the "firsts" next to sleep and feeds (Yorix)

**Yorix** lets you add notes to any day, so the first roll or the first laugh is saved next to naps and feeds. That's handy when your pediatrician asks "when did that start?". It is a support for parents, not a medical device and not a developmental screening tool.

## Related reading

- [6 month old sleep schedule](/6-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [6 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/6-months)
- [4 month milestones](/4-month-milestones)
- [9 month milestones](/9-month-milestones)
- [When to start solids](/when-to-start-solids)
- [Tummy time by age](/tummy-time)

4. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "Milestones by 1 Year." Updated 16 May 2026. <https://www.cdc.gov/act-early/milestones/1-year.html>.
5. Zubler JM, et al. "Evidence-Informed Milestones for Developmental Surveillance Tools." *Pediatrics*, 2022. <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9680195/>.

8. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Corrected Age For Preemies." Last updated 10 December 2018. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/preemie/Pages/Corrected-Age-For-Preemies.aspx>.

title: 9 Month Milestones: Sitting, Babbling & Shyness | Yorix
heading: 9 Month Milestones: Development Checklist for a 9 Month Old
description: 9 month milestones from CDC's 2022 checklist: sitting alone, babbling, raking food, stranger shyness, object permanence. Plus crawling facts and when to ask.
body:
# 9 Month Milestones: Development Checklist for a 9 Month Old

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. If you are worried about your baby's development, hearing, vision, or feeding, contact your pediatrician.*

Nine months is when many babies discover that the world keeps existing when they can't see it. A dropped spoon is searched for, a parent who walks out is protested, and a stranger may be met with a suspicious stare. This guide lists the skills most babies show by 9 months, explains the one milestone that surprises parents most (crawling isn't on the list), and covers the developmental screening your pediatrician will do at this visit. For naps, bedtimes, and dropping the third nap, see our [9 month old sleep schedule](/9-month-old-sleep-schedule).

## Short answer

By 9 months, most babies **are wary of strangers, show a range of facial expressions, look up when you call their name, react when you leave, enjoy peek-a-boo, babble strings like "mamama" and "bababa", raise their arms to be picked up, look for things that drop out of sight, bang two objects together, get into a sitting position alone, sit without support, pass toys from hand to hand, and "rake" food toward themselves with their fingers.** These come from CDC's 2022 checklist, which only includes skills that **75% or more** of babies have by this age. **Crawling is not on it.** The AAP recommends a standardized developmental screening for every baby at the **9-month** checkup.

### Key facts at a glance

| Question | Answer | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Checklist | CDC "Learn the Signs. Act Early." 9-month list (2022 revision) | CDC |
| Number of milestones | 13, in four areas | CDC |
| Threshold | 75% or more of babies by 9 months | CDC; Zubler et al., 2022 |
| Crawling | Not a CDC milestone; most babies crawl at about 7–10 months | CDC; Cleveland Clinic |
| Developmental screening | Recommended for all babies at 9, 18, and 30 months | AAP |
| Stranger and separation anxiety | Normal at this age; separation anxiety tends to build between 8 months and 1 year | CDC; KidsHealth |

## 9 month milestones checklist (CDC, in our words)

| Area | Most babies by 9 months… |
| --- | --- |
| Social and emotional | Act shy, clingy, or afraid around unfamiliar people; show different faces (happy, sad, angry, surprised); turn when you say their name; react (look, reach, or cry) when you leave; smile or laugh at peek-a-boo |
| Language and communication | Make lots of different repeated sounds such as "mamama" and "bababa"; lift their arms to ask to be picked up |
| Thinking and learning | Search for an object that falls out of view; bang two things together |
| Movement and physical | Sit up from lying down without help; sit steadily without support; pass an object from one hand to the other; use fingers to drag food closer |

Source: CDC "Milestones by 9 Months" (updated May 2026); Nemours KidsHealth shows the same list.

## Why crawling isn't on the checklist

Parents often expect crawling to be *the* 9-month milestone, but CDC's checklists up to 1 year don't include it. CDC's milestone pages don't explain this omission. A likely reason is that the 2022 revision kept only skills that at least three in four babies reliably show by a given visit, and crawling varies a lot *(our interpretation)*. Cleveland Clinic says most babies crawl between 7 and 10 months, that one baby may start at 7 months and another closer to 11, and that both are fine. Babies also get around in different ways first: rolling across the room, belly ("commando") crawling, bottom scooting, or bear crawling on hands and feet.

What matters more at 9 months is that your baby is **moving with purpose and using both sides of the body**: sitting steadily, getting into sitting alone, reaching and transferring toys. If your baby isn't moving across the floor in any way and you're worried, mention it.

## Stranger shyness and "where did you go?"

The social part of the 9-month list can look like a step backward: a baby who happily went to anyone at 5 months may now cling and cry. It's the opposite of a problem. KidsHealth explains that between 4 and 7 months babies develop **object permanence**, the understanding that people and things still exist out of sight, and that between 8 months and 1 year many become more upset about being separated from a parent.

What helps (CDC and KidsHealth):

- Say a quick, cheerful goodbye instead of slipping out, so your baby learns what to expect, and greet them when you come back.
- Give new caregivers time; let your baby warm up while you're still in the room.
- Stay close as your baby explores, so they can check you're there.
- Play hiding games (a toy under a cloth, peek-a-boo) that practice "gone and back".

Clinginess often spills into bedtime; our [9 month old sleep schedule](/9-month-old-sleep-schedule) page covers that side.

## Hands, food, and the road to self-feeding

Raking food toward the body with the fingers is on the 9-month list. The neat thumb-and-pointer-finger pinch for small bits of food comes later, on the 1-year list. CDC suggests letting your baby practice feeding themselves with their fingers and drinking from a cup with a small amount of water, sitting with them at meals, and offering foods that are smooth, mashed, or finely chopped. Learn which foods are choking risks before offering finger foods; our [baby-led weaning](/baby-led-weaning) guide lists them.

## The 9-month checkup

The AAP asks pediatricians to check development at every well visit and to use a **standardized screening questionnaire at 9, 18, and 30 months**, with autism-specific screening at 18 and 24 months. If you've filled in CDC's checklist (in the free Milestone Tracker app or on paper), bring it along. The AAP also suggests using the checklist for the younger age if your child is between two checklist ages.

## Play ideas for a 9 month old

Based on CDC's tips for this age:

1. **Turn sounds into words.** When your baby says "bababa", repeat it, then add a word: "ba-ba... ball!"
2. **Toys a little out of reach** on the floor to encourage crawling, scooting, or rolling, and cheer when they get there.
3. **Wave "bye-bye"** every time you leave, and try simple signs for "more" or "all done".
4. **Fill and dump.** Put blocks in a container, tip them out, and fill it again together.
5. **My turn, your turn.** Pass a toy back and forth.
6. **Find it.** Hide a toy under a blanket while your baby watches.
7. **Say what you want to see:** "time to sit" instead of "don't stand".
8. **Baby-proof** as your baby gets mobile: sharp and breakable things out of reach, medicines and cleaners locked away, and the Poison Help number (800-222-1222 in the U.S.) saved in your phone.

## Premature babies

Use **corrected age** for the first 2 years. A 9-month-old who was born 2 months early is usually compared with the 6-month list (AAP).

## When to talk to your pediatrician

Don't wait for the next visit if:

- by 9 months (corrected age), your baby isn't doing one or more items on the checklist, especially **sitting without support**, **babbling with consonants**, or **responding to their name**;
- your baby has lost skills they used to have;
- your baby doesn't react to sounds or doesn't seem to see well;
- your baby uses one hand or one side of the body much more than the other, or seems unusually stiff or floppy *(clinical warning signs, not CDC milestones)*;
- you have any other concern; the AAP notes parents' concerns are often right.

In the U.S. you can also call your state's early intervention program for a free evaluation for children under 3 (HealthyChildren.org; find the number at cdc.gov/FindEI).

## Frequently asked questions

**What should a 9 month old be doing?**  
Most can sit alone and get into sitting by themselves, pass toys between hands, rake food with their fingers, babble "mamama" or "bababa", look when called by name, enjoy peek-a-boo, and look for dropped toys.

**My 9 month old isn't crawling. Should I worry?**  
Not by itself. Crawling isn't on CDC's checklist, and Cleveland Clinic notes that most babies crawl between 7 and 10 months, with some starting closer to 11. Talk to your pediatrician if your baby isn't sitting alone or isn't moving around in any way.

**Should a 9 month old be pulling up to stand?**  
Many do, but pulling up to stand is on CDC's 1-year checklist, not the 9-month one.

**Is stranger anxiety normal at 9 months?**  
Yes. Being shy, clingy, or fearful around strangers is one of CDC's 9-month milestones.

**Should a 9 month old say words?**  
Not necessarily. Babbling repeated syllables is expected; calling a parent "mama" or "dada" is on the 1-year list.

## Keep a record for the 9-month screening (Yorix)

**Yorix** lets you jot notes next to naps and feeds, so you can bring the dates of a first sit, first babble, or anything that worries you to the 9-month checkup. It is a support for parents, not a medical device and not a developmental screening tool.

## Related reading

- [9 month old sleep schedule](/9-month-old-sleep-schedule)
- [8 month sleep regression](/sleep-regression/8-months)
- [6 month milestones](/6-month-milestones)
- [12 month milestones](/12-month-milestones)
- [Baby-led weaning](/baby-led-weaning)

## Sources

All pages below were opened and checked on 15 November 2026. App pages are used only as labeled examples.

1. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "Milestones by 9 Months." Updated 16 May 2026. <https://www.cdc.gov/act-early/milestones/9-months.html>.
2. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "Milestones by 1 Year." Updated 16 May 2026. <https://www.cdc.gov/act-early/milestones/1-year.html>.
3. Zubler JM, et al. "Evidence-Informed Milestones for Developmental Surveillance Tools." *Pediatrics*, 2022. <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9680195/>.
4. Nemours KidsHealth. "Your Child's Development: 9 Months." Reviewed April 2022. <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/development-9mos.html>.
5. Nemours KidsHealth. "Separation Anxiety." <https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/sep-anxiety.html>.
6. Cleveland Clinic. "When Do Babies Start To Crawl?" 6 February 2026. <https://health.clevelandclinic.org/when-do-babies-crawl>.
7. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "American Academy of Pediatrics: Universal Screening Urged for Developmental Delays." Published 16 December 2019. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/news/Pages/Identifying-Developmental-Disorders-Through-Surveillance-and-Screening.aspx>.
8. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "What should I do if I am worried about my child's development?" Last updated 29 March 2019. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/tips-tools/ask-the-pediatrician/Pages/What-should-I-do-if-I-am-worried-about-my-childs-development.aspx>.
9. HealthyChildren.org (AAP). "Corrected Age For Preemies." Last updated 10 December 2018. <https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/preemie/Pages/Corrected-Age-For-Preemies.aspx>.

title: Baby-Led Weaning: First Foods, Safety & How to Start | Yorix
heading: Baby-Led Weaning (BLW): First Foods, Safety, and How to Start
description: Baby-led weaning (BLW): when to start, first finger foods and how to cut them, gagging vs choking, iron and allergens, and what research says about safety.
body:
# Baby-Led Weaning (BLW): First Foods, Safety, and How to Start

**By the Yorix team**  
**Published:** November 15, 2026 · **Updated:** November 15, 2026

*This article is for general information and is not medical advice. It is not a substitute for care from your baby's pediatrician or another qualified clinician. Talk to your pediatrician before starting baby-led weaning, especially if your baby was born early, has trouble sitting, chewing, or swallowing, has severe eczema, or has a known allergy.*

Baby-led weaning means skipping (or mostly skipping) the spoon and letting your baby feed themselves soft pieces of real food from the first meal. Fans love the shared family meals and the mess-is-learning attitude; worried parents mostly ask one question: "Won't my baby choke?" This page explains how BLW works, when your baby is ready, which first foods to offer and **how to shape them**, how to tell normal gagging from choking, and how to make sure iron and allergens aren't missed. For general timing and purees, see [when to start solids](/when-to-start-solids).

## Short answer

**Baby-led weaning** is a way of starting solids in which your baby **picks up and eats soft finger foods themselves**, usually from **about 6 months**, once they can sit upright with little support, reach for food and bring it to the mouth, and no longer push everything out with the tongue. Offer **soft foods that squash between your fingers**, cut into **finger-length strips** (about the size of a small baby carrot), never round coins or hard chunks. Include **iron-rich foods** (meat, fish, eggs, beans, iron-fortified cereal) and **common allergens** early. A 2016 randomized trial of a modified BLW approach found **no more choking** than with spoon-feeding when parents were taught which foods to avoid. Always seat your baby upright in a high chair and stay with them for every bite.

### Key facts at a glance

| Question | Answer | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When to start | About 6 months (corrected age if born early) | AAP; Cleveland Clinic |
| Readiness signs | Sits upright with little or no support, reaches for and mouths objects, tongue-thrust reflex fading | Cleveland Clinic; CDC |
| Food shape | Finger-shaped pieces, like a small baby carrot; no round coin shapes | AAP |
| Texture test | Soft enough to mash with gums or a few teeth | AAP |
| Choking risk vs spoon-feeding | No significant difference in a 206-baby trial (BLISS) | Fangupo et al., 2016 |
| Gagging | More common with BLW at 6 months, less common by 8 months | Fangupo et al., 2016 |
| Main nutrition | Breast milk or formula until the first birthday | Cleveland Clinic; AAP |

## What is baby-led weaning?

The word "weaning" here means *introducing foods*, not stopping breastfeeding. In BLW:

- your baby sits with the family and is offered **small portions of the same meal**, adapted to be safe (AAP, Cleveland Clinic);
- **your baby decides** what to pick up, how much to eat, and when to stop;
- spoon-feeding isn't banned: you can preload a spoon with oatmeal or yogurt and hand it to your baby (AAP, Cleveland Clinic).

**Possible benefits** cited by the AAP and Cleveland Clinic include independence, earlier practice with textures and flavors, better self-regulation of appetite, fine-motor practice, and shared family meals. The AAP stresses that there are **very few studies** on the health benefits, so treat them as plausible rather than proven.

**Possible downsides** the AAP lists: some babies take in too few calories, self-chosen foods can be low in **iron** and other micronutrients, and choking is a real risk if food isn't prepared safely.

## When to start BLW: readiness signs

Most babies are ready around **6 months**, not earlier (Cleveland Clinic). Look for all of these:

- sits upright in a high chair with little or no support and steady head control;
- reaches for objects and brings them to the mouth;
- the tongue-thrust reflex is fading (food isn't automatically pushed out);
- shows interest in what you're eating.

The AAP advises waiting longer if your baby was born prematurely, has trouble sitting on their own, or struggles to chew and swallow even soft food. Cleveland Clinic suggests using **corrected age** for preterm babies and talking to your pediatrician or a speech-language pathologist if you're unsure.

## BLW first foods (6 months)

Pick foods that are **soft, easy to grip, not sticky, and served at room temperature** (Cleveland Clinic). A simple test: if you can squash it between your thumb and finger, it's soft enough *(practical tip)*.

| Food group | Good first options | How to serve |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vegetables | Sweet potato, carrot, squash, broccoli | Steamed or roasted until very soft; long wedges or florets with a "handle" |
| Fruit | Ripe banana, avocado, mango, pear, kiwi | Banana in half-peel "handle" or thick strips; avocado in wedges; ripe pear or mango in long slices |
| Protein | Shredded or ground meat and fish, tofu, eggs | Shredded meat, meatballs or patties that crumble easily, omelet strips, well-cooked egg |
| Dairy | Plain whole-milk yogurt, cheese | Yogurt on a preloaded spoon; soft cheese in thin strips or grated |
| Grains | Iron-fortified infant cereal, oatmeal, well-cooked pasta, toast strips | Oatmeal on a preloaded spoon; pasta shapes that are large and soft |
| Legumes | Lentils, beans | Mashed or smashed, never whole beans (CDC) |

Sources for this table: AAP, Cleveland Clinic, CDC. Small round fruits such as grapes, berries, and cherry tomatoes must be **cut into small pieces** (CDC, Cleveland Clinic).

### How to cut BLW foods

- **Finger shapes, not coins.** Long strips your baby can hold in a fist with food sticking out of the top (AAP).
- **Round foods** (grapes, cherry tomatoes, blueberries): cut into small pieces (CDC). Round slices of hot dog or sausage are a classic choking hazard; avoid hot dogs and meat sticks altogether in the first year (AAP).
- **Hard foods**: cook until soft enough to mash with a fork (CDC).
- **Nut butters**: spread thinly on toast strips or stir into oatmeal; never a spoonful or a chunk (AAP, CDC).
- **As your baby develops a pincer grasp** (around 9–12 months; it is on CDC's 1-year checklist), you can offer smaller, bite-size soft pieces. The AAP recommends pieces no larger than ½ inch for young children.

## Foods to avoid in baby-led weaning

From CDC, AAP, and Cleveland Clinic lists:

- whole nuts and seeds, chunks or spoonfuls of nut butter;
- popcorn, chips, pretzels, crackers or bread with whole seeds or nut pieces;
- whole grapes, uncut berries or cherry tomatoes, whole corn kernels, raisins and other dried fruit;
- raw hard vegetables and fruit (raw carrot, celery, apple chunks);
- hot dogs, sausages, meat sticks, tough or large chunks of meat, bones in meat or fish;
- large chunks of cheese, especially string cheese;
- marshmallows, hard or gummy candy, chewing gum;
- honey before 1 year (CDC), salty foods, and added sugar;
- fish high in mercury (Cleveland Clinic);
- cow's milk or juice as drinks before 12 months (Cleveland Clinic).

## Gagging vs choking

Knowing the difference is the single most useful thing you can learn before starting.

| | Gagging | Choking |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A protective reflex that pushes food forward | The airway is blocked |
| Sounds | Loud: coughing, retching, sputtering | Little or no sound; can't cry or cough effectively |
| Face | Red, watery eyes, tongue thrust forward | May turn bluish |
| What to do | Stay calm, keep your baby upright, let them work it out | Act immediately: infant first aid and call emergency services |

The choking signs come from the AAP: can't breathe, gasping or wheezing, can't talk, cry, or make noise, bluish color, panicked movements, going limp. In the BLISS trial, gagging was common in the early weeks and **fell faster** in BLW babies than in spoon-fed babies by 8 months. Huckleberry (app example) describes gagging as "loud and protective" and choking as quiet.

**Before you start:** the AAP recommends taking an infant **CPR and first-aid class** (American Red Cross or American Heart Association), so you know what to do if your baby chokes.

## Is baby-led weaning safe?

The best evidence is the **BLISS randomized trial** in New Zealand (Fangupo et al., *Pediatrics*, 2016): 206 healthy babies were assigned either to usual feeding or to a modified BLW approach in which parents got extra support and advice designed to reduce choking risk.

- About **35% of all babies choked at least once** between 6 and 8 months, and there was **no significant difference** between the BLW and spoon-fed groups.
- **Worrying finding:** at 7 and 12 months, **52% and 94%** of babies in both groups were offered at least one food that posed a choking risk during a 3-day record.

The takeaway: BLW done *with* safety guidance doesn't appear riskier than spoon-feeding, but **parents in both groups often offer unsafe foods**. The AAP also notes that some studies suggest BLW doesn't raise choking risk, while stressing that choking is a leading cause of accidental death in infants. Safety comes from the food shape and supervision, not from the method's name.

## Iron, calories, and allergens in BLW

- **Iron:** around 6 months, babies (especially breastfed ones) need iron from food (CDC). Offer an iron-rich food at most meals: soft meat, fish, egg, beans or lentils, or iron-fortified cereal on a preloaded spoon (AAP, CDC).
- **Calories:** babies who choose mostly fruit may not get enough energy (AAP). Keep offering breast milk or formula between or alongside meals.
- **Allergens:** the AAP says most babies should have small portions of peanut, dairy, and egg around 6 months, and you may need to "flex" BLW rules to make sure your baby actually eats them, for example thinned peanut butter on a preloaded spoon. See [introducing allergens](/introducing-allergens).

## BLW vs purees: do you have to choose?

No. The AAP says you can adapt the baby-led idea to your family; purees are nutritious too, more portable for travel, and a few days or weeks of spoon-feeding won't stop your baby from learning to feed themselves. Many families do a **mixed approach**: finger foods at family meals plus preloaded spoons of yogurt, oatmeal, or mashed lentils.

| | Baby-led weaning | Spoon-feeding purees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who controls the amount | Baby | Shared; follow baby's cues |
| Textures early on | Varied from day one | Smooth first, then lumpier |
| Mess | A lot | Less |
| Watch-outs | Iron, calories, safe shapes | Moving on to lumps and finger foods in time |

## A first week of BLW (example only)

**Example only.** Your baby may eat almost nothing at first, and that's normal while milk is the main food.

| Day | Offer at one meal a day |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Steamed sweet potato wedge |
| 2 | Avocado strip |
| 3 | Soft shredded chicken or a soft meatball |
| 4 | Ripe banana with a peel "handle" |
| 5 | Omelet strip (egg allergen) |
| 6 | Steamed broccoli floret |
| 7 | Toast strip with a thin layer of smooth peanut butter (if no allergy risk factors) |

## When to talk to your pediatrician

- **Before starting**, especially if your baby was premature, has trouble sitting or swallowing, or has severe eczema or a food allergy (AAP).
- If your baby gags on every food after several weeks, coughs or chokes often, or seems to have trouble swallowing.
- If your baby isn't gaining weight well or eats very little after a few months of solids.
- **Call emergency services** if your baby shows choking signs that don't clear, or swelling of the face, trouble breathing, or repeated vomiting after a new food.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is baby-led weaning?**  
A way of starting solids in which babies feed themselves soft, finger-shaped pieces of family food instead of being spoon-fed purees.

**When can I start BLW?**  
At about 6 months, when your baby sits upright with little support, reaches for food, and no longer pushes everything out with the tongue.

**What are the best BLW first foods?**  
Soft, finger-shaped foods such as steamed sweet potato, avocado, banana, omelet strips, and soft shredded meat, plus iron-rich options.

**Is baby-led weaning safe?**  
In a randomized trial, BLW with safety guidance didn't lead to more choking than spoon-feeding. Safe food shapes and constant supervision matter most.

**Is gagging normal in BLW?**  
Yes. Gagging is a loud, protective reflex and usually decreases within a couple of months. Silent struggling, a bluish color, or no sound means choking.

**Can I combine BLW and purees?**  
Yes. The AAP supports adapting the approach; many families use both.

## Track new foods and reactions (Yorix)

**Yorix** lets you note each new food next to milk feeds, naps, and nights, so you can see what your baby tried, how it went, and whether a new allergen came before a reaction. It is a support for parents, not a medical device and not a diagnosis.
